News.title: The convicted £33m tax fraudster evading justice and living it up in Dubai
News.content:
In the early part of the millennium, Arif Patel appeared to be a businessman very much on the up.

His company, Faisaltex, headquartered in his home city of Preston, was known for manufacturing textiles, such as socks and nighties, which it supplied to retailers.

Patel was a fixture in the Sunday Times Rich List with his wealth in 2006 estimated to be Â£105m. He was also investing heavily in property across the city and beyond.

In 2007, his teenage son bought a minority stake in Preston North End Football Club. There was even a plan to build a Â£100m, 19-storey tower block - complete with botanical gardens and restaurant - in the centre of the city.

Behind the facade, though, something very different was going on.

In the early 2000s, organised crime groups had turned to large-scale attacks on the tax system through what became known as carousel fraud.

Chains of fake business transactions are created as a way of stealing VAT repayments from HMRC.

Goods move between different companies, into and out of the country, to generate false tax refunds.

The same shipments of goods are often moved around repeatedly, hence the name carousel fraud.

This type of fraud was costing taxpayers billions of pounds a year and experts like Stone were at the vanguard of the fightback.

This is how Patel's textiles empire appeared on his radar.

"When we started to look at them we did notice some very strange shipments of goods - a container load of hats to Switzerland seemed odd because they were actually Swiss hats," he said.

News.title: GP says she was forced out of job after raising concerns about gender treatment
News.content:
Although Doyle at first denied to the tribunal he knew Hall before this, it emerged during the tribunal that he had previously had a number of mentoring meetings with the GP.

The GMC investigation was not taken forward. However, the NHS launched an investigation into Redvers, bringing in an external investigator.

The tribunal heard she was called to what she described as a "brutal" four-hour interrogation.

"It was oppressive, very upsetting. I didn't feel I had the chance at all to explain what had happened," she said. "I broke down at one point".

She said she was off sick for several months as a result and received treatment for trauma.

Other colleagues who were interviewed as part of the investigation into Redvers also complained about the process and the NHS upheld most of their complaints.

The investigation concluded the CEO and trust should apologise to Redvers.

It also warned that Redvers' treatment would have a "broader negative impact" on the willingness of staff to raise concerns.

In 2023, a year after the grievance outcome, when a trans campaigner suggested in an NHS meeting that she was transphobic, Redvers told the tribunal she felt the NHS did not do enough to support her. She felt she had no choice but to leave her job as a safeguarding GP.

"I just felt there's no way I could carry on working in this organisation," she told the BBC.

At about that time, a group of parents, school governors and social workers began raising concerns about WellBn and Hall.

The co-founder of campaign group PSHE Brighton, Rachel Cashman, said: "It is a travesty that Sarah Redvers was punished for doing her job safeguarding and expecting the best standards of care for gender distressed children."

Redvers is now waiting for the outcome of her employment tribunal. She may not get the judgment for several months.

She described what has happened as "personally and professionally difficult" and said the NHS "needs to remember that patients come first" and it should "listen to staff who raise legitimate concerns."

In a statement NHS Surrey and Sussex said: "We engaged professionally and supportively with the Employment Tribunal. We recognise that some employment processes should have been handled differently and have apologised whilst Dr Redvers was employed with us, before, and during the hearings. We await the findings of the tribunal to make any further comment."

NHS England said: "When concerns about prescribing practices by an individual GP were escalated to NHS England national directors in 2023, they met directly with an affected family and asked regional professional standards leads to undertake formal investigations.

"Wider concerns were subsequently identified, and the WellBN practice was asked to stop providing a specialised prescribing service. Further new information led to NHS England and NHS Sussex initiating an independent patient safety investigation in 2025."

Dr Sam Hall and WellBN have been contacted for comment.

In response to the investigation report in June, WellBN said it recognised "the seriousness and sensitivity of the matters raised" and that its priority remained providing "compassionate, safe and effective care for all patients".

News.title: Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water
News.content:
The prime minister has advised people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies.

With storms battering the UK, and in the wake of online disruption caused by a major security flaw, Andy Burnham said "unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common".

The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster.

Burnham added: "It's not about panicking... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation."

At Labour's conference last month, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner joked that her emergency box, external would include a bottle of wine.

She said she'd include: "Mascara, concealer, I don't know, a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, a tin of baked beans because you've gotta have some baked beans, and I like a good tin of custard as well so I think that'll keep me going for a while."

Asked whether he agreed with her, Burnham told BBC Radio 5 Live's Matt Chorley: "Well, I'm not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you're in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you've done the hard work.

"But I'll stick to the basics I think - I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup.

"I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have, as well as Twiglets, I'm not sure I can get by for too long without those."

Last month, the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis and said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.

The chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, also told the BBC the UK is being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system".

Speaking at a wildfire resilience summit in Liverpool, Burnham denied the government had failed to properly prepare, saying: "No, we're having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we're living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.

"Obviously, weather events, and we're in a situation today where the UK is facing storms and obviously, we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now.

"It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments. So we are having that conversation about resilience."

News.title: Trump says Burnham 'getting it done' after Jackdaw decision
News.content:
Burnham announced the decision to approve the drilling of the Jackdaw gas field earlier this week.

Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.

Environmental campaigners say the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.

Based on official forecasts for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.

Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.

Trump responded to the decision on Friday, but appeared to confuse oil and gas.

He said: "They're opening up the North Sea oil. I've been after them to do that for two years."

Trump added: "Andy is getting it done, and I guess it's against the liberal principle, but he knows what's right. It's going to make UK a very wealthy country."

In a discussion on Friday, Burnham and Trump spoke about the decision to approve Jackdaw.

The two leaders "agreed on the significant benefits this will bring to the UK, boosting the economy and supporting jobs for British workers", a statement from Number 10 read.

It added that Trump and Burnham "welcomed the continued collaboration between UK and US companies, especially on nuclear power".

Earlier this week, on Wednesday, Trump said the decision was "great news for the wealth and prosperity" of the UK.

Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump urged the UK to go "full blast" and called the North Sea "one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of oil in the world".

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.

News.title: Former NBA star Malik Beasley negotiating plea deal over gambling charges
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Former NBA player Malik Beasley is negotiating a plea agreement with the Department of Justice after initially pleading not guilty to charges that he altered his play in certain games in 2024 to enrich sports bettors and ease his own debts, his attorney said Saturday.

In July, Beasley entered a not guilty plea in New York federal court. He was among the latest big names caught up in a sweeping federal gambling investigation.

Beasley's attorney, Steve Haney, told The Associated Press in a text message that they were negotiating an agreement with the government “with an expected direction in the coming days.”

Beasley, 29, and sports agent Paolo Zamorano, who has also pleaded not guilty, were among six people charged in an indictment unsealed this summer detailing a gambling scandal that has involved more than three dozen arrests.

Zamorano, 39, formerly represented another co-defendant, ex-NBA player Ed Davis, who had lent money to Beasley and is accused of acting as his “gatekeeper” in the alleged scheme.

Beasley is accused of fixing or trying to fix his performance in at least four games while playing for the Milwaukee Bucks in 2024 by under or overperforming bookmakers’ expectations. In exchange, the indictment said, the bettors bribed Beasley — and his debts to Davis were reduced or eliminated.

“Only way you can beat Vegas is sports betting,” Davis told Beasley in a Jan. 26, 2024, text message, according to the indictment. “Everything else they got the edge.”

Beasley borrowed money from Davis, a former teammate, after racking up millions of dollars in gambling losses. His widely reported financial problems include disputes with a Detroit landlord, a Milwaukee barber and a Minnesota dentist. A 2025 lawsuit from a sports marketing agency resulted in a $1 million default judgment against him.

Beasley has been out of the NBA since playing with the Detroit Pistons in 2024-25 on a one-year, $6 million contract. He averaged 16 points per game and scored 20 in his last game, a playoff loss to the New York Knicks. He is one of five players in NBA history with more than 300 three-pointers in a season. ___

AP Sports Writer Larry Lage contributed to this report from Ann Arbor, Michigan.

News.title: Airbnb’s new cleaning rules spark internet fights with hosts whining they can’t make guests wash dishes and do laundry
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Airbnb’s new cleaning rules have sparked internet fights, with hosts whining that they can’t make guests wash dishes and do laundry anymore and guests celebrating the controversial move.

“Running the dishwasher and taking the trash out isn't hard. It's the courteous thing to do,” Joe Peters, who identifies himself as a “short-term rental pro” on X, wrote.

“Airbnb hosts are so out of touch with how the world works,” one X user hit back. “Customers are increasingly avoiding the platform because they don’t want to deal with cleaning responsibilities.”

The social media feuds have sprung up in the last few days after the vacation rental site announced plans to rein in hosts after guests complained about arriving to a list of chores at their temporary home—all while hosts charge a cleaning fee.

Starting November 20, hosts can only make reasonable requests for guests. For example, guests can be asked to put dirty dishes in the sink, but they shouldn’t be asked to wash them. Hosts can also ask guests to gather used towels, but they shouldn’t be asked to strip the bed or start a load of laundry.

open image in gallery Starting November 20, Airbnb hosts can only make reasonable requests for guests when it comes to cleaning, which some hosts have criticized as uncourteous ( Getty Images )

Some Airbnb hosts are up in arms over the new changes, with one saying they thought the notice couldn’t have been real, but instead “a malicious cyberattack on the platform.”

“I cannot accept that guests who lack common decency should be within their rights to leave a place dirty,” the host who goes by Marie from Mulhouse, France, wrote on an Airbnb community forum. “So, for the time being, I have suspended my listing, signed the petition, and expressed my dissatisfaction to Airbnb.”

Another host, Stuart from Campbell River, Canada, wrote on the forum: “As hosts, we have a responsibility to protect our investments, our homes, and, in many cases, our personal living spaces.”

But Airbnb guests and real estate experts aren’t buying it.

“Too many people with zero customer service skills decided they wanted to run a single Ritz-Carlton and provide Motel 6 service,” one X user who says they’ve been in the real estate business since 2001 wrote.

Another X user said she was “vindicated” by the new rules after complaining in a December 2024 post about a cabin she had rented that she said had “like 20 things to do before check-out.”

open image in gallery One social media user called Airbnb hosts ‘so out of touch with how the world works,’ adding, ‘Customers are increasingly avoiding the platform because they don’t want to deal with cleaning responsibilities’ ( AFP via Getty Images )

There were some social media users who defended hosts, saying that cleaning rules some find excessive are things people should normally do.

“Putting the dishes in the dishwasher, taking out the trash, pulling the sheets off the bed....they are just standard things any normal person would do when staying at a house,” one person wrote on X. “Why wouldn't a host be allowed to say that?”

Another replied: “Because they’re not houseguests. They’re paying customers.

“The same way no one helps the restaurant cleanup or do dishes after dinner is over, even though that would be totally normal if you went to a friends dinner get together.”

One X user speculated that Airbnb’s new changes were because the company was losing guests over how hosts were treating them.

“I think the Airbnb hosts need to realize that Airbnb aren't changing the rules out of the goodness of their hearts,” the person wrote. “Your poor treatment of guests is making them lose money. They are losing customers because you want to have your cake and eat it too.”

open image in gallery The new changes were based on customer demand, with Airbnb saying, ‘House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we’ve heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage’ ( Getty Images )

While Airbnb reported strong earnings for the second fiscal quarter in August, with $3.6 billion in revenue, the rental site had help from their expanded services. Airbnb now offers grocery delivery, car rentals and even some boutique and independent hotel listings — slightly detouring from its original goal of being an alternative to hotels.

But most U.S. travelers still prefer a traditional hotel over short-term rentals such as Airbnb, according to an October 2025 survey by Upgraded Points, a website that helps people maximize their travel rewards.

The survey found that about 60 percent of U.S. travelers preferred hotels. When asked why Americans prefer hotels, another roughly 60 percent said it was because of no cleaning rules or fees.

Airbnb has said that the rule change was based on customer demand.

“House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we’ve heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage,” the company said in a statement.

“So we’ve redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises.”

News.title: Husband pays tribute to ‘hero’ mum who died saving two sons during Bahamas holiday
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A British mother who died while rescuing her children after they were dragged away by sea currents in the Bahamas was a "hero", her husband has said.

Leanne Gregory, 36, died after attempting to save her two sons while snorkelling in the Caribbean islands.

The Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers on the island of Bimini launched an enquiry into the sudden death of a 36-year-old British woman on Tuesday.

The force said they believed the woman was snorkelling alongside her husband and two young sons near the southern tip of the island when strong currents swept both children away.

In an effort to rescue her sons, "the woman was also swept away", police confirmed.

The children were subsequently pulled to safety.

In a GoFundMe post, Nathan Gregory wrote that his wife, from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire, was "sadly taken from us after saving my sons life in a rip tide".

He added: "She held him until he was rescued but didn’t have the energy to save herself, after a freak wave swept the boat away from her."

Mr Gregory said: "This loss is unimaginable for our family, she was our foundation, our support, she made us who we are.

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

"We were childhood sweethearts, my one and only. 22 years into our relationship at only 36-years-old.

"We had our whole lives ahead of us and it has all been taken away.

"I just have to be thankful for the hero she was in life and in death, and totally grateful for the fact my boys got out safely.

"Thankful for the people in the boat that noticed me flag it down after I struggled out the water, and got them out.

"Thankful to the lady that helped me try bring her back when the boat returned.

"Thankful for my boys for remaining strong after seeing something nobody should ever see.

"But mainly thankful to my brave, amazing wife for keeping my boy above the water even as you were sinking.

"You will be forever loved by everyone you knew and I know you will continue to watch over us."

In a statement released on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said: "According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.

"Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.

"Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.

"In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.

"She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered.

"Foul play is not suspected at this time.

"An autopsy will be conducted to assist in determining the exact cause of death."

A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office spokesperson said: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.

"We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."

News.title: Pakistan urges Afghanistan to act against militants and denies recruiting Afghan fighters
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Pakistan urged Afghanistan’s Taliban government on Saturday to take verifiable action against militants it says operate from Afghan territory, dismissing Kabul’s assertion that Islamabad was shifting blame for its own security failures.

In a separate statement on X, Pakistan’s Information Ministry rejected allegations that it was arming Afghans to fight the Taliban or recruiting them to fight anti-Pakistan insurgents. Former U.S. envoy to Afghanistan Zalmay Khalilzad had cited reports of both activities a day earlier.

The exchanges come amid heightened tensions between the two sides over militant activity, repeated border clashes and Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan, deepening a longstanding dispute over responsibility for cross-border violence.

Khalilzad on Friday wrote on X that there had been reports of Pakistan arming Afghans to fight the Taliban inside Afghanistan and of the Pakistani military recruiting Afghans to fight anti-Pakistan insurgents. He offered no evidence, and did not identify the sources of those reports.

Last month, Afghanistan said its forces killed 28 fighters and captured 32 others, including alleged members of the Islamic State group said to have crossed from neighboring Pakistan.

Pakistan frequently accuses Kabul of sheltering the Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, as well as the outlawed Baloch Liberation Army, or BLA, and al-Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent, an affiliate of the global extremist network. The TTP is separate from but closely allied with Afghanistan’s ruling Taliban.

On Friday, the Afghan Taliban government spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid said that Kabul was not responsible for insecurity in Pakistan. He accused Pakistani military and security agencies of shifting blame when they failed to maintain security at home. He said Kabul had neither an interest in destabilizing Pakistan nor the capability to foment or finance unrest in other countries.

In Islamabad, the Information Ministry on X said those assertions did not address what it described as documented security concerns. It cited attempted cross-border infiltration, the deaths of Afghan nationals and members of militant groups during Pakistani counterterrorism operations, and the recovery of foreign-origin weapons as matters requiring scrutiny.

According to the ministry, the U.S. report covering January through March 2026 estimated the strength of the Pakistani Taliban at 4,000 to 6,000 fighters.

Pakistan is currently conducting multiple operations against militants near the Afghan border.

The ministry said these security measures were aimed at targeting militant threats, not the Afghan people. It urged the Taliban government to end any tolerance, facilitation or support for militant organizations, including the TTP and the BLA, and prevent Afghan territory from being used to plan or launch attacks against Pakistan.

Militant violence has surged in Pakistan in recent years, with much of it blamed on TTP and BLA. Pakistan says many TTP leaders and BLA insurgents have found sanctuary in Afghanistan since the Taliban returned to power there in 2021, an allegation Kabul denies.

Pakistani authorities say more than 2,800 militant attacks since January have killed 3,000 people across Pakistan, mainly in the northwest and Balochistan province.

News.title: James Maddison suffers another heartbreaking injury setback for Tottenham in London derby
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

James Maddison has suffered another injury setback in a gut-wrenching blow for the Tottenham midfielder.

Maddison, who missed nearly the entirety of last season with an ACL tear, was forced off in Spurs’ London derby with Chelsea on Saturday afternoon.

He went down soon after the second half got underway at Stamford Bridge, crouching and looking to the bench before hitting the deck as his team-mates signalled team doctors onto the pitch.

Maddison walked off the pitch visibly dejected and was replaced by former Chelsea midfielder Conor Gallagher, who was booed as he entered play.

He went straight down the tunnel after being substituted, receiving a pat on the back from opposition manager Xabi Alonso.

open image in gallery James Maddison went straight down the tunnel after being replaced ( PA )

Maddison has had his entire Tottenham career plagued by fitness issues and only made his first start since May 2025 against Coventry, when the midfielder scored and starred in a 3-1 win - the club’s first of the season.

He missed 24 games in his debut campaign in north London due to an array of issues before suffering a serious knee injury last term, which ruled him out for eight months.

The 29-year-old suffered an early injury scare this season when he was forced off in the damning opening day defeat to Brentford due to a shoulder issue, though this setback wasn’t as bad as initially feared.

However, Roberto De Zerbi will now face another nervous wait to learn the extent of Maddison’s latest injury, compiling Tottenham’s woes in the medical department.

Several key players were missing for the trip to Chelsea, with Destiny Udogie missing while Tosin Adarabioyo was unable to recover in time to face his former club. Pedro Porro could only start on the bench.

But despite a growing injury crisis, De Zerbi defended Tottenham’s medical team, saying: “It’s football. I am convinced our medical staff this season is high level.

“I follow them. I believe in them. I have big confidence because I know how they are working.

“I think they are good enough to believe in them. Nothing more. We are suffering a normal situation in football.”

De Zerbi will be expected to provide an update on Maddison after full-time at Stamford Bridge.

News.title: Pollock at heart of scuffle that inspires Leicester to thumping win in feisty derby
News.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Leicester Tigers v Northampton Saints.

The Prem’s derby weekend continues today at Mattioli Woods Welford Road, where Geoff Parling’s side go head-to-head in with their East Midlands rivals.

Both Leicester and Northampton have two wins from the opening three rounds of the season and with both sides involved in a number of high-scoring encounters already in the new campaign, we could be in for a real treat.

Tigers started the season with a 38-40 loss at home to Saracens, but bounced back quickly with wins over Gloucester and Newcastle Red Bulls. They will be itching to right a few wrongs after suffering a chastening Champions Cup defeat in Pau last week.

Northampton, meanwhile, have notched up wins over Newcastle Red Bulls and Bath either side of loss to Bristol Bears.

A win today for Saints would be their first on the road since defeating Exeter Chiefs at Sandy Park in April.

“It (the East Midlands derby) means a lot to everyone, we know it will be a great atmosphere at Mattioli Woods Welford Road,” said Parling.

“I don’t think with this sort of game either team has to build it up too much emotionally because that just comes, so I think it’s actually about being really really calm in the moment.”

“Hopefully we can put the best of ourselves out there and I’m sure Saints will be able to do exactly the same.”

Saints are without a victory in Leicester since January 2023, when a single point decided the 18-19 result.

Since then, the last five meetings between the sides have been won by the hosts on the day – with Saints last taking home the bragging rights when a Tom Litchfield hat-trick helped Northampton to a 45-31 win on home soil in last season’s league play-off.

Kick-off gets underway at 3.05pm. Stay with us here for all the latest updates.

News.title: Saliba has fight on his hands to usurp ‘unbelievable’ Konsa
News.content:
Hello and welcome to coverage from the Emirates as Premier League champions Arsenal host Everton.

Mikel Arteta’s men produced a good performance in midweek to draw with Bayern Munich in the Champions League while David Moyes’s squad have had the week off following their 2-0 defeat by Chelsea last weekend.

Arteta said: “We’re having three games in six days so we know what’s happening, especially when the games are so demanding and the necessity is to win. We know that, so we prepare the players for those scenarios and do the best we possibly can.

“I know David so well and how he sets the team, the quality they have in their organisation and individually. It’s no coincidence they didn’t lose before their last game. They have a really good team, which we know because in recent clashes, it’s always been a really difficult game for us.”

Both teams enter this game having been beaten just once this season but eight points separate them with Arsenal in second and Everton in eighth.

Moyes said: “It’s not an easy game and never has been over many years. We look forward to it; they had a game in midweek, and we have to try and capitalise on that. I thought we did really well last year against them; we played really well down at Arsenal, and I hope we can do the same.

“When I look back at the team we had out, we were pretty threadbare at that time, but we did a good job, and I hope we can do it again. Obviously Arsenal have some many different tools in their bag and people they can use in different positions, so we’re fully aware of the team we’re up against and the level.”

Former Arsenal players Ainsley Maitland-Niles and Christian Norgaard could feature for Everton this afternoon.

News.title: ‘Tactical genius’ Emery outsmarts Maresca as City crash to first league defeat
News.content:
It was four years ago to the day that Emery grabbed this famous club by the shirt and collar and gave them an almighty shake. After a summer of much instability including many player sales, he appears to have already struck a formula with his newly assembled team.

There were a number of fine individual performances from many of the summer arrivals, such as Jackson, goalkeeper Zion Suzuki and Johan Manzambi.

Emery said: “We were very motivated and Manchester City is the best team in the world so this is the level. This year we started so poorly and we needed time to understand how we improve. The players showed the capacity to retrieve the level we’ve had over the last few years.

“Nicolas is more mature and very demanding of himself to improve. Earlier this season he was shooting over the crossbar but he is now finding the corners. There is still work to do and 11 points is not enough but we are feeling better.”

Villa were fierce from the start and ahead after six minutes. Guéhi’s mistake was punished by John McGinn, with the ball dropping to Jackson who crashed a shot into the roof of the net.

The home team did require Suzuki to produce saves to stop efforts from Iliman Ndiaye, Rayan Cherki and Abdukodir Khusanov as City responded. Ndiaye also struck the outside of the post and City were level seven minutes into the second half with Erling Haaland nodding in Ndiaye’s cross at the far post. Haaland had touched the ball just eight times in the opening 45 minutes but invariably only needs one chance.

News.title: England hammer France to keep Rugby League World Cup hopes alive
News.content:
With Samoa beating Papua New Guinea 64-6 earlier on Saturday, England’s task was put into stark and imposing focus. The Pacific Islanders have a points difference of plus-132. Courtesy of this mauling, England’s is plus-64. So they must see off Papua New Guinea by a big number next Friday and then pray that Tonga defeat Samoa two days later. That is their only route through.

In truth, that is as much as McDermott could hope after their initial shortcomings, as they seek to avoid missing out on the last four for the first time in the World Cup’s 72-year history.

“What we’ve done today, given the context, is just enormous,” McDermott said. “We had to win big but, as any coach will tell you, nobody thinks like that. You think, ‘we’ve got to win’.

“We had some real good, candid conversations this week about what that actually means and we’ve been able to do that without getting distracted in chasing points.”

It should be remembered that this was only McDermott’s second game in charge and, even allowing for the poor opposition, they were dramatically improved.

“We’ve been together for five field sessions only,” he said. “We’re building something here and there was a little bit of that on show today.

“Certainly the six tries we scored in the last 17 minutes or so before half-time are what we’ve been chasing. We can see how good that’s going to be.

“If this group’s together for a process or a long build-up to a tournament, we could achieve some special things but, over a short space of time, it’s been remarkable really.”

It is incredible to think that England took 22 minutes to break the deadlock, when the ever-excellent Dom Young burst through. From there, they averaged a try every four or so minutes, with France looking increasingly forlorn and fatigued.

News.title: How an aid initiative maimed thousands of children in war-torn Africa
News.content:
Tormented by pain from severe internal burns, Amza Kebbie is one of thousands of children in Sierra Leone damaged for life by an aid intervention which went horribly wrong.

It has been five days since the four-year-old boy drank caustic soda, one of the two main ingredients for making soap, after mistaking it for drinking water. The highly corrosive liquid, also known as sodium hydroxide, has stripped the lining of his oesophagus and part of his stomach, causing life changing damage.

He’s now in intensive care, clinging precariously to life. An intravenous drip provides fluids and there’s a nasal cannula that enables him to breathe. Medics and relatives look over him around the clock.

If he can gather enough strength (which the nurses say is by no means guaranteed) the dangerously sick child will undergo a gastrostomy, an operation that will see a tube directly inserted into his stomach so that he can be fed long term.

Amza drank caustic soda while being looked after by a neighbour who was making soap at home Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

He can no longer swallow properly and may never be able to do so again, say his doctors.

This is not an isolated tragedy. Across Sierra Leone, there are thousands of children like Amza, and their number is growing every year.

At the Goderich Surgical Centre in the capital Freetown, around 200 children are admitted annually with caustic soda poisoning. Many more are thought to die in remote regions where emergency medical treatment is unavailable.

Behind the calamity is a humanitarian initiative that has spectacularly backfired. It’s a prime example of the law of unintended consequences; of a seemingly sensible and undoubtedly well meaning public health intervention doing more harm than good.

Fatmata Kamara accidentally drank caustic soda at her grandmother’s house in 2014 and has had a feeding tube ever since Credit : SImon Townsley

The story starts in the aftermath of Sierra Leone’s vicious civil war, which ran between 1991 and 2002.

Fought between the government and the Revolutionary United Front – backed by Liberian warlord Charles Taylor – the war claimed an estimated 50,000 to 70,000 lives, displaced 2.5 million people and left the country brutalised and in ruins.

In its aftermath, international aid agencies and NGOs desperately sought ways to revive the country and alighted on DIY soap making as a way of killing two birds with one stone.

Siblings Aminata Fofana and Salieu Bangura help out with the family soap-making business Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Organisations including UNHCR, UNICEF and World Vision thought the practice would both improve sanitation in the country’s disease-ridden shanty towns and provide home-bound women with the means to earn a sustainable income.

It seemed like an obvious “win-win”, and schemes to help women set up in the soap making business rapidly proliferated.

An annual report by the International Federation of the Red Cross, published in May 2002, promoted a micro-finance scheme to fund small-scale soapmaking.

Saieu Bangura, 13, with a tub of soap flakes Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

In 2005, the Centre for War Affected Women in Sierra Leone’s Kono district, backed by the UNHCR, listed soap making as one of the main training courses for war widows and female amputees.

And at about the same time, the Freetown-based Safer Future Youth Development Programme, supported by UNICEF and the charity War Child, provided “a tool kit for soap production” at its training workshops.

As recently as 2020, Action Aid ran a promotional article on its Sierra Leone website showing how soap making had enabled women to become financially independent of their husbands.

The article ran under the headline: “With Soap Making Skills – I'm Empowered!”

Mabinty Bangura is taken to theatre for an endoscopy Credit : Simon Townsley

It is for good reason that the ancient Greek physician Hippocrates urged doctors “first, do no harm”.

To follow the rule literally is not possible as all health interventions entail some risk but it's a reminder never to underestimate the capacity of a new intervention to backfire.

There are plenty of examples from history to choose from.

During the British Raj in India, the government offered a cash bounty for every dead cobra as a way of reducing the danger of venomous snakes.

The surgical team examine the internal damage via an endoscopy Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But rather than leading to a decline in snake numbers, the plan resulted in entrepreneurial individuals breeding cobras just so they could kill them and then claim the reward.

Once officials realised what was happening and the scheme was stopped, thousands of the then worthless cobras were released into the wild, greatly increasing the risk of snakebite.

In the late 1950s, the Chinese Communist regime introduced an equally calamitous public health campaign involving sparrows.

They issued a directive ordering the birds to be destroyed because they were thought to spread disease and destroy crops.

A child’s gastrostomy scar with a feeding tube in place Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

What those behind the idea failed to consider was that sparrows are natural predators. As their numbers declined, the locust population exploded, decimating agriculture and contributing to the Great Chinese Famine in which millions died.

So what went wrong in Sierra Leone? What did those behind the soap making scheme fail to foresee?

Experts say the initiative simply failed to consider the danger inherent in encouraging people to use toxic chemicals in their homes.

The brightly coloured buckets in which caustic soda is made, and then mixed with oil and scent to make soap, are the same buckets used across the country to fetch and hold drinking water. And just like drinking water, the lethal solution is cool, clear and inviting.

Just a drop is enough to cause the most horrific burns. So when a thirsty young child like Amza runs in from play and mistakenly scoops up a cup of it to quench their thirst they will lose their oesophagus, if not their lives.

Giuseppe Meucci, chief surgeon at the Goderich Surgical Centre Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Giuseppe Meucci, chief surgeon at the 56-bed Goderich hospital in Freetown where four year old Amza is being cared for, has been treating patients burned by sodium hydroxide nearly every day since arriving in Freetown in 2019.

Three quarters of patients seen by the hospital’s specialist programme for oesophageal burns, set up in response to the crisis and run by the Italian medical charity Emergency, are under five.

“It’s a struggle in this country,” says Dr Meucci. “Almost every family knows someone who has suffered because of this problem. But they just keep coming.”

Hospital director Jasna Sundic Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“In most countries you remove the source of danger for the child, but here that doesn’t seem to happen,” he says.

“It’s one of the main health problems of this country. Soda is there with malaria, malnutrition and typhoid complications. It’s one of the reasons why so many children die before they reach five years old.”

Hospital director Jasna Sundic agrees.

“This is a very severe issue but one which is very preventable,” she tells the Telegraph. “[But] however much we do here, we have not been able to decrease the overall number of soda patients being admitted.

“We cannot stop mothers who have no other source of income except making soap.”

Ibrahim Kerah is fed by his father Mohamed Credit : SImon Townsley

In a handful of rare cases, burns victims are sent abroad for complex oesophageal reconstruction surgery but this is not an option for the vast majority of children injured in Sierra Leone.

More than 60 per cent require surgery, but for these children, like Amza, a feeding tube that bypasses the oesophagus is the only option.

The hospital has many of these gastrostomy patients.

Critically underweight Mabinty Bangura Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

In a ward dedicated to soda burns, four-year-old Ibrahim Kerah is being fed through his stomach tube by his father Mohamed.

They travelled together on the back of a motorbike taxi for nearly 10 hours to get here for his third check-up appointment.

The Telegraph watches as Mohamed carefully prepares his son’s meal, adding spinach leaves to the porridge-like mix which is fed into a syringe at the end of the tube.

At an adjoining bed two-year-old Mabinty Bangura is critically underweight after ingesting soda about six months ago. Nurses have put her on a high protein drip so she can regain enough strength to undergo the same bypass surgery.

In the courtyard outside, mothers whose children have just had a gastrostomy are being taught how to prepare the liquid food.

Ibrahim and his father Mohamed endured a 10-hour motorbike journey to attend his hospital check-up Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Isatu Alie, 24, has been living with a stomach tube for 12 years, and now works for Emergency as a patient ambassador.

She is eight months pregnant with her second child and proud to have overcome her injury and the stigma of having to feed through a tube.

“I remember what happened so well,” she says. “I had just got back from school. I took my cup and dunked it into the water bucket. My aunt made soap and, on that day, I didn’t ask about the liquid in the bucket. The pain was incredible”.

More than a decade has passed since her surgery, and Isatu has adjusted well.

“I’m okay with it now. I feel like a normal human being; I’m blessed to be here,” she says.

“Now I speak to children and their parents who have just experienced the same thing and tell them not to lose hope.”

Pregnant Isatu Alie now works as a patient ambassador Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

A small proportion of the patients needing treatment following caustic soda burns are adults.

Among them is 21-year-old Junisa Bundeh, who is on a follow-up visit to check his stomach tube. He explains that he gulped down what he thought was a cup of water from a basin while eating at his grandmother’s house three months ago.

“It was so painful,” recalls Junisa. “I realised what it was straight away because it was so harsh. I tried to spit it all out but the liquid was already going down my throat.”

Mothers are taught how to prepare liquid food; Junisa Bundeh shows his feeding tube Credit : SImon Townsley

In the muddy lanes of Freetown’s Waterloo district there are makeshift soap making operations all over.

The coloured plastic buckets full of either soda or water are everywhere.

Against the backdrop of the rainy season’s persistent gloom, the containers symbolise a measure of cleanliness for families sheltering from torrential downpours under mouldy concrete awnings.

As the Telegraph watches Yabom Kapro, a village elder, making soap, the risks involved are immediately obvious.

Chief Yabom Kapro makes soap at her Waterloo town home, near Freetown Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

As she tips a purple bucket of caustic soda solution into a large basin and then adds palm oil from a plastic jerrycan, local children hover round the cluster of colourful containers.

Yabom uses a wooden paddle to stir the mixture into a creamy paste and then pours it into a mould held in place by an old motorcycle tyre.

Buckets containing caustic soda dissolving, top. Caustic soda crystals, below Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Once set, the beige-coloured cake of soap is cut into blocks which are then grated on a wire mesh contraption to be sold at the local market.

“When you dilute the caustic soda, it is completely clear like water at first,” says another soap maker, 43-year-old Cilina Bangura.

“Afterwards a white scum forms on the top, but you cannot be watching all of the time, [even] with all of these children around.”

Cilina knows the risks but says she can't afford to stop making soap. It has, as the NGOs intended, become an economic lifeline for her and her family.

“I want my children to continue making soap when I stop working,” she says. “I took out a loan to buy everything I needed, and now it is the only way I can make a living.

“Of course, I know how dangerous soda is – it has burned my skin many times – but I don’t have another option.”

Home-made soap, in Waterloo Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Maimunatu Sankoh, three, whose family lives in a nearby tin-roof shack, is sadly too well aware of that danger from her own bitter experience of soda poisoning.

As she feeds her daughter through a stomach tube, Maimunatu’s mum Iyesatu complains: “I have never seen any public information about soda.

“There are warnings on the packets but that is no use once the product is dissolved in water. They need to tell people to keep buckets out of the way.”

Iyesatu Kamara feeds her daughter Maimunatu Sankoh at their home Credit : SImon Townsley

Incidents of children consuming harmful chemicals are not confined to developing countries and were once common in the west.

In the US, the Poison Prevention Packaging Act was introduced in 1970, mandating childproof containers and the labelling of harmful household products.

The UK followed suit in 1975 with the introduction of child-resistant safety caps on containers of caustic soda and most other noxious household substances.

Despite the risks, Cilina says she can't afford to stop making soap Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Such legislation is still a long way off in Sierra Leone and is anyway far too late for four-year-old Amza.

Under heavy sedation in the intensive care unit, his glazed eyes open only occasionally.

The only visible evidence of his injuries is some scarring on his lips, but the doctors say his throat, oesophagus and stomach have all been seared by several large gulps of soda.

The boy’s mother, Mamie Kebbie, 30, keeps a watchful vigil, stroking his listless head tenderly. She says he used to be a playful and vivacious child.

If they are taken to hospital quickly, children with soda burns are normally given an oesophageal dilation endoscopy – a procedure which aims to keep the oesophagus open – but for Amza this has not been possible.

Freetown, Sierra Leone Credit : Simon Townsley

“This is a very severe case,” explains nurse Annette Turay, who heads the hospital’s intensive care unit. “When he was brought in, about 10 hours after he had ingested the soda, we were unable to conduct an endoscopy because he already had respiratory problems.

“He has pneumonia and he cannot feed through his mouth. He cannot even swallow his own saliva.

Mamie Kebbie keeps a vigil at her son's bedside Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“It will be a week before he is strong enough for us to be able to operate. We will insert a gastric tube into his stomach. He will have to keep this as his main way of being fed for a long time, potentially forever.”

But nurse Turay has seen worse.

“I have seen so many children suffering a lot after ingesting soda, so many dying too.

“A few weeks ago, we had a child in the ward who died because his stomach was completely gone”.

The Telegraph contacted all the NGOs involved in the setting up of and promotion of soap making schemes in Sierra Leone that are mentioned in this story for comment.

“Now I speak to children and their parents who have just experienced the same thing and tell them not to lose hope.”

Pregnant Isatu Alie now works as a patient ambassador Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

A small proportion of the patients needing treatment following caustic soda burns are adults.

Among them is 21-year-old Junisa Bundeh, who is on a follow-up visit to check his stomach tube. He explains that he gulped down what he thought was a cup of water from a basin while eating at his grandmother’s house three months ago.

“It was so painful,” recalls Junisa. “I realised what it was straight away because it was so harsh. I tried to spit it all out but the liquid was already going down my throat.”

Mothers are taught how to prepare liquid food; Junisa Bundeh shows his feeding tube Credit : SImon Townsley

In the muddy lanes of Freetown’s Waterloo district there are makeshift soap making operations all over.

The coloured plastic buckets full of either soda or water are everywhere.

Against the backdrop of the rainy season’s persistent gloom, the containers symbolise a measure of cleanliness for families sheltering from torrential downpours under mouldy concrete awnings.

As the Telegraph watches Yabom Kapro, a village elder, making soap, the risks involved are immediately obvious.

Chief Yabom Kapro makes soap at her Waterloo town home, near Freetown Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

As she tips a purple bucket of caustic soda solution into a large basin and then adds palm oil from a plastic jerrycan, local children hover round the cluster of colourful containers.

Yabom uses a wooden paddle to stir the mixture into a creamy paste and then pours it into a mould held in place by an old motorcycle tyre.

Buckets containing caustic soda dissolving, top. Caustic soda crystals, below Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Once set, the beige-coloured cake of soap is cut into blocks which are then grated on a wire mesh contraption to be sold at the local market.

“When you dilute the caustic soda, it is completely clear like water at first,” says another soap maker, 43-year-old Cilina Bangura.

“Afterwards a white scum forms on the top, but you cannot be watching all of the time, [even] with all of these children around.”

Cilina knows the risks but says she can't afford to stop making soap. It has, as the NGOs intended, become an economic lifeline for her and her family.

“I want my children to continue making soap when I stop working,” she says. “I took out a loan to buy everything I needed, and now it is the only way I can make a living.

“Of course, I know how dangerous soda is – it has burned my skin many times – but I don’t have another option.”

Home-made soap, in Waterloo Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Maimunatu Sankoh, three, whose family lives in a nearby tin-roof shack, is sadly too well aware of that danger from her own bitter experience of soda poisoning.

As she feeds her daughter through a stomach tube, Maimunatu’s mum Iyesatu complains: “I have never seen any public information about soda.

“There are warnings on the packets but that is no use once the product is dissolved in water. They need to tell people to keep buckets out of the way.”

Iyesatu Kamara feeds her daughter Maimunatu Sankoh at their home Credit : SImon Townsley

Incidents of children consuming harmful chemicals are not confined to developing countries and were once common in the west.

In the US, the Poison Prevention Packaging Act was introduced in 1970, mandating childproof containers and the labelling of harmful household products.

The UK followed suit in 1975 with the introduction of child-resistant safety caps on containers of caustic soda and most other noxious household substances.

Despite the risks, Cilina says she can't afford to stop making soap Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Such legislation is still a long way off in Sierra Leone and is anyway far too late for four-year-old Amza.

Under heavy sedation in the intensive care unit, his glazed eyes open only occasionally.

The only visible evidence of his injuries is some scarring on his lips, but the doctors say his throat, oesophagus and stomach have all been seared by several large gulps of soda.

The boy’s mother, Mamie Kebbie, 30, keeps a watchful vigil, stroking his listless head tenderly. She says he used to be a playful and vivacious child.

If they are taken to hospital quickly, children with soda burns are normally given an oesophageal dilation endoscopy – a procedure which aims to keep the oesophagus open – but for Amza this has not been possible.

Freetown, Sierra Leone Credit : Simon Townsley

“This is a very severe case,” explains nurse Annette Turay, who heads the hospital’s intensive care unit. “When he was brought in, about 10 hours after he had ingested the soda, we were unable to conduct an endoscopy because he already had respiratory problems.

“He has pneumonia and he cannot feed through his mouth. He cannot even swallow his own saliva.

Mamie Kebbie keeps a vigil at her son's bedside Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“It will be a week before he is strong enough for us to be able to operate. We will insert a gastric tube into his stomach. He will have to keep this as his main way of being fed for a long time, potentially forever.”

But nurse Turay has seen worse.

“I have seen so many children suffering a lot after ingesting soda, so many dying too.

“A few weeks ago, we had a child in the ward who died because his stomach was completely gone”.

The Telegraph contacted all the NGOs involved in the setting up of and promotion of soap making schemes in Sierra Leone that are mentioned in this story for comment.

News.title: Carrick weighs up stripping Bruno Fernandes of Man Utd captaincy
News.content:
A defiant Michael Carrick refused to rule out stripping Bruno Fernandes of the captaincy as the Manchester United manager told his players to cut out their public sniping and start doing their talking on the pitch.

Carrick struck a bullish tone as he came out fighting and moved to reassert his authority after a tumultuous past fortnight that has left him battling to save his job ahead of Sunday’s must-win game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

The United manager began his press conference on Friday afternoon with a stirring five-and-a-half-minute monologue in which he issued an emotional call to arms to his players to demonstrate the values of hard work, sacrifice, humility and resilience that define the club.

Referencing Sir Matt Busby, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Bobby Charlton, Ryan Giggs and Wayne Rooney, Carrick warned there could be no “entitlement” culture in echoes of complaints from his predecessor Ruben Amorim.

United are actively considering their options in the event Carrick cannot quickly arrest a shocking start to the season that hit a new low with Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation by Como. The likes of Julian Nagelsmann, Eddie Howe, Unai Emery, Fabian Hürzeler and Antonio Conte are in the frame.

But Carrick insisted he was “100 per cent” convinced he was the right man to take United forward and, while he claimed the dressing room was “not divided”, he has had to contend with first defender Lisandro Martínez and then Fernandes venting in public.

Martínez was fined and publicly apologised for an extraordinary tirade at Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and the Old Trafford board last week before Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics in the wake of the Como debacle.

Carrick responded at the time to having his set-up and approach questioned by suggesting tactics count for little if players are unprepared to run.

Asked if he would consider taking the captaincy off Fernandes, Carrick said: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”

News.title: Oil hits five-month high amid fears of fresh strikes on Iran
News.content:
The price of oil has hit a five-month high amid fears Donald Trump will ramp up strikes in the Middle East following the midterm elections.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, climbed as much as 2.8pc to more than $116 a barrel, pushing down stock markets in the US and Europe.

It followed a New York Times report that the US and Israel had drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the midterm elections.

Oil has climbed more than 4pc this week, increasing pressure on stock markets at the same time as fears grow about the valuations of AI companies.

European shares fell on Friday, with the FTSE 100 down as much as 0.8pc, the Cac 40 in Paris down 1pc and the Dax in Frankfurt down 1.1pc.

On Wall Street, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell as much as 1pc, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite fell at a slower pace than the previous day.

Traders were rattled on Thursday after Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, warned that a “scarcity of capital” was hampering the rollout of the technology.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq in New York dropped by 2.6pc on Thursday while the S&P 500 fell 1.2pc on its worst day since July.

Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta was one of the worse hit in the sell-off, as its shares finished trading almost 7pc lower.

Overnight, the sell-off spread into Asian markets. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by as much as 2.3pc and was down more than 4pc on the week.

The Kospi index in South Korea declined as much as 4.1pc on Friday but recovered to be marginally higher as markets closed.

The stock market turmoil led to a jump in safe haven assets like bonds.

The yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds, a benchmark for the cost of borrowing for governments around the world, fell by the largest amount since March 2023.

Sports.title: Erling Haaland gives Man City teammate dressing down as he pulls rank during loss
Sports.content:
Erling Haaland gives Man City teammate dressing down as he pulls rank during loss

Erling Haaland wore his frustration on his sleeve during Manchester City's 2-1 Premier League defeat to Aston Villa

View 3 Images Erling Haaland was not pleased with a team-mate as Manchester City lost to Aston Villa (Image: Getty)

Erling Haaland lambasted Gianluigi Donnarumma during Manchester City's 2-1 loss to Aston Villa. The defeat at Villa Park ended City's perfect start to the top-flight campaign.

‌



‌



Enzo Maresca's side travelled to face Villa looking to make it eight wins from eight in the league but found themselves 1-0 down inside six minutes. Nicolas Jackson capitalised on a Marc Guehi error and thundered home.

‌



The visitors battled back and after some valiant Villa defending, City were level. None other than Haaland headed in an Iliman Ndiaye cross in the 52nd minute. But the striker's joy was short-lived.

‌



On the hour mark, Jackson popped up once more and unleashed a strike straight at City shot-stopper Donnarumma. But the Italian let the shot slip under him and into the back of the net for 2-1. The scoreline stayed this way for all of City's efforts in the final stages.

Premier League clubs learn individual cost of independent regulator after fees double READ MORE :

Arsenal capitalise on Man City slip-up but Mikel Arteta still left with glaring concern READ MORE :

Haaland was visibly frustrated at full-time but footage from the first half shows that his grievances had started long before City's fate was sealed. In the 33rd minute, an interaction with the eventually culpable Donnarumma was rather unsavoury.

View 3 Images Donnarumma came out to protest the free-kick decision (Image: TNT Sports)

‌



Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

City conceded a free-kick shortly after the half-hour mark as Guehi brought down Jackson on the break. The Villa players started to line up the set piece, just outside the penalty area.

‌



But Donnarumma briefly stepped off his line as the free-kick was being prepared and approached the official in protest of it being given. Other City players had been speaking to the referee about the decision.

Haaland did not take kindly to the Italian leaving his net and could soon be seen gesturing at the 27-year-old, appearing to tell him to get back.

‌



Donnarumma didn't have to make a save from the eventual free-kick as Johan Manzambi put the effort over. But in the second half, Jackson's powerful strike did slip under him in a costly error.

View 3 Images Haaland gestured at the goalkeeper (Image: TNT Sports)

‌



Speaking after the match, manager Maresca told TNT Sports that both goals City conceded could have been avoided. He said: "Absolutely, both.

"Sometimes you have to be a bit more lucky because we only conceded those two chances, but we created a lot of chances. We played most of the game in their box.

Article continues below

"But you have to be clinical and avoid mistakes like the two goals we conceded. The overall performance was good. Second half, we conceded in transition.

"We needed to defend that a little better and be a little bit luckier in that transition but that is football," he added. "We will learn from that."

Sports.title: Arsenal capitalise on Man City slip-up but Mikel Arteta still left with glaring concern
Sports.content:
Arsenal capitalise on Man City slip-up but Mikel Arteta still left with glaring concern

ARSENAL 2-0 EVERTON: Goals from Ezri Konsa and Gabriel Magalhaes gave the Gunners a vital victory, moving them level with Manchester City at the top of the Premier League table

View 4 Images Arsenal took advantage of Manchester City losing (Image: David Price/Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

Arsenal capitalised on Manchester City dropping points and beat Everton 2-0 to go joint-top of the Premier League table. The Gunners were boosted by City's first defeat of the campaign, with the pacesetters having lost 2-1 away to Aston Villa in the early kick-off.

‌



‌



Ezri Konsa gave Arsenal an early lead, scoring the Gunners' first goal from a corner this season. In truth, the soaking wet conditions at the Emirates made it a slog for both teams.

‌



But Gabriel Magalhaes' goal midway through the second half - one of his many important contributions after having an injury scare - was like a ray of sunshine for Arsenal and a storm cloud for Everton. The Toffees had a decent start to the season but remain winless since the international break and they now go into a cup-league double-header against Newcastle.

‌



After Wednesday's thrilling 2-2 draw away to Bayern Munich, and with a trip to Fleetwood in the Carabao Cup coming next Tuesday, Arteta rotated his starting XI. Riccardo Calafiori's run of starting every league game this season came to an end while Viktor Gyokeres got the nod up front over Kai Havertz, with Mikel Merino also replacing Bruno Guimaraes.

Everton's slim resources were on show as David Moyes named two goalkeepers on the bench. Jarrad Branthwaite (concussion) and Jack Grealish (illness) were both ruled out of their trip to face the reigning champions.

Make sure you don't miss the best Arsenal coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

The return of Set Piece FC

It was the match fact that pessimistic Everton fans will've winced at. Seven games into last season, Arsenal had scored from a corner six times on their way to a record-breaking 19. Their record prior to Saturday: zero.

‌



Sadly for the Toffees, was only a matter of time until that changed.

In the seventh minute, a delivery swung in by Martin Odegaard caused chaos and the ball hit the crossbar via an Everton man. Viktor Gyokeres was first to get something on it before Konsa prodded home to score his first goal for Arsenal the day after his 29th birthday.

‌



Will Arsenal win the Premier League? Give us your prediction in the comments section.

View 4 Images Ezri Konsa scored Arsenal's first goal from a corner this season (Image: Mark Leech/Offside/Offside via Getty Images)

‌



Moyes' half-time rant

After Arsenal dominated the first half and missed chances to extend their lead, David Moyes had every right to be upset with his team. But he was also furious with the referee.

Moyes, donning a cap in the pouring North London rain, waited in the tunnel at half-time and was seen telling Tony Harrington exactly what he thought of his performance. Everton captain James Tarkowski also wasn't happy with Harrington, and there was a feeling that the visitors had been on the wrong side of one too many decisions in the opening 45 minutes.

‌



Harrington couldn't please Arsenal either. After Tarkowski won a soft foul from Gyokeres in the second half, the Gunners bench were up in arms and Arteta was given a yellow card for their protestations.

View 4 Images David Moyes vented his fury towards Tony Harrington (Image: Alex Pantling/Getty Images)

‌



Gyokeres' drought leaves Arteta with concern

A goal-a-game for Sweden, but none in 10 for Arsenal. Rarely is a striker so prolific for his country and yet can't score for his club.

Arteta handed Gyokeres first league start of the season, a big opportunity to break his duck. But the Swede couldn't find a way through Everton's backline to even register a single shot.

‌



Kai Havertz replaced him in the 68th minute and remains Arteta's first-choice striker. A goal against Fleetwood could kickstart Gyokeres' season, but right now, Arteta - rather concerningly - can't rely on his £64million signing to get on the scoresheet.

View 4 Images Viktor Gyokeres hasn't scored for Arsenal this term (Image: Henry Nicholls/AFP via Getty Images)

Article continues below

Moyes would love to have two options up front, having been left reliant on Thierno Barry. The 24-year-old did nearly equalise with Everton's best chance of the game on the brink of half-time. Ben White's header back towards goal fell short and allowed Barry to sneak in, only for David Raya to pull off a sharp save low down.

Sports.title: Senne Lammens goes against the grain with Michael Carrick comments as Man Utd boss under pressure
Sports.content:
Senne Lammens goes against the grain with Michael Carrick comments as Man Utd boss under pressure

Michael Carrick is fighting for his job at Manchester United

View 2 Images Man United goalkeeper Senne Lammens has revealed what the dressing room thinks of Michael Carrick. (Image: (Photo by Emmanuele Ciancaglini/Ciancaphoto Studio/Getty Images))

Manchester United goalkeeper Senne Lammens insists the dressing room remains behind under-fire manager Michael Carrick, despite the likes of Lisandro Martinez and Bruno Fernandes voicing concerns in recent weeks. United have endured a difficult campaign since their Champions League return, securing just two victories from their 11 fixtures across all competitions.

‌



‌



The scrutiny on Carrick has intensified following public criticism from two of his star players in the wake of losses to Atletico Madrid and a humiliating 4-1 defeat at Como. Martinez aimed his criticism at United director of football Jason Wilcox, suggesting the club failed to provide sufficient backing in the summer transfer market to support Carrick, leaving the squad stretched for their European fixtures.

‌



Meanwhile, Fernandes took aim at Carrick's tactics. But Lemmens insists he is fully behind the United head coach. Speaking to Sky Sports, the United goalkeeper said: "For me personally, I think it [the dressing room] is [behind Carrick].

‌



"Of course, the people at home can't see that, so we need to also try to look like that when we are on the pitch in the weekend, but I can assure you that we're doing everything we can and we're all together behind the coach, as a staff, players, front office.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Make sure you don't miss the best Man Utd coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



"Everyone knows, of course, they have to do better, but I think we are united and we are trying to get better as a team and together."

Lammens was asked further about Fernandes' comments in midweek and whether tactics were responsible for their difficulties this campaign.

‌



He said: "Last season I felt like, playing-wise, maybe we played sometimes better this season, but last season everything just clicked and went the right way for us.

View 2 Images Michael Carrick during his pre-Bournemouth press conference (Image: Sky Sports)

‌



"We struggled as a team together when they pressed us, but we didn't concede that many goals, and then I think as a counter team a bit more last season we did really well, but you also know, I think everybody knew that we had to improve as well from that, that teams were going to change the way they played against us.

"So that's why we had to evolve this season and in preseason, we tried to do some different things to get us in the best position to win games.

‌



"I think we need a little bit more like last season, the way we fought together, even when it wasn't going the best and just trying to fight as a team and defend as a team, I think that's probably something we need to try to get back to."

Antonio Conte's two demands to take Man Utd job emerge after giving green light READ MORE :

Fernandes voiced his concern at Carrick and his backroom team following the woeful performance against Como, telling TNT Sports after the defeat in northern Italy: "It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence."

‌



FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

When pressed on whether he believed the manager had got his tactics wrong, Fernandes said: "That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable."

Article continues below

Carrick was questioned over whether he would strip Fernandes of the captaincy in the wake of the Como defeat, but remained tight-lipped and insisted he would do whatever he deemed right for the football club.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick told Man Utd squad revolt 'wouldn't have happened' under Sir Alex Ferguson
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick told Man Utd squad revolt 'wouldn't have happened' under Sir Alex Ferguson

Sir Alex Ferguson ruled Manchester United with an iron fist during his 26 years in charge at Old Trafford and is witnessing a squad revolt under Michael Carrick

View 2 Images Sir Alex Ferguson has watched several Manchester United matches this season (Image: NurPhoto, NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Owen Hargreaves is convinced that Sir Alex Ferguson would bomb Bruno Fernandes out of the team if he were still Manchester United manager. The former United midfielder reckons Fernandes' remarks after their loss to Como would have proved fatal under Ferguson's reign.

‌



‌



Hargreaves went so far as to suggest he would not have dared make such comments in the first place, knowing what the repercussions would be. Fernandes will seemingly escape any punishment for questioning Carrick's approach following their Champions League defeat.

‌



The Portugal international retains the club captaincy. He also looks set to feature for United against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.

‌



Jadon Sancho given crushing reality check with contract offer after Man Utd and Chelsea flops READ MORE :

Hargreaves was questioned on TNT Sports about who he would direct his frustration towards as a player in such circumstances. He said: "To be fair, I would have never looked at my manager.

"First of all, you would have never said that under Sir Alex because you would never have played again for the football club. Second of all, you've got to look at yourself first.

"Not one Man United fan thinks Manchester United should be competing for the Premier League, not one. But the best you can do is put your best effort in every game, every time you step out there."

‌



View 2 Images Bruno Fernandes has left Michael Carrick with a huge decision to make for Manchester United's match against Bournemouth (Image: NurPhoto, NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Fernandes told the same broadcaster on Wednesday evening: "It's a decision from the staff not to press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball."

‌



When pressed on whether Carrick had misjudged his tactics, he said: "That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me."

Questioned over whether the remarks could prove divisive, Carrick said at Friday's pre-match press conference: "The most important thing for me is the team, first and foremost, the squad, the dynamics in the squad. Again, it's about the football club. I'll always do what's best for the football club."

‌



Make sure you don't miss the best Man Utd coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Pressed on the dressing room atmosphere, Carrick was emphatic: "It's not divided, no. It's not divided. We just need to get back to doing what we do best, and we will."

‌



He was also quizzed on whether the club might contemplate removing the captaincy from Fernandes as a consequence. Carrick responded: "I'm just saying, whatever the situation is, I'll always do what's best for the football club."

United's head coach declined to confirm whether he had held talks with Fernandes: "If I've spoken to him or haven't spoken to him, I don't think this is the time to go into too much detail."
