Sports.title: Fabio Wardley reveals why he wanted to get straight back into the ring with Daniel Dubois as he defends his team after they came under fire for not pulling him out earlier in first defeat
Sports.content:
Fabio Wardley is not supposed to be here again so soon.

Not, at least, according to those who watched him endure 11 gruelling rounds against Daniel Dubois in Manchester in May. Not according to those who questioned whether his corner should have pulled him out earlier, as his face became increasingly battered and his right eye swelled shut. And certainly not according to those who believe the punishment he absorbed makes a rematch a risk too far.

But Wardley has never been one to follow the script.

When the 31-year-old first faced Dubois, 29, he did so as the WBO heavyweight champion. He dropped his opponent twice in the opening three rounds, threatening to produce one of the biggest victories of his career before Dubois fought his way back into the contest and eventually stopped him in the 11th.

Now, with the WBO title back on the line, Wardley finds himself in more familiar territory in one respect: he is the challenger, the underdog and the man many expect to lose again.

And, as he explains when we sit down ahead of the rematch, he rather likes it that way.

Fabio Wardley is not supposed to be here again so soon but he's never one to follow the script

Dubois (right) and Wardley (left) will go toe-to-toe for a second time on Saturday evening

'It's been the staple of my career for as long as I can remember, well, since I started. It has been the main focal point. After the first five or six fights, when I started to step up the level, even incrementally, even slightly, people were saying I was going to lose, that it was a step too far, and all the rest of it. It's all the stuff everyone's heard before,' he says.

'It's a side of the coin I'm very much used to, and the pressure's off. I'm the challenger here. I'm expected to lose and expected to go even quicker, and Daniel's supposed to put on a better performance, and all the rest of it. So there's no pressure on me. There's nothing on my shoulders.'

It is a strikingly relaxed assessment from a fighter preparing to walk back into the ring with the man who inflicted the first defeat of his professional career.

Wardley, however, insists that defeat has done little to change him. He is not pretending that losing a world title is enjoyable, but nor does he regard it as a defining moment in his life.

'Not a lot has changed. I'm not that different. Don't get me wrong, a loss is never fun. It's never nice, it's never enjoyable. But for me, at least, it wasn't soul-crushing or devastating, and it hasn't had any effect on me as a person, my character or anything else.

'The job’s the job, the game’s the game. From the very beginning, I’ve accepted that getting through heavyweight boxing unscathed isn’t guaranteed, especially given the way I compete at the highest level and my desire to take on the biggest challengers out there.

'I think people forget that the first time around, I picked Daniel. I asked for that fight because I looked at the crop of heavyweights and thought, "That's the best one to challenge myself against."

'Knowing that about myself, and knowing that's my angle, was I ever going to get through this undefeated like Floyd Mayweather? Probably not. So, look, it comes how it comes. But as long as I'm happy with myself in terms of the performances, that I've given my all and all the rest of it, I can sleep at night.'

Their first fight in May was a brutal affair, with the contest being stopped in the 11th round

Wardley took a lot of punishment in the latter rounds of their first encounter in May (above)

It is that willingness to put himself in the firing line which has made Wardley such a compelling heavyweight. His fights are rarely short on drama, and the first meeting with Dubois was no exception. He started at a blistering pace, dropping DDD in the opening 10 seconds, only for the momentum to swing as the punishment began to accumulate.

By the later rounds, Wardley was absorbing heavy shots and fighting through considerable damage. His condition between rounds prompted questions about whether the contest should have been stopped sooner, with particular scrutiny falling on his corner for allowing him out ahead of the 10th.

Wardley disagrees with the suggestion that his team failed him. He regards the people around him as family and trusts them to put his welfare first, even when the decisions they make are questioned from the outside.

He is equally dismissive of the noise surrounding the timing of the rematch, arguing that those watching from the outside cannot know the full picture of his recovery. His position is that he and his team are best placed to judge the damage he sustained and whether he is ready to fight again.

For Wardley, the prospect of another brutal encounter is not something he has brushed aside or refused to think about. It is a reality he has had to confront with himself, knowing that by stepping back into the ring with Dubois, he is willingly putting himself in a position where he could once again withstand a frightening amount of punishment.

It is a remarkable thought process: to acknowledge the possibility of enduring the same damage all over again, to ask himself whether he is prepared to go through it, and then to make peace with the answer before he has even thrown a punch.

'It's a level of early acceptance. The second I triggered the rematch clause, even before that, I had to have a conversation with myself and ask, "This could go the exact same way. Are you ready for that? Are you OK with that?"

'As long as the answer is yes from me to me, then cool, let's go. But by now, it's nowhere near my brain as a question mark or something I'm having to deal with, battle with or anything else. It's already been ticked off, boxed and put away. It is what it is.'

Wardley was checked by the doctor and spoken to by the referee multiple times in the fight

As a result, Dubois became a two-time heavyweight champion and will now defend his belt

There is little melodrama in his delivery. When the possibility of going through the same ordeal again is put to him, Wardley does not attempt to dress it up as fearlessness or pretend that the risks do not exist.

'It's an acceptance of the game and the sport we got into, and especially the way I fight as well,' he says.

That approach is perhaps best illustrated by what goes through his mind when he is taking punishment in the ring. Wardley is not a heavyweight who is inclined to retreat quietly after being caught cleanly. His instinct is to make sure his opponent knows there will be a response.

'Especially in those moments, it's about getting back at them. All right, you took one… let your hands go. Don't just let them get away with it for free. At least let them know. Let them have it in their brain that if they get off a few shots, I'm not just going to take them, run away and roll over.'

It is a mindset that makes for spectacular viewing, but one which also places enormous demands on a fighter's corner.

Wardley describes those 60 seconds between rounds as almost too precious to waste on anything other than the information he needs to continue. With the clock ticking and another round approaching, he wants tactical instruction rather than an emotional check-in.

'No, I think it's 90 per cent tactical, 10 per cent everything else, because in those moments, compassion doesn't need to come into it. That's not where the compassion needs to be.

'Those 60 seconds are so precious, such a small moment. It feels like a click. It feels like nothing. It feels like it's done and gone so quickly that you're on your stool, you're off your stool and the next round has started.

'In that time, you need to get the information. It's not time for, "Oh, a little rub on the shoulder. Are you doing OK, Fab? Is everything alright? Are you going to be alright, mate? Do you want me to dab your face a bit?" No. Let me know what I need to know. Let's get this going again.'

Wardley knows that the rematch will be gruelling. He knows his durability will continue to be questioned. But he also knows why he wanted the first fight in the first place.

For Wardley, the pursuit of the biggest challenges has always mattered more than protecting an unbeaten record. Defeat by Dubois has not changed that. He is back because in his mind, the possibility of the same ending has already been accepted and because it’s a risk worth taking.

Sports.title: Daniel Dubois' second clash with Fabio Wardley promises to be even MORE brutal than their first, writes JEFF POWELL MBE - as May's champion vows to 'bash and smash' his rival
Sports.content:
Daniel Dubois' second clash with Fabio Wardley promises to be even MORE brutal than their first, writes JEFF POWELL MBE - as May's champion vows to 'bash and smash' his rival

Even the most hardened boxing fans can be taken aback by the depths of brutality which two men are capable of inflicting on each other. Especially the heavyweights.

So it was on the Saturday night this May when Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley battered hell's bells out of each other in Manchester’s Co-op Live Arena. Wardley dropped his world title challenger twice in the first three rounds. Just 28 seconds into the 11th, Dubois had to be pulled off the champion he had reduced to a bleeding and battered but still-standing wreck.

We mere mortals can only ask: How on earth do they do it? ‘We’re fighters,’ says Dubois. ‘Honoured to share a ring with him.’

‘Born to do it,’ says Wardley, who found out that truth of himself when he tried white collar boxing. ‘Love being in with such a great fighter.’

What in heaven goes through their minds at the prospect of doing it again, as they are on Saturday night at the O2? Do they not realise the danger this sledgehammer head-banging presents to their health?

Prepare yourselves, dear gentle readers, for this stunning answer from Dubois: ‘Dementia? If you’re talking about dementia, no point worrying. We’ve probably got it already.’

Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley have both spoken of their love for stepping into the ring with one another ahead of their rematch on Saturday

But as brutal as their meeting in May was, tomorrow night's clash at the O2 has been teased as even bloodier

A chilling insight, this, into the mentality of men who fight not only for a living but for the lust for glory, the thrill of battle, the roar of the crowd, the smell of the greasepaint, the glare of the lights and not least their manly pride.

And on nights like this, for a world championship. This time the WBO belt which Dubois ripped from Wardley’s fairy-tale grasp five months ago.

What, no nerves? ‘I live with the chaos,’ says Dubois. ‘Chaos all day every day and specially on the night. I love the fear. It gives me the power. I hold the chaos in until it’s at its peak when the first bell goes. Then it explodes as I let it out. Which brings power and clarity.’

Wardley comes not only from his different background in commerce but also with an opposite mindset. He says: ‘No one wants to lose a world title but if it has to be, then what really matters is how it happens.

‘I feel more relaxed and confident having proved I can engage a top-level fighter in a great fight, which everyone expected me to lose easily. Calm makes me better.’

That and the lessons he learned in the five months since his gladiatorial — and only — defeat thus far. ‘We’ve studied every critical moment of the first fight,’ he says. ‘And I’ve adapted where necessary. Had to because I have more to work on than Daniel with all his experience.

‘But we’ve not only looked at me. We’ve looked at him. He’s not as adaptable as me. He’s not suddenly going to become light-footed and free moving. I’ll give him something different.’

To which Dubois says: ‘I’ll give him another beating. Bash him up. Smash him worse than before. And quicker. We didn’t know quite what he might do in the first fight. Now I know what to expect.

‘I also know that he’s not good enough to adapt. I’m his daddy now.’ That is clarity, Dubois style. He also discounts those two knock-downs. As a man who has been a slow starter at times — although not when he demolished Anthony Joshua from the get-go — he says: ‘Things happen in boxing. You can get caught. But I also know now that he doesn’t have the power. No real power.’

Wardley, for his part, denies that he was as badly hurt as it appeared in fight one. Their respective trainers have disagreed about the 11th-hour stoppage. Dubois’ coach Don Charles says the towel should have been thrown in earlier.

Wardley supports his man Ben Davison’s assertion that he was still in the fight throwing punches, saying: ‘The optics looked bad, what with the blood and the bruising and the punches. But I trust my team to take care of me. Trust them with my life.

‘A lot of the punches were glancing and in the 10th round I shook him with an uppercut. If the big right that followed had connected cleanly we might have had a different ending.’

This man who escaped office drudgery to chase his dream hopes to go on to meet the December winner of Joshua v Tyson Fury. Dubois fancies some of that big money but is also looking beyond, to unifying all the other world titles vacated by Oleksandr Usyk.

Will the ending on Saturday be different from Wardley v Dubois One? Probably not. Dynamite Dan likely added the more valuable knowledge to his wider experience and has never looked this bullish before a fight.

What we do know for sure is that this pair will give us another thriller.

Sports.title: The intrigue caused by Cadillac's F1 boss dodging driver market question
Sports.content:
The US GP weekend naturally means the spotlight gravitates towards Formula 1’s two American-owned teams. That has led to some awkward questions for Cadillac amid ongoing speculation over its driver line-up for 2027 and beyond.

Both Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas are on “multi-year” contracts, understood to be a so-called one-plus-one arrangement in which the second year is optional, subject to either party fulfilling various conditions. Such has been the disparity in performance between the two drivers that Bottas’s position has been the object of paddock gossip for months.

Recently appointed team principal Marcin Budkowski has already had to do some firefighting on this, as had his predecessor Graeme Lowdon. But a rather peculiar moment in the FIA’s press conference for team representatives on Friday in Austin suggested Cadillac’s plans aren’t as fixed as previously billed.

The catalyst was a soft question from one of the broadcasters on the theme of Perez’s upcoming 300th grand prix start: “How difficult is it to evaluate a driver who’s fighting at the back of the grid, at the same time as the impression is that he’s having a better season than his team-mate? And quickly on drivers, would you be interested in having any conversation with Esteban [Ocon] regarding maybe a reserve role?”

In trying to give a suitably anodyne non-answer, Budkowski began to flounder.

“Look, for a driver like Checo, who, as you said, has a huge amount of experience and a number of races, I can tell you he doesn’t behave or drive like a driver who is anywhere close to retirement,” he said.

“He’s pushing very hard behind the wheel. He’s pushing us very hard also behind the scenes, in the debrief rooms and outside, and regularly texting me and other members of the team to push us to improve. He’s hungry, he’s motivated, and that’s actually really good to see. He does it in his own style.

Marcin Budkowski, Cadillac Team Principal Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

“We have two drivers: one is more hot and one is probably more cold, if we could say, from there. And they both push the team in their own particular ways, but Checo is, yes, pushing us very hard. And just looking at the way his body language on the grid, when he gets his helmet on and he gets in the car, he’s getting ready for a fight. There’s a lot of fire, there’s a lot of motivation there, so it’s really impressive for a driver of this experience.

“And at the same time, we’re getting his feedback and his input in terms of, as an experienced driver. So yes, it’s a very good combination.

“And sorry, the second question was about Esteban Ocon? Well, look, as a team principal, and I’m sure it’s the same with my colleagues, you’re getting calls and contacts from every driver or driver manager that is on the market. So, there are a number of drivers and managers who have contacted me.

“I’m not going to say who it is or who it isn’t, but pretty much all of them that are on the market have been in touch, as you’d expect. But yes, I think it’s the last place here, as you can imagine, where I would communicate anything on driver line-up.”

Were William Shakespeare present, he would no doubt have put quill to parchment and scratched out a note to the effect that the gentleman doth protest too much. Fortunately for the Cadillac team principal, perhaps, Adrian Newey was in the room and acted as a natural magnet for the majority of further questions.

Autosport understands that Ocon is highly unlikely to go to Cadillac, since he and Perez mixed like oil and water when they last coexisted under the same roof. It’s believed he will probably become Aston Martin’s third driver.

Whether or not Cadillac retain Bottas for 2027, it’s known that the team’s owners wish to have an American driver in a race seat as soon as possible. Lowdon’s surprise replacement this summer is an indication of how General Motors and TWG Motorsports’ expectations appear to be running somewhere ahead of the team’s current progress.

Cadillac ran Colton Herta in FP1 at the Circuit of The Americas, but he is a left-field candidate for any race opportunities since he is one point short of qualifying for a superlicence, owing to the FIA having changed the qualifying rubric. If he has meaningful running in another session this year he will qualify – but his rather patchy Formula 2 campaign this season isn’t a very strong calling card.

“Obviously having an American driver in an American team is a great story,” Budkowski told Sky Sports this weekend. “It needs to be the right time and the right driver. But we're working on that. We're working on that with Colton.

“There are some really exciting American talents coming up through the ranks as well. We've seen Ugo Ugochukwu winning F3. We've got [Sebastian] Wheldon coming through to F3 next year.

“So there's a lot of potential here and we'll look into that obviously.”

Read Also: Formula 1 When Cadillac will open its F1 engine factory

Sports.title: The unexpected issue Honda faced with upgraded F1 power unit
Sports.content:
Following a surprisingly successful Formula 1 weekend in Malaysia, expectations were also high at Aston Martin for Singapore, a venue that should have suited the AMR26 on paper.

However, the competitive picture at the Marina Bay Street Circuit proved rather disappointing, with Fernando Alonso pointing to problems with the Honda power unit after the race, particularly in terms of driveability.

Honda subsequently sent both its engineers and power units back to Sakura for more in-depth investigations. Those checks did not reveal any specific hardware fault. Instead, it emerged that the Japanese manufacturer was primarily struggling with turbo lag – the time it takes for the turbo to spool up, and therefore the delay between pressing the accelerator and feeling the effect of the turbo kicking in.

That is not a new problem in itself. In fact, it was one of the factors that hampered driveability with the new power unit specification introduced at Zandvoort. But it was precisely for that reason that Honda used its second ADUO token of the year in Madrid to introduce a new turbocharger intended to eliminate the problem.

However, when asked by Autosport, Honda's chief trackside engineer Shintaro Orihara revealed that it had unexpectedly become an issue again in Singapore.

“Even though we introduced a new turbocharger to manage turbo lag, we still struggled to manage that lag in Singapore because of the unique track lay-out and also the energy-rich situation. That has given some unstable acceleration to the driver,” Orihara admitted.

Shintaro Orihara, Honda Racing Corporation Trackside General Manager and Chief Engineer Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

Asked whether the turbo lag could be partly compensated for by deploying the MGU-K in different places than usual, Orihara explained that this only works to a certain extent, although he stressed that the MGU-K had contributed to the problem in a different way.

“MGU-K deployment can help [against] turbo lag, but not enough to compensate for it,” he said. “If we go to energy-rich tracks, we normally use the MGU-K harvesting to compensate for turbo lag. If we have enough MGU-K harvesting power, then the engine can run at a high operation point in the off-throttle sections.

“That helps turbo lag and is nice, but if we go to energy-rich circuits, sometimes it's difficult to get enough MGU-K harvesting value because of the energy-rich situation. In that case, the operation mode of the engine is not enough to control turbo lag and that's why we struggled at Singapore.”

The fact that Honda found no specific problems during its checks at the Sakura facility could potentially raise concerns. After all, it suggests that the same issue could arise again when Aston Martin returns to an energy-rich circuit.

However, Honda stressed that lessons have been learned, leading to new measures – not in terms of hardware, but rather in how Honda operates the power unit through software and settings.

Lance Stroll, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

“Yes, we have learned some things from Singapore, so we are preparing countermeasures for the future,” said Orihara. “We understand that we need to improve our control of the turbo lag. At the moment, our control is not meeting the driver demands, so we apply some countermeasures. But again, we need to check how those work on our power unit.”

The mental lesson Aston Martin learned in Singapore

As for Singapore, Aston Martin's chief trackside officer Mike Krack said the disappointment was compounded by expectations being too high heading into the race weekend. That, too, is something Aston Martin has learned from and will seek to avoid repeating in Austin.

“I always call them the emotional dynamics,” Krack said when asked about the disappointment by Autosport. “I think Sepang probably surprised us in terms of outcome and it raised the expectation level [for Singapore] maybe even beyond what was realistic.

“And when you do not deliver it for various reasons, then everybody becomes disappointed and it gets more difficult over the weekend. That is very clear.”

However, such factors are difficult to predict, particularly because driveability cannot be fully captured by simulation tools, as Krack also acknowledged.

“It is something that in simulations you cannot really have this clear picture,” he said. “How much will this cost you, for example? If you have lag or what Orihara was mentioning about the MGU-K stopping, and how it affects the drivability. This goes beyond simple sensitivity simulations.”

Mike Krack, Aston Martin Chief Trackside Officer Photo by: James Sutton / LAT Images via Getty Images

Aside from understanding the exact cause and the measures Honda has taken, Krack stressed that the team has also learned a mental lesson from the setback in Singapore.

“I think it is important to regroup after such an event and try to understand why it happened, in which areas did we lose out and then take the right learning from it,” he said.

“And [it’s also important] to manage our expectations a little bit better, or at least when you manage expectations, that you have a set of risks that could affect it, which we didn't do in Singapore.”

Sports.title: Verstappen enjoys promising start to US GP - but Red Bull pinpoints areas of improvement
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen finished Friday's practice sessions for the Formula 1 United States Grand Prix in second and third place. In each outing, the four-time world champion was less than two tenths behind Charles Leclerc, who set the benchmark on both occasions.

Red Bull is not immediately standing out from the rest of the field as it did in Malaysia, for example, but Verstappen is nevertheless largely satisfied with the early signs from the RB22 in Texas.

"It's been a positive start to the weekend. This track is never easy when it comes to finding the right compromise between the low and high-speed corners," the Dutchman said after FP2.

"The bumps make it even more difficult, so you’re trying to find a good balance in the car and get into a rhythm. That’s what we’ve been working on between FP1 and FP2. There’s still a bit more work to do to fine-tune that balance, but it wasn’t a bad day at all."

In practical terms, this means teams have to find a compromise in two different ways this weekend. Given the varied layout of the Circuit of the Americas, the first concerns the balance between high-speed and low-speed corners. Based on the GPS data, Red Bull appears competitive in the high-speed sections, making technical director Pierre Wache very clear about what needs to improve.

"It's clearly the low speed performance that we are focused on at the moment. Low speed is the key for us," said the Frenchman.

That is reflected in the data. Comparing the fastest laps of Leclerc, Kimi Antonelli and Verstappen, the slowest corners on the circuit are predominantly coloured red – in other words, Ferrari territory. Leclerc is strong both on the brakes and on the exit of Turn 1, and shows the same pattern at Turn 11, the slow left-hander before the long straight.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

At the end of that long straight – just before the braking point – Verstappen is almost a tenth ahead of Leclerc's time, while Antonelli is more than two tenths ahead. However, Verstappen loses considerable ground through Turns 12 to 16, another slower section of the circuit.

This underlines Wache's comments, although the challenge in Austin is not just about finding the right balance between different types of corners. Equally important is the compromise between outright performance and a car that can cope reasonably well with the bumps, which Verstappen described as "unacceptable" and "out of control" during Thursday's media day.

"The car reacts to those bumps how you would expect, it's jumping a lot," Wache said when asked how the RB22 is dealing with the track conditions.

"The track is massively bumpy, especially at Turn 1 under braking. You have to be very careful. But yeah, that’s the problem with this type of set-up that we are using. It is not as stiff as last year, but also not so far [away from that]. The car is not very compliant on the bumps here."

By using the term set-up, Wache is not referring specifically to Red Bull's choices, but to the current generation of F1 cars. In theory, these should be slightly more comfortable over the bumps than the ground-effect cars of recent years, but Verstappen explained on Thursday that the opposite is actually the case.

Thanks to active aerodynamics and straight mode, the cars rise slightly on the straights. This limits wear on the skid blocks and gives teams the freedom to push the limits even further in terms of ride height. As a result, the ride height is low under braking and through the corners, precisely the areas where the Circuit of the Americas is extremely bumpy.

According to Wache, improving the car's behaviour over those bumps and its low-speed performance are Red Bull's two main priorities ahead of qualifying.

Sports.title: McLaren's aims for its final F1 2026 upgrades amid decline in form
Sports.content:
"To get the car to be quick, we just have to try so hard to be perfect, and you cannot be perfect," said Lando Norris after practice for the Formula 1 United States Grand Prix in Austin.

"We're just a step behind."

Two mid-season wins for Norris now appear to be a 'purple patch' rather than harbingers of a competitive renaissance for McLaren after a troubled start to the 2026 season. At the US GP it introduced the first elements of what will be the final upgrade package of the year, due to be introduced in stages between this event and the Las Vegas GP.

Although by mid-season McLaren had developed the MCL40 to the point where it was among the fastest cars through quick corners, straightline speed and slow-corner performance have continued to be problematic, as has its nervous demeanour. Development has had to balance the process not just of creating theoretical performance, but also of making the car benign enough for the drivers to tap into that potential.

"It's just on a knife edge on every single corner," said the reigning world champion in Singapore. "You've just got to drive it within an exact percent, and you have to force the car in every single way. You can't let the car do any work. You can't just let the front do the work, or the rear do the work. You have to force the front; you've got to force the rear.

"You've got to drive it in a way that takes so much concentration and so much ability. It's just full-on and mentally draining because of how hard you have to work behind the wheels.

"It's just too difficult and it makes it impossible to put laps together in qualifying, which just shows how good of a job we were able to do when we were getting on pole [in Hungary, the Netherlands and Spain], and how rewarding that felt."

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Angela Weiss / AFP via Getty Images

Slow-corner performance isn't just a function of aerodynamics. Although Norris has a more adaptable style than many other drivers, even this requires the car to have a certain set of virtues. He takes a shallower approach to the apex than others, overlapping throttle and brake to a higher degree. His strength is a tremendous feel for where the front tyres pick up lateral grip mid-corner, which he exploits to help rotate the car.

What operates against him is the trend towards running a high degree of anti-squat, anti-dive geometry in the suspension. Although this stabilises the car's aerodynamic platform, it smothers the transmission of 'feel' about the changing state of grip at each axle. Shorn of this, Norris can't trust either end of the car – which is why, last year, his performances picked up dramatically after a slow start when McLaren developed an alternate front suspension geometry suspension for him.

In that context it's no surprise that McLaren has led with a revised front-end geometry for this latest update in Austin, along with reprofiled diffuser furniture. It's understood that the next phase of the upgrade will be applied in Brazil, with more arriving for Las Vegas depending on manufacturing timescales.

The new components McLaren will bring to the car in the coming races were signed off between the Dutch GP in late August and the Italian GP in the first week of September, and have been making their way through the production process. McLaren's design resources have been fully focused on the 2027 car ever since.

Insiders say the team identified a new aerodynamic direction during the April interregnum caused by the cancellation of the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian grands prix. The belief was that it would ultimately lead to a higher performance ceiling than the concept with which the team started the season.

This is a relatively typical occurrence in F1, especially during a new rules cycle. But it is very easy to leap to the conclusion that an upgrade package has somehow been a failure if it doesn't deliver an immediate and significant lap time uplift. From an engineering point of view it is simply establishing a new baseline.

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

McLaren introduced the first iteration of its new aerodynamic concept in the Azerbaijan GP weekend, centring around a dramatically different sidepod profile, along with heavily revised geometries for the flow conditioners in and around the diffuser, the leading edge of the floor, and the rear suspension fairings. The team was careful to manage expectations, emphasising that it wasn't expecting a major improvement in lap time straight away.

Circumstances then combined to make the new configuration appear, superficially, to be ineffective: Norris was stymied by a fuel injection problem while Oscar Piastri laboured to keep the Red Bulls of Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar behind him in the early phase of the race, then dropped out of the points after locking up at the second safety car restart. Later the team admitted that at least some of the straightline speed deficit was a consequence of not getting the most out of its Mercedes power unit.

"We will be having some more upgrades coming for the final part of the season, which is the kind of upgrades that follow the foundation set with the upgrades we delivered in Baku," said team principal Andrea Stella after the Singapore round.

"The step in Baku wasn't expected to be big, but it was foundational for some stuff that we will start taking trackside as of Austin and for the coming races. So what's most important for me is that I look forward to seeing our competitiveness from the next race. And hopefully we will be back to being in condition to score podiums and hopefully, once the full package is delivered, to compete for the victory."

McLaren isn't the only team to find itself combatting instability as it tries to add performance to its car. Mercedes went to the extent of running two different car specs in Singapore to try to understand the behaviour of its latest upgrade – but, notably, it has opted for the latest spec in Austin. As Norris explained ahead of the US GP weekend, upgrading an F1 car isn't a predictable and linear process.

"Upgrades are not always just you put them on and things work," he said. "They're not always easy to get the full potential out of. I think we've had a car which has just been still so, so difficult to drive. Yes, we won two races and I had a couple of podium positions, but it was by tiny margins. With a car like that, you'll not be able to do that consistently.

"We need to also improve the car in terms of ease of driving and ease of extracting performance."

Sports.title: F1 United States GP: Leclerc pips Antonelli to top FP2 while McLaren struggles
Sports.content:
Ferrari's Charles Leclerc has led the way in Friday practice for Formula 1's United States Grand Prix, narrowly beating Kimi Antonelli to the top spot in Austin as McLaren struggled for grip.

Leclerc set a 1m35.291s just before the halfway mark of Friday afternoon's second practice session on Austin's demanding Circuit of the Americas, pipping Max Verstappen's initial benchmark as Antonelli slotted into second.

As was the case earlier in FP1, COTA's bumpy and varied combination of low-speed and high-downforce corners caused teams headaches as they homed in on the best set-up compromise for the 5.5km loop.

As George Russell beat Verstappen's early medium-tyre benchmark, Oscar Piastri went wide in the McLaren and Isack Hadjar was struggling for overall grip in the Red Bull.

The paddock collectively unwrapped fresh sets of soft tyres shortly before the halfway mark. Those qualifying simulations further highlighted COTA's challenges, with the circuit's relentless combination of first sector Esses chewing through the soft tyres.

Russell dramatically lost and then saved his Mercedes through the fastest part of the Esses. Grip was low in the final sector too, with Lando Norris fighting a bucking bronco of a McLaren as he went off the road.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Chris Graythen / Getty Images

Verstappen put his soft tyres to good use to claim top with a 1m35.480s. The Dutchman didn't stay there for long, though, as on his first soft-tyre flyer Leclerc stopped the clocks after 1m35.291s, two tenths clear of the Red Bull man thanks to a superior third sector.

Championship leader Antonelli split his two rivals in second, falling just 0.042s short of Leclerc's benchmark.

The trio enjoyed a significant gap to the rest of the field, with Lewis Hamilton shipping six tenths in fourth as he was one of several frontrunners not to turn an optimal lap before shifting to long runs.

Russell recovered from his near crash in the Esses to take fifth, with Liam Lawson a promising sixth for Racing Bulls.

McLaren's handling issues left Norris and Piastri down in seventh and eighth, one second behind Leclerc.

A frustrated Hadjar was ninth with Haas driver Oliver Bearman rounding out the top 10.

Sports.title: The reasons behind Ferrari's US GP upgrades
Sports.content:
Ferrari's latest clutch of updates for the Formula 1 United States Grand Prix feature a unique approach to the 'fingers' situated at the front edge of the floor, although both drivers have played down the significance of the new parts.

The SF-26 has also been given a minor rework to the sidepods, with a small change to the inlet and the undercut to link up with a minor change to the floor board upstream. Ferrari's pre-event technical notes state that these changes intend to increase the energy of the airflow passing to the rear of the car, with the intent of getting the diffuser to work harder.

The diffuser has also been updated to increase the expansion of the flow released from the rear of the car, by modifying the overall volume of the diffuser itself along with small tweaks to the internal floor fences.

At the front of the floor, the five floor fences (or fingers) help to control the airflow passing underneath the floor, minimising the overall turbulence present in that flow to ensure the diffuser works efficiently. Ferrari has extended the outermost finger to reach over the top, offering a horizontal flow conditioner to further improve the airflow quality here.

Ferrari sidepod detail Photo by: Stuart Codling

Lewis Hamilton kept a lid on expectations for the weekend, suggesting pre-FP1 that the tweaks are worth "less than a tenth" and that its car chiming with the Circuit of the Americas would generate a bigger performance swing, while Charles Leclerc equally downplayed the effect of the new parts.

"They are not major upgrades; I've heard quite a lot about them, but they are not as big as maybe what's going around," Leclerc stated.

"It's a small step in the right direction, obviously, as always, that's the target. Then we still need to put it on the car and do the first few laps and see whether that's the step we expected is there.

"However, there are other teams I think I've heard that are bringing big upgrades, and so we'll have to see how it is compared to them. But I don't expect anything hugely significant, but I hope it can help us just do that little step forward and help us win the races."

Ferrari demonstrated solid pace in the opening practice session of the Austin weekend with Leclerc going fastest, although Max Verstappen's short-lived benchmark was deleted for track limits.

Why introduce an upgrade worth "less than a tenth?"

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

If Hamilton's assessment about the Ferrari update is correct, it does sound like small potatoes given the cost outlay required in producing and shipping new parts to the US. But there's more to an update package beyond the headline numbers.

By energising the flow to the rear end of the car, the car can generate higher levels of downforce more consistently. It might not change the peak lap time by a great deal, but it should ensure that there are fewer fluctuations in aero performance due to any changes in airspeed. If you can control that airspeed moving to the rear of the car, even during the car's axial motion when braking and cornering, it provides a more stable platform.

Improving consistency is one thing, and the developments can also become a jumping-off point for 2027. The number of floor fingers will be reduced from five to three next season, so potentially exploring that floor finger extension could help to reclaim any of the performance lost next season.

These are largely speculative examples, but do partly explore the idea of why a team would press an upgrade into service when the headline numbers only yield a small improvement. Ultimately, it's about either creating a platform for whatever comes next, or enhancing the properties of the existing aerodynamics to minimise the variance in lap time.

Sports.title: F1 United States GP: Leclerc beats Verstappen to top FP1 in upgraded Ferrari
Sports.content:
Ferrari driver Charles Leclerc pipped Red Bull's Max Verstappen to top first practice at Formula 1's United States Grand Prix in Austin.

Leclerc was just under a tenth faster than Verstappen in an upgraded Ferrari as he aims to deny the Dutchman and his in-form Red Bull team a hat-track of grand prix wins.

On a hot Circuit of the Americas, Ferrari hit the ground running as it trialled its latest, and understood to be the final, round of 2026 aero upgrades. The update package for Texas features revisions to the floor, bargeboard, sidepod and diffuser.

While impressive sounding on paper, the team was keen to play down expectations, calling it a minor improvement. Whatever the case, Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton quickly managed to get up to speed in the early running on the undulating 5.5km circuit, with Leclerc's 1m36.61s on medium tyres 0.074s off Hamilton's first personal best.

McLaren's Lando Norris was third ahead of Mercedes duo Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, who donned the slower hard compound for their opening runs and shipped four and five tenths respectively.

Feedback on balance issues permeated the airwaves at COTA, which typically is a tough circuit to get right due to its varied track layout and bumpy surface.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Chris Graythen / Getty Images

Just after the halfway mark, Leclerc took seven tenths off his previous benchmark as he switched to the softest tyre compound. Mitigating early balance and steering rack woes, Verstappen shot up the timesheets to take second, 0.084s behind Leclerc's 1m36.052s lap.

Verstappen's Red Bull, which featured an additional update to its new front wing, looked particularly impressive through COTA's first sector and its fast and flowing Esses. A lap that would see the four-time world champion usurp Leclerc was scratched for track limits at COTA's penultimate corner.

After suffering a couple of snaps of oversteer, Norris took third 0.245s behind, ahead of Russell as the top four teams all appeared in the same ballpark based on FP1's limited sample size.

World champion-elect Antonelli settled for fifth ahead of Hamilton and Piastri. Gabriel Bortoleto led the midfield in the Audi, taking eighth-place and just under a second off the pace of the frontrunners. That was slightly quicker than Arvid Lindblad in the Racing Bulls car, which has been comfortably leading the battle for fifth in the constructors' championship.

Liam Lawson held off Haas driver Oliver Bearman to round out the top 10, while Aston Martin showed glimpses of improvement as Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll took 12th and 13th. That put the pair ahead of Isack Hadjar in the second Red Bull, who lost his one-lap run due to exceeding track limits.

FP1 featured one rookie runner in Cadillac's Colton Herta, who took the reins of Sergio Perez's car on home soil. The former IndyCar star was handed additional Friday practice sessions as he aims to collect the last couple of missing FIA superlicence points, making up for a curtailed FP1 session in Italy.

Williams man Alex Albon was the only driver not to set a competitive lap, as his team opted to conduct aero testing to aid its 2027 development.

Sports.title: Renault to sell former F1 engine facility in Viry
Sports.content:
Renault has agreed to sell its Viry-Chatillon engine facility to Belgian company Dumarey Group.

According to an official statement, the Dumarey Group, which specialises in technology and development of powertrains and engineering components for mass-produced vehicles, is prepared to take control of the French site.

The acquisition proposal has already been submitted to Alpine Racing. Both parties are now working diligently to analyse the entire organization and its financial aspects, with the goal of determining how to move forward quickly.

The deal will see Dumarey Group acquire Alpine Racing SAS, located in Viry-Chatillon, including "the teams and the tangible and intangible assets required to operate the site".

Located in the southern suburbs of Paris, Viry was the home of Renault's Formula 1 engine programme for several decades and was seen as an important hub for motorsport in France.

But Renault pulled the plug on its in-house engine department at the end of last year in favour of Alpine signing a customer deal with Mercedes, threatening the future of hundreds of employees at Viry.

Alpine is also exiting the World Endurance Championship at the end of the year, having used Viry to maintain and assemble the Mecachrome-built engines that power its A424 LMDhs.

#35 Alpine Endurance Team Alpine A424: Antonio Felix Da Costa, Ferdinand Habsburg, Charles Milesi Foto di: FIA WEC / DPPI

WEC future

The deal could also have implications for Alpine's Hypercar programme, with its factory partner Signatech keen to run the A424 under a different brand in 2027.

Signatech appeared poised to finalise a deal with Chinese brand Geely after last month's Fuji 6 Hours, but the talks between the two firms appear to have broken down.

The deadline for entry into the 2027 season is 25 November; the necessary formal documentation must be finalised by then to secure a spot in the Hypercar class. For weeks, team principal Philippe Sinault has maintained that everything is in place, in terms of engineers, mechanics and all other resources required, to continue the A424 program in the championship next year.

Naturally, organising a new team also entails signing the necessary drivers (noting, for instance, the departure of Antonio Felix da Costa) and confirming those already involved in the programme.

In its statement, the Dumarey Group stressed that it is "seeking to diversify its activities into motorsport", saying the deal "creates opportunities to leverage Renault's Formula 1 engine expertise for racing teams in the future".

Axel Plasse, VP Alpine Tech, said: “This transaction represents a strong and coherent opportunity to secure and further develop the expertise of the Viry-Châtillon site. It opens up new prospects for employees and for the engineering business. This development is a recognition of the site’s longstanding motorsport expertise, particularly in Formula 1.”

Sports.title: Formula 1’s ruined season diminishes Antonelli’s inevitable championship triumph | Comment
Sports.content:
Mercedes and Andrea Kimi Antonelli are making all the usual noises about the championship fight not being over until it’s over.

As well they should: after all, for Antonelli to be crowned this weekend he needs the team’s other driver to finish no higher than ninth. That’s not a result Mercedes are looking for.

All the same, it’s hard to imagine Mercedes doesn’t have a pile of ‘Kimi Antonelli: F1’s youngest world champion’ T-shirts stashed away somewhere.

Barring some incredible turnaround over the coming races, there is an inevitable sense of anti-climax to this year’s championship conclusion. Any realistic hope Antonelli’s rivals had was extinguished long ago. The title will almost certainly be awarded long before the final race, wherever that might be.

Last year three drivers went into the final round of the season with a chance of winning the world championship. But that was a rare treat. More often than not someone wins the title before the last race. The fact that is possible is what makes occasions like last year special.

But this year’s championship fight would not feel special under any circumstances. I have been following F1 for almost 40 years and in that time it has never been harder to appreciate the drivers’ abilities, or be impressed by their efforts.

The hideously overcomplicated, energy-starved 2026 power units disguise the skills of the world’s greatest drivers so effectively it’s hard to imagine how they could do it better. The faster and more demanding the track, the more inadequate the power units are to tackle them.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

F1 and the FIA have tried desperately hard to keep selling the show. But they know they have committed a terrible mis-step which has ruined the championship. The reality of the situation can be gauged by the haste with which they rushed in fixes and prepared to ditch the disastrous new formula after potentially just four seasons – one-third the life of its predecessor.

While F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali reassures everyone that fans are too stupid to understand the shortcomings of the current cars, the reality is rammed home by the depressing accounts of those who have to drive this year’s cars, such as Charles Leclerc.

“In Q3 at Spa I did a very good turn one, but by being a tenth-and-a-half quicker through turn one I lost two-and-a-half tenths on the straight,” explained the Ferrari driver earlier this year. “So in the end I was a tenth slower despite having done a better job through the corner.”

A world driving championship title has no value in a series which punishes drivers for driving well. F1’s hype cannot change that.

Following F1 has always involved a degree of filtering out the variables to understand who is really performing well. Which driver has the best chassis or engine? Who has been affected more by unreliability? I have always found making sense of this part of its appeal.

But in 2026 that has gone from being merely difficult to impenetrable. This is even more so in race situations, where the invisible Overtake Mode tips the balance, ensuring no pass can ever be taken at face value.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

There is little sign the modest tweaks to the 2027 engine regulations will significantly improve the situation. The best-case scenario is most of the grid turns up for IndyCar’s new race at the Circuit de Catalunya, conveniently timed to fall between the Austrian and Belgian grands prix. Surely there will be at least one driver who fancies getting back into a single-seater which doesn’t automatically slow down before reaching a quick corner?

I wish I could say Antonelli’s performance this year, and his likely coronation as F1’s youngest ever champion, has convinced me he is one of the series’ all-time great talents. I certainly see no reason to believe he isn’t.

But I can’t truthfully say I believe he is, nor that I would feel differently whoever won this year’s title. When the contest is this bad, who cares who wins it?

Sports.title: Newey says Honda are “disappointed” with their progress in first year back | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Aston Martin team principal Adrian Newey says their power unit supplier Honda are disappointed with their lack of progress since returning to Formula 1.

Honda has introduced upgrades to its power unit since then. However Aston Martin remains 10th in the championship, only ahead of Cadillac, and Newey believes Honda expected greater gains.

“I think it’s fair to say that Honda have probably been a little bit disappointed with how much progress they have managed to make this year,” said Newey. “But as always, or as is so often the case in that situation, it only strengthens resolve to go forward in the future.

“I think the future is obviously the important bit for both companies. They are very determined. These things don’t change overnight, but they have a lot of good people and a lot of good processes now in place.”

Newey said the situation does not compare directly with his previous experience of working with Honda at Red Bull from 2019.

“At the moment, in all truth, Honda are a little bit behind where Red Bull, as the works team, picked up Honda in ’19. That obviously was four seasons after they first came back in ’15.

“So, this is the first year back in. They are a great company. I have every confidence that they will accelerate quickly and understand the problems of these particular PU regulations.”

Sports.title: Leclerc stays on top in second practice at COTA, narrowly ahead of Antonelli | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc was quickest again in the second practice session for the United States Grand Prix, but once again there was only a narrow margin between the Ferrari driver and his closest rival.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli set the second-quickest time, several minutes after Leclerc produced a 1’35.291 on softs to lead the session. His early progress was disrupted by a loose seat in his Mercedes.

Max Verstappen, who had been second-quickest earlier in the day, fell to third place in the second session, but remained within two-tenths of a second of Leclerc.

The leading trio had almost half a second in hand over everyone else, including their team mates. Lewis Hamilton looked less comfortable in his Ferrari and managed only fourth. George Russell was even further behind his team mate after a snap of oversteer on his quickest run.

Isack Hadjar could only manage the ninth-fastest time, almost a second slower than Verstappen, and was deeply unhappy with his car’s balance. “That’s disgusting,” he exclaimed to race engineer Richard Wood, calling his tyre degradation at high-speed “a joke”.

There was little to separate the McLaren pair, who were kept out of the top six by Liam Lawson, who produced a strong lap for Racing Bulls. Lando Norris appeared to have time in hand after his soft tyre run but not enough to significantly cut his deficit of over a second to Leclerc.

Oliver Bearman put his Haas, in its one-off minty blue livery, inside the top 10 at the team’s home race. Fellow American racers Cadillac, meanwhile, ended a session somewhere other than bottom of the times for a change.

That unwanted distinction fell to Williams, whose drivers struggled with their evil-handling FW48. Alexander Albon failed to set a competitive time for the second session in a row after several off-track excursions, ending up over four seconds off the next-slowest driver. “The car is a mess right now,” said his team mate Carlos Sainz Jnr. “I have no confidence in the rear.”

Sports.title: Leclerc puts upgraded Ferrari on top ahead of Verstappen in first practice | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc led the opening practice session at the Circuit of the Americas with Max Verstappen close behind.

The Red Bull driver was just six hundredths of a second off Leclerc’s best time of 1’36.052. Lando Norris set the third-quickest time ahead of George Russell, meaning four different cars filled the top four places.

Ferrari has introduced a significant upgrade for its SF-26 this weekend. Leclerc ran the new package in full while team mate Lewis Hamilton had the majority of the upgrade. He ended the session sixth-quickest behind Andrea Kimi Antonelli.

The SF-26s looked in good shape earlier in the session when they ran the medium compound tyres. Leclerc led the early times by around four-tenths of a second. However Red Bull and Mercedes preferred to use the hard tyres early on.

Several drivers lost their quickest lap times due to track limits infringements, including Isack Hadjar. He ended the session 14th-quickest.

That helped Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto take the eighth-quickest time. His team mate Nico Hulkenberg suffered a technical problem and brought his session to an early end.

The Racing Bulls drivers completed the top 10 led by Arvid Lindblad. However the rookie will take a grid penalty in the grand prix for exceeding his maximum allocation of power unit components.

The Circuit of the Americas’ notorious bumps appear to be no less of a problem than usual this year. The track has been patched in several places in an attempt to alleviate the worst of the bumps.

Sports.title: Palou gets home race as IndyCar adds new Spanish round to 2027 calendar | IndyCar
Sports.content:
Five-times IndyCar champion Alex Palou will race in his home country next year as the series has added a round in Spain.

IndyCar will race outside North America for the first time in over a decade when it visits the Circuit de Catalunya in July.

“I’m so excited to be part of IndyCar’s first race in Barcelona,” said Palou, who was born in the nearby town of Sant Antoni de Vilamajor. “It is an amazing opportunity, and it means so much to me to have a race at home in Barcelona, it’s hard to put into words.”

The permanent circuit will not hold a Formula 1 race next year for the first time since it was built in 1991. It will hold its first IndyCar race on July 18th, the Sunday between F1’s races at the Red Bull Ring in Austria and Spa-Francorchamps in Belgium.

F1 moved the Spanish Grand Prix to the new Madring this year. The Circuit de Catalunya is due to return on the 2028 F1 calendar, hosting the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix.

Mark Miles, president and CEO of Penske Entertainment Corporation which owns IndyCar, said the announcement is “a monumental day for our sport.”

“We are pleased to be able to take our ultra-competitive brand of wheel-to-wheel racing to Europe and thrilled that we can showcase IndyCar in Alex Palou’s home town. We have seen Alex’s remarkable skill and talent for several years and know his fans in Spain have been clamouring to watch him race in person.”

Palou has become the dominant force in IndyCar racing since making his debut in the series six years ago. Following one season at Dale Coyne, he moved to the top Ganassi outfit the following year and has won five of the last six championships for them.

Sports.title: Rafael Espinoza Gets Ricardo Blandon After Parra Rejected
Sports.content:
Rafael Espinoza has a replacement opponent for October 31 in Riyadh, with the WBO approving No. 15 contender Ricardo Blandon after the local commission refused to authorize Lorenzo Parra’s participation.

The change comes just one week before the event, leaving Blandon little time to prepare for a featherweight title opportunity against the unbeaten champion.

In an official advisory shared by WBO president Gustavo Olivieri, the organization confirmed that Canelo Promotions informed it of the Middle East Professional Boxing Commission’s decision regarding Parra. The notice attributed that refusal to the commission’s rules, regulations, and policies.

The advisory does not identify the specific reason Parra was rejected. It offers no basis for attributing his removal to a medical issue, failed test, or any other particular cause.

Canelo Promotions subsequently requested approval for Blandon, whose No. 15 position places him at the bottom of the WBO’s ranked contenders.

The organization cited the short notice, limited time to find a qualified replacement and the interests of those involved in the event when explaining its approval. Blandon must still satisfy all applicable medical and regulatory requirements.

That keeps Espinoza’s planned defense alive, although finding an eligible challenger and producing a competitive title fight are separate questions. A ranking gets Blandon through the sanctioning body’s door. It does not give him additional preparation time.

Espinoza also has to adjust to a different opponent during the final week. His camp has been preparing for Parra, and the replacement forces a late change to whatever tactical work was already completed.

For Blandon, the opportunity comes with an obvious cost: he is accepting a world championship fight under circumstances that give him little room for a full camp.

The WBO has explained its decision to approve the substitute. The unanswered question is what specifically prevented Parra from competing. Until the commission or those involved provide that explanation, the confirmed news is limited to his removal and Blandon’s conditional approval.

Sports.title: Naoya Inoue And Bam Rodriguez Near March Deal
Sports.content:
Update: Naoya Inoue’s agent, John Lewis, tells The Ring’s Mike Coppinger that he is working with Eddie Hearn and Frank Smith to finalize a deal for Inoue to fight Jesse “Bam” Rodriguez in March in Tokyo.

The fight is not yet finalized, but the update indicates that Inoue is pursuing the matchup following the scheduling disagreement discussed below.

Robert Garcia Scrambles To Save Naoya Inoue Fight

Robert Garcia is suddenly scrambling to get Jesse “Bam” Rodriguez into the ring with Naoya Inoue. Not long ago, the trainer talked about making the Japanese superstar hold off until April or May 2027. Now he wants ink on paper immediately because he realized the chance might slip away completely.

Garcia wanted everything on his terms. The catch is that Inoue runs his own schedule. Tell an elite champion with featherweight plans to sit around, and he will just pack up and go.

“Send the fking contract,” Garcia told BoxingScene, suddenly daring Inoue’s side to lock down a March date.

That urgency tells the whole story. Garcia previously wanted another 118-pound tune-up first. By mid-October, he tried shrinking that timeline, telling The Ring that Bam could jump into the ring in December, then turn right around for Inoue in March.

Everyone is wondering if that scramble happened too late.

Giving Bam another look at bantamweight made sense in theory. Jumping up to meet Inoue is a massive leap, so wanting extra prep time makes total sense. Still, that plan only worked if Inoue decided to play along, and the Japanese star already hinted he had plenty of other targets.

Garcia clearly misjudged his leverage. Inoue showed he has zero problem walking away, flipping the entire script. It stopped being about what Bam preferred, turning into a fight to keep the chance alive at all.

Demanding a contract flips the pressure into the public eye. Garcia can claim Bam is ready right now, yet that does not wipe away months of trying to stall for a later date.

Nobody knows if Inoue shut the door for good. Still, the sheer threat of him moving up division ranks gave Robert every reason to panic.

Bam might watch the biggest payday of his life vanish without throwing a single punch. Garcia’s sudden shouting just sounds like a corner realizing their dream matchup will not wait on their calendar.

Sports.title: Christian Mbilli May Not Need His Best Against Canelo
Sports.content:
Christian Mbilli could walk away with a victory over Canelo Alvarez without needing the fight of his life next Saturday, October 31, in Saudi Arabia. His relentless pace and trademark volume might easily suffice against a 36-year-old fighter whose offensive engine visibly sputters when pressed to maintain high-gear work.

Canelo clearly talks like the WBC super middleweight champion needs a miracle.

“He’s going to come 100% because he’s going to need it,” Canelo insisted to DAZN Boxing.

That mindset clings to the idea that defeating him demands career-best perfection. His one-sided loss to Terence Crawford last September completely shattered that myth. Crawford used nothing more than crisp footwork, sharp feints, and an active jab to leave Canelo completely flat-footed, snatching the undisputed 168-pound crown with tactical clarity.

Crawford never looked pushed to the brink. He dictated terms using distance, precision combinations, and smart angles, while Canelo simply followed him around the ring unable to pull the trigger with any consistency.

Mbilli presents a very different stylistic problem. He will naturally offer Canelo cleaner counterpunching lanes, yet he will relentlessly drag the Mexican star into deep water by forcing an uncomfortable pace.

Whenever Canelo turtles behind his high guard, Mbilli will let his hands go. Even if those punches crash into elbows and gloves, judges reward activity, and Canelo will have to respond. Landing an occasional explosive counter cannot bail out long stretches of ring hibernation.

Naturally, Canelo still carries dynamite timing and wicked rib-cracking hooks. Careless, head-down rushes could give the decorated veteran the exact highlight-reel openings he craves. Blind aggression rarely secures a victory against elite counterpunchers.

Nevertheless, Mbilli has no obligation to pitch a flawless twelve-round masterpiece. He simply needs to keep the pressure going, deny Canelo the rest breaks he desperately seeks, and make the aging star sweat for every single exchange.

Canelo might be living on past reputation if he thinks Mbilli must deliver a superhuman performance to win. The real question is whether Canelo can muster enough gas in the tank to survive Mbilli on a routine, rock-solid night.

Sports.title: Andy Ruiz vs Dave Allen Targeted For Spring
Sports.content:
Andy Ruiz Jr. and Dave Allen could meet in Sheffield in March or April 2027, with Allen revealing that Matchroom’s Frank Smith has told him the company is targeting that window for the heavyweight fight.

The Fight Wire reports Allen also indicated that he would likely retire afterward. The fight has not been officially announced, and the proposed dates remain a target.

Ruiz (35-3-1, 22 KOs) would enter the bout coming off a defeat against Damian Knyba in September. His last victory came against Luis Ortiz in September 2022, with a draw against Jarrell Miller and another lengthy absence between that win and the Knyba loss.

That represents a dismal drop for a man who battered Anthony Joshua to win the unified heavyweight crown in 2019. Ruiz held all the gold, dominated global sports headlines, and blew the chance to become a generational heavyweight star. He surrendered the titles in the rematch and spent the next seven years fighting just four times.

Allen keeps fighting to stay relevant and earn a living, but nobody expected him to rule the division. He has spent much of his career taking punishment from better heavyweights. Ruiz reached the top, won three world titles, and then wasted the opportunity.

A win over Allen gets Ruiz back in the win column, but beating a domestic trialhorse proves nothing about his ability to mix with elite heavyweights. An upset loss drops him off the boxing map entirely.

Take Allen’s retirement talk with a grain of salt. Sharing the ring with Ruiz hands him a big-name scalp to target along with a solid payday. Even in defeat, a decent showing will keep promoters dialing his number.

Expect Allen to stick around if matchmakers keep waving checks in his face. Giving a former unified champion a real scrap will open doors for future paydays, not push him into retirement.

Right now, the story is Matchroom penciling in that spring date in Sheffield. Calling it a farewell bout looks like wishful thinking, especially since another decent payday will easily tempt him back into the ring.

Sports.title: WBO Set To Strip Denzel Bentley Of Title
Sports.content:
Denzel Bentley is set to lose his WBO middleweight title after allowing the deadline to commit to mandatory challenger Yoenli Hernández to pass, leaving his November 7 fight against Shane Mosley Jr. as his next bout.

WBO president Gustavo Olivieri told EverythingBoxing’s Darshan Desai that the organization received no formal communication from Bentley’s team confirming he would go ahead with the Hernández defense within the allotted 24 hours. According to Desai, the WBO will now strip him.

Bentley has already signed to face Mosley Jr. in his Zuffa Boxing debut. That looks like a more winnable fight than defending against Hernández, although Bentley would enter it without the championship he had hoped to keep.

Hernández (11-0, 9 KOs) would be a dangerous fight for Bentley, with the power to knock him out. A loss like that would be a rough way to begin his time with Zuffa.

Bentley would have a chance against Hernández, but this would be a dangerous defense against a challenger who has been finishing most of his opponents. From a career standpoint, accepting the loss of his belt and going ahead with Mosley Jr. is understandable. He keeps his scheduled fight and avoids the immediate possibility of a punishing defeat.

The WBO cannot justify letting him keep the belt while pursuing a side attraction. Hernandez did the work to earn his mandatory ranking, and he shouldn’t be put on hold just because Bentley decided to take a different path.

Vito Mielnicki Jr. could step into the opposite corner against Hernandez for the vacant belt. Mielnicki holds the number two spot in the WBO ratings just behind the Cuban, positioning the American contender as the frontrunner if he accepts an invitation to fight for the strap. Sanctioning body officials have not made an official announcement regarding the pairing.

Bentley can still get off to a good start with Zuffa by beating Mosley, but he’ll be giving up his world title to take the easier fight.

Hernández would then get his shot at the vacant belt against someone prepared to face him.

Sports.title: Devin Haney Talks DAZN Benefits As Inactivity Continues
Sports.content:
Devin Haney credits DAZN with offering the opponents he needs to build his legacy. After 11 months outside the ring, however, he still needs a fight date to turn that explanation into something fans can judge.

Haney has not fought since beating Brian Norman Jr. last November. His DAZN agreement gives him a broadcasting home, but the next opponent and an official event announcement remain the real test of its value.

“All the opponents are on DAZN. Zuffa Boxing, they offered me a ton of money. I’m thankful for that,” Haney told Chris Mannix on DAZN. “I’m thankful for them to reach out to my team, but all the opponents are on DAZN. It’s not just about money for me. It’s about me being the best and me putting on the best fights.”

That is a reasonable explanation for choosing a platform. It is also a promise that requires action. Having potential opponents under the same broadcasting umbrella does not put their names on Haney’s record.

“I’m a legacy fighter. I love the money. The money is massive at DAZN as well. It’s great, but I need to have the opponents too to showcase my skills.”

Haney is getting paid well by his own account. The missing part is the opportunity to showcase those skills. Interviews can explain his intentions, but they cannot replace rounds, title defenses, or victories.

A unification with Liam Paro has reportedly been agreed, although an official announcement is still pending. Getting that fight scheduled would give Haney something concrete to support his comments. Until then, it remains another proposed contest following a lengthy absence.

The inactivity does not establish that Haney alone caused the delays. Negotiations require cooperation. Still, the time comes out of his career regardless of who holds up an agreement.

Prime years pass quickly. Haney can prefer DAZN and have sound reasons for doing so, but his legacy benefits when he fights. Right now, he is explaining what the platform can offer while fans wait to see it delivered.

Sports.title: Rocky Marciano vs Mike Tyson: Speed Against Stamina
Sports.content:
Rocky Marciano against Mike Tyson would match relentless pressure against explosive speed. Both heavyweight champions could end a fight with one punch, but the deciding factor might be whether Marciano could survive Tyson’s early attacks and force him into a longer fight.

The comparison should involve both men at their best. Tyson’s late-career defeats tell us little about how the fighter who demolished Michael Spinks would have handled Marciano.

Tyson would have the advantages in hand speed and weight. Although similar in height, he generally fought substantially heavier than Marciano. His quick combinations to the body and head would present an immediate threat to a fighter who needed to get close to do his best work.

Marciano retired at 49-0 with 43 knockouts and six successful heavyweight title defenses. His unbeaten record did not mean he avoided trouble. Jersey Joe Walcott dropped him in the opening round and led on the scorecards before Marciano knocked him out in the 13th.

Against Ezzard Charles in their rematch, Marciano fought through a severe nose injury to secure an eighth-round knockout. Those victories demonstrated his ability to remain dangerous when a fight was going against him.

Tyson’s first championship reign showed how quickly he could take control. He stopped Trevor Berbick in two rounds to win the WBC title and later knocked out Pinklon Thomas, Tyrell Biggs, Larry Holmes, Tony Tubbs and Spinks. James “Bonecrusher” Smith and Tony Tucker took him the distance, with Tyson winning both fights on points.

Against Marciano, Tyson’s uppercuts would be particularly dangerous. Rocky often advanced from a low crouch, bringing him into range of short punches as he worked his way inside. Tyson could also attack the body before bringing his hooks upstairs.

Marciano’s answer would be to keep punching and deny Tyson comfortable breaks. He attacked the chest, shoulders, and arms when an opponent’s head was protected. Those punches could contribute to wearing Tyson down, although they would leave Marciano close enough to be countered.

Tyson’s peek-a-boo style was more than a stationary high guard. At his best, he used head movement and quick changes of angle to create openings. Marciano would have to deal with that movement before he could establish his own attack.

A longer fight would give Marciano more opportunities. His conditioning and sustained output were major strengths, particularly over 15 rounds. If he could survive the early combinations and continue forcing Tyson to work, his chances would improve.

That does not make an early Tyson knockout inevitable or a late Marciano victory automatic. Marciano could be dropped, while Tyson could win over the distance, as his victories over Smith and Tucker demonstrated.

Tyson would have the stronger chance of an early stoppage because of his speed, combinations, and greater size. Marciano’s best route would be to withstand that opening assault and turn the contest into a prolonged, punishing fight.

Would Tyson’s speed settle it early, or could Marciano survive and wear him down?

Ghana News.title: Ellen White Foundation brings free breast cancer screening to Bono East police women
Ghana News.content:
In a heartwarming display of commitment to women's health, the Ellen White Sustainable Foundation, in partnership with the Awat Foundation and the Police Ladies Association, has provided free breast cancer screening to nearly 100 female police officers across the Bono East Region.

The screening exercise, held at the Techiman Divisional Police Command, formed part of efforts to promote early detection and awareness of breast cancer among women in uniform.

The programme was held under the theme: "Investing in Women's Health, Investing in Stronger Communities."

Mrs. Ellen White Opoku, founder of the Ellen White Sustainable Foundation and a 2023 Joy Impact Makers Award recipient, said the initiative was born out of the need to reach officers who cannot easily access health facilities due to their busy schedules.

"This exercise is to help bring the screening to the doorstep of the police, who are unable to attend to health facilities for the same due to their busy work schedules," she noted.

Police Ladies Association Weighs In

ASP Beatrice Okrah, Crime Officer for the Jema District Police Command and a regional executive member of the Police Ladies Association, commended the organizers and encouraged women to prioritize their health.

She said the time had come for women to own up and get themselves screened to know their statuses and be treated when diagnosed with the condition.

"The time has come for women to own up and get themselves screened to know their statuses and be treated when diagnosed with the condition," she stated.

ASP Okrah added that the awareness talk had been helpful in creating awareness about what the condition is, equipping participants with knowledge to share with colleagues and family members.

"The talk has been helpful in creating awareness about what the condition is," she noted.

Service to Support Officers Diagnosed

In a reassuring message to personnel, ASP Okrah disclosed that officers found to have the cancer will be taken care of by the Police Service.

She explained that the welfare of officers remains a priority, and those diagnosed through the screening will receive the necessary support and care from the Service.

A Community Investment

The event reflects a growing push to make healthcare accessible to women in security services, who often sacrifice personal wellness for public duty. By investing in the health of these officers, organizers say the ripple effect will be felt across entire communities.

The Ellen White Sustainable Foundation has indicated its commitment to sustaining such initiatives, with plans to reach more districts in the Bono East Region and beyond.

Ghana News.title: Ghana’s U-15 Boys thrash Uzbekistan 4-1 as Abdul Aziz Issah and Jerry Owusu hit brace each
Ghana News.content:
The National U-15 Boys team made a flying start to the FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival with an emphatic 4-1 victory over Uzbekistan in their opening Group W match on Saturday.

Abdul Aziz Issah and Jerry Owusu were the heroes for Ghana, scoring a brace each to secure all three points in Azerbaijan.

Ghana dominated proceedings from the blast of the whistle, showing flair, composure and attacking intent against their Asian opponents.

Aziz Issah opened the scoring before doubling Ghana's advantage, while Jerry Owusu added two more goals to put the game beyond the reach of Uzbekistan, who managed a consolation strike late in the game.

The win gives Ghana a strong start in Group W, which also includes Myanmar, Guam, Bahamas and Kazakhstan.

Ghana will next face Myanmar and Guam on Sunday, before wrapping up the group phase against Bahamas and Kazakhstan on Monday.

The FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival, part of FIFA's Talent Development Scheme, is aimed at giving every talent a chance to showcase their skills on the world stage.
