World.content:
Jallah had pleaded not guilty to all charges, while his defense challenged the prosecution’s evidence, citing alleged inconsistencies in the complainant’s account and limitations in the medical and forensic findings.

— Acquits NSA Staff of Gang Rape; Defense Announces Supreme Court Appeal

MONROVIA, Liberia — Criminal Court “E” at the Temple of Justice has found 63-year-old Peter Bon Jallah, a staff member of the National Security Agency (NSA), guilty of statutory rape and kidnapping but not guilty of gang rape in a case involving a 16-year-old boy.

By Victoria Wesseh



The verdict was handed down Friday, October 23, 2026, by Assigned Circuit Judge Wesseh Alphonso Wesseh Sr., following final arguments by the prosecution and defense on Thursday.

Following the verdict, Judge Wesseh ordered Jallah’s remand at Monrovia Central Prison. However, the court had not announced the sentence at the time of reporting.

Defense lawyer Cllr. Wilfred Sayeh has announced plans to appeal the ruling to the Supreme Court of Liberia, setting the stage for another legal battle over the verdict.

The court acquitted Jallah of gang rape. The two other individuals allegedly involved in the incident on Camp Johnson Road were not presented during the trial.

Prosecution Presented 12 Witnesses

During the trial, prosecutors presented 12 witnesses, including the complainant, police investigators, medical personnel, and Rwandan forensic examiner Pascal Bavugirije.

The prosecution also relied on DNA findings that linked Jallah’s DNA profile to biological material recovered from four clothing exhibits.

However, the forensic examiner reportedly testified that the findings could not establish when or how the biological material was deposited.

Jallah had pleaded not guilty to all charges, while his defense challenged the prosecution’s evidence, citing alleged inconsistencies in the complainant’s account and limitations in the medical and forensic findings.

Defense Challenges Evidence, Plans Appeal

During Thursday’s final arguments, prosecution lawyer Cllr. Calvin H. Momolu urged the court to convict Jallah, arguing that the evidence presented during the trial supported a guilty verdict.

Defense lawyer Cllr. Sayeh countered that the prosecution had failed to establish the allegations beyond a reasonable doubt. The defense questioned the interpretation of medical and forensic findings, as well as aspects of the police investigation.

The competing arguments centered on witness testimony, medical findings, forensic evidence, and whether the prosecution had sufficiently established the elements of the charged offenses.

With the guilty verdict on two charges and the defense’s announced intention to appeal, the case is expected to proceed to the Supreme Court, where Jallah’s lawyers will seek a review of the lower court’s decision.

World.title: Liberia Poised to Surpass 2026 Intellectual Property Registration Target
World.content:
The Government of Liberia, through the Liberia Intellectual Property Office (LIPO), has announced that it is on track to surpass its annual intellectual property registration target after recording 526 registrations by the end of the third quarter of 2026.

Speaking at the Ministry of Information’s regular press briefing on Thursday, LIPO Director General Hon. Garmai Koboi noted that the Office had achieved 95.6 percent of its annual target of 550 registrations — expressing confidence that the current pace of registrations would push the year-end figure beyond the projected benchmark.

According to Hon. Koboi, trademarks accounted for the overwhelming majority of registrations, with 483 recorded during the period, followed by 40 copyright registrations and three industrial designs.

Of the total, Hon. Koboi further disclosed that 174 of the registrations were by Liberian-owned businesses and foreign nationals with established business operations in the country.



“With 526 applications recorded against an annual target of 550, we have achieved 95.6 percent of our FY2026 intellectual property registration target, leaving an outstanding balance of just 24 applications, representing 4.4 percent of the annual target,” Hon. Koboi added. “This performance reflects the work we are doing to strengthen intellectual property awareness and engagement among businesses, entrepreneurs, and other key stakeholders through targeted outreach, capacity-building initiatives, and stakeholder collaboration.”

According to Hon. Koboi, the uptake in registration is down to LIPO’s ongoing efforts to make intellectual property services more accessible, particularly to entrepreneurs, creators, and small businesses seeking to protect and commercialize their innovations, brands, and creative works.

“These achievements reflect the progress we are making toward building a stronger and more inclusive intellectual property ecosystem in Liberia,” the Director General said. “By supporting enterprise development, promoting creativity and innovation, strengthening intellectual property protection, and expanding access to IP services for SMEs and creators, we are seeing a lot of uptake in our registration and use of the IP system.”

Highlighting LIPO’s other achievements, Hon. Koboi pointed to the implementation of the Business and Intellectual Property Management Clinic (BIPMC), undertaken in partnership with the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) through its GROW-2 Project.

The initiative, according to LIPO and UNIDO, reached 142 entrepreneurs across Lofa, Bong, Nimba and Margibi counties, providing practical training, business advisory support and technical guidance on intellectual property identification, registration and management.

At the closure of the clinic, 90 intellectual property applications were filed for the first time by enterprises in these counties, of which 39 resulted in the issuance of intellectual property registration certificates to applicants who satisfied the legal and regulatory requirements under the Liberia Intellectual Property Act of 2016.

The project, according to Hon. Koboi, forms part of a broader national effort by the Government to integrate intellectual property protection into business development, particularly in agriculture, food processing, fashion, manufacturing and other sectors where entrepreneurs increasingly rely on brands, creative designs and product differentiation to compete in the marketplace.

Speaking also, Hon. Koboi noted that LIPO, in collaboration with the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), has expanded the 2nd edition of the Intellectual Property Management Clinic (IPMC) to 40 SMEs in four counties, providing specialized one-on-one mentorship support to 40 small and medium-sized enterprises across Montserrado, Nimba, Bong and Lofa counties.

The initiative provides training and technical advisory support to participating businesses in order to help them strengthen their intellectual property management practices, minimize infringement risks and identify opportunities for business growth and market expansion.

“These projects support the government’s commitment under the ARREST Agenda to its 2029 vision of developing a robust intellectual property ecosystem, as they expand access to intellectual property protection services for businesses and creators while equipping them with the knowledge and practical guidance needed to understand, protect, and effectively manage their intellectual property assets,” Hon. Koboi noted.

Meanwhile, Hon. Koboi has noted that one of the greatest achievements for the office this year has been the successful completion of the national stakeholder validation of Liberia’s National Intellectual Property Policy and Strategy (NIPPS), describing the exercise as an important step toward establishing a coordinated framework for intellectual property development.

The document is intended to strengthen coordination among public institutions and other stakeholders while positioning intellectual property as a tool for innovation, enterprise development, creativity and economic diversification.

The completion of the validation exercise represents a key milestone in Liberia’s efforts to establish a more structured national approach to intellectual property development, although further steps will be required before the framework becomes fully operational.

The LIPO Director General has also disclosed that the institution is preparing to digitize its intellectual property registration services through the Intellectual Property Administration System (IPAS), with technical assistance from WIPO. The planned introduction of the system is expected to modernize the administration of intellectual property applications, streamline registration procedures, and improve the efficiency of service delivery.

In a separate development, the LIPO Director General has appealed to the Liberian Senate to give attention to outstanding international instruments submitted by the President for ratification, emphasizing their potential importance to the country’s agriculture, tourism and creative sectors.

Hon. Koboi noted that the ratification of relevant instruments could strengthen Liberia’s ability to benefit from international intellectual property protection frameworks, particularly in areas involving geographical indications and the protection of products associated with specific geographical origins.

“We also want to appeal to the Senate to look at all outstanding instruments submitted by the President for ratification,” Hon. Koboi noted. “These instruments are very cardinal to our agriculture sector, for example, looking at our potential geographical indications, including our Liberian coffee, the tourism sector, our local government and the creative industries.”

Geographical indications are intellectual property protections used to identify products whose qualities, reputation or other characteristics are linked to a particular geographical origin.

World.title: Liberia’s Supreme Court Weighs Whether Parliament Defied Its Order in Expelling Outspoken Lawmaker
World.content:
MONROVIA, Liberia — Liberia’s Supreme Court on Thursday reserved judgment in a case that could determine whether the country’s House of Representatives defied a court order when it expelled one of its most outspoken members, Yekeh Kolubah, in April.

By Victoria G. Wesseh

The case turns on a narrow but consequential question: was the House leadership legally served with a Supreme Court order instructing it to halt proceedings against Kolubah before it voted to remove him? If it was, the vote may have been taken in breach of a binding judicial directive. If not, the House may have been free to act.



How the Dispute Began

Kolubah represented District 10 of Montserrado County, which includes the capital, Monrovia, and was long one of the Legislature’s most combative voices. The disciplinary case against him followed a controversial statement he made about the Makona River boundary dispute, one that many considered provocative, even offensive.

Kolubah was formally notified on April 9, 2026, to appear before the House Committee on Rules, Order and Administration on April 13. He and his lawyers walked out of a later committee hearing after it refused to grant them an additional five days and access to evidence.

His lawyers then asked the Supreme Court for a writ of prohibition, an order used to stop a body from exceeding its authority. Associate Justice Yussif D. Kaba granted the petition on April 16, summoning House leaders to a conference on April 20 and ordering them to stay all further proceedings pending its outcome. The directive was addressed to Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon, Deputy Speaker Thomas Fallah, the House Chief Clerk, the Sergeant-at-Arms and everyone acting under their authority.

The next day, the House went ahead. Kolubah was expelled by the full House on Friday, April 17, after a resolution was signed by 49 of the chamber’s 73 members, the two-thirds majority the Constitution requires. The resolution said he was removed for acts and utterances deemed unpatriotic and detrimental to the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

The Service Dispute

The House says it was never properly served. Its lawyers cited Rule 26.5 of the House rules, which names the Sergeant-at-Arms as the only officer authorised to receive court orders on behalf of the House. Court records show the Supreme Court Marshal instead served the documents on a receptionist and a computer operator attached to the offices of the Speaker and the Chief Clerk.

That argument has already succeeded once. In May 2026, Justice Kaba dismissed Kolubah’s follow-up complaint, known as a bill of information, for improper service, reportedly finding that the House had not been properly served with the writ and stay order. Kolubah appealed to the full five-member bench, which heard arguments on Thursday.

Jonathan Massaquoi, who leads Kolubah’s legal team, told the justices that the validity of service should be judged by Liberia’s Civil Procedure Law, not by the House’s internal rules for handling correspondence.

He cited Section 3.38(9), which states: “Personal service upon a subdivision of the government subject to suit or upon a municipal corporation shall be made by reading and delivering the summons to the chief executive thereof.”

On that basis, the petitioners argued that delivering the order to the office of the Speaker, the House’s presiding officer, was sufficient. A court officer identified as Joshua B. delivered the document there, they said, and a receptionist acknowledged receipt and signed for a copy.

Whether the provision covers the House at all is an open question. It refers specifically to “a subdivision of the government subject to suit” or “a municipal corporation,” and the Court must decide whether a branch of the national Legislature falls into either category.

Did the House Defy the Court?

The justices must weigh the wording of the order, the Marshal’s report of service, the receptionist’s acknowledgment and the legal standing of the office that received it.

Even a clear answer on service may not end the dispute. If the Court upholds the dismissal, it will not necessarily have examined or endorsed the disciplinary proceedings; and a win for Kolubah on service would not automatically prove the expulsion unconstitutional.

Other questions hang over the vote itself. A Bomi County lawmaker has denied backing the expulsion, raising questions about whether the House reached the legally required majority. A media adviser to Speaker Koon also told FrontPage Africa the expulsion took place on April 22, not April 17, before abruptly ending the conversation. A later date could matter, because it would fall after the scheduled court conference.

The case has become a test of the balance between Liberia’s branches of government. Critics have likened it to the recent standoff over former Speaker Fonati Koffa, which tested the limits of legislative authority. Prominent lawyer Tiawan Saye Gongloe has said the Court’s options include voiding the expulsion, holding House leaders in contempt, or ordering Kolubah’s reinstatement pending a hearing that satisfies due process.

The Court did not say when it would rule.

World.title: Liberia: PLP Elevates Zarwolo to Two Top Posts as Party Eyes New Political Framework With Bility’s CMC
World.content:
MONROVIA, Liberia — The People’s Liberation Party (PLP) has appointed education policy expert Tonzeah N. Zarwolo to two senior leadership positions, a move that could position him to help shape the party’s policy direction as it explores political collaboration with Musa Hassan Bility’s Citizens Movement for Change (CMC).

Zarwolo, a former PLP National Youth Chairman, has been named National Vice Chairman for Political Affairs and Acting National Secretary General, according to two appointment letters dated October 22, 2026.

The appointments come as the PLP engages in discussions with Bility’s CMC about a possible political collaboration intended to offer an alternative to the country’s established political blocs, the Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC) and the ruling Unity Party (UP).

While neither appointment letter explicitly links Zarwolo’s elevation to the discussions, his combination of political, administrative and education policy experience could make him a significant figure in developing the principles and policy priorities of any proposed arrangement.

A Possible Role in Policy Development

Zarwolo’s professional background could be particularly relevant if the proposed collaboration moves beyond political consultations toward developing a formal policy document.

An education policy expert, he has worked on national education projects involving the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and CODE Canada. He is also a university lecturer.

That experience could provide a foundation for contributing to discussions on education reform, public-sector performance, institutional accountability and national development priorities.

Zarwolo’s appointment as National Vice Chairman for Political Affairs could place him in a position to coordinate discussions on behalf of the PLP, while his role as Acting National Secretary General could give him a hand in documenting decisions and coordinating the party’s internal processes.

However, there is no confirmation in the appointment letters that he has been assigned to lead or draft a policy document for the proposed collaboration.

The Search for a Different Political Arrangement

The PLP’s reported discussions with Bility’s CMC come amid wider efforts by Liberian opposition parties to determine how they might cooperate ahead of the 2029 general and presidential elections.

In September, the CMC withdrew from a proposed opposition coalition process convened by former President George Weah, arguing that the draft arrangement did not adequately reflect its objectives. The party has emphasized the need for cooperation built around a clear reform agenda rather than political unity alone.

That position underscores a central question for any alternative political framework: whether participating parties can agree not only on political cooperation but also on a defined program for governing and addressing Liberia’s challenges.

For the PLP and CMC, a formal arrangement could require decisions on policy priorities, accountability mechanisms, internal decision-making, the roles of participating parties and how commitments would be communicated to the public.

Zarwolo’s policy background could be relevant to that process, particularly if the parties seek to develop proposals grounded in sectoral experience and implementable public policy rather than a general declaration of political unity.

Zarwolo Accepts Both Appointments

Zarwolo thanked the Political Leader, Tapple Doe, Bernard Blue Benson, National Chairman, David Woods Beyan Sr. National Vice Chair for Administration and the wider PLP membership for the confidence placed in him.

“I hereby formally accept these appointments and assure the Party of my unwavering commitment to discharging my responsibilities with diligence and loyalty,” he said.

He pledged to work with the party’s leadership and fellow partisans to advance its collective vision and strengthen its ideals.

World.title: Liberia: Commerce Minister Designate Plan Meets a Market That Isn’t Waiting
World.content:
MONROVIA — Stephen M. Yekeson Jr. told senators Wednesday that he wants to be “judged by what is delivered.” His confirmation statement gives the Senate one promise it can test within 100 days, and many more it cannot.

By Rodney D Sieh

Appearing before the Senate Committee on Commerce and Industry, the acting Commerce and Industry Minister set out a vision to have Liberia “produce more of what Liberia consumes” by 2029. He pledged to protect consumers, enforce Liberian-only business sectors and cut the cost of moving goods “between the ship and the shop.”



His firmest commitment: within 100 days, the ministry will publish weekly prices for rice, fuel and cement in all 15 counties. Beyond that, the statement leans on verbs such as “work with,” “engage” and “address,” with few numbers, dates or budgets attached. Set against the problems now pressing on traders and households, the distance between promise and mechanism is where the scrutiny belongs.

A stronger dollar that isn’t reaching the market

Yekeson’s most striking admission was that prices have kept rising “in spite of a stronger Liberian Dollar.” The Liberian dollar was Africa’s best-performing currency in September, closing the month at about L$172 to US$1.

Small traders in Monrovia say the gains are not passed on. They report that some wholesalers still price stock at about L$190 to the dollar while the market rate sits near L$170, a gap of nearly 12 percent.

On October 6, Yekeson announced a five-point plan under which the ministry would work with the Central Bank to require supermarkets, wholesalers and retailers to post the bank’s daily exchange rate. That measure does not appear in his Senate statement. Instead, he cites a “reengineered” Price Analysis Department and a better-resourced Inspectorate. Whether the posting rule is still coming, and when, is a question the committee should put to him.

Fuel: a review, but no formula

Fuel is where the Senate already has its own findings. A Senate probe found that diesel rose from L$840 to L$1,235 a gallon between October 2024 and September 2026, a 47 percent increase. Gasoline climbed from L$775 to L$985 over the same period. The probe also found that Bea Mountain paid nothing on 16.4 million gallons of diesel.

The senator leading that inquiry proposed that the Liberia Petroleum Refining Company (LPRC) publish its full pricing formula every week. Yekeson’s statement moves in that direction but stops short. He promises to review pricing with the LPRC, and says regulated prices should be “transparent, rule-based and regularly reviewed,” reflecting verified import costs, duties, transport and a reasonable margin.

He does not commit to publishing that formula. His weekly price list would show what motorists pay at the pump, not how the figure was reached. He also names the LPRC, a petroleum body, as his partner in reviewing rice and cement pricing, a pairing he did not explain.

Rice: a global squeeze is coming

The next test may arrive before his 100 days are up. World rice prices are up about 67 percent on the year and hit a 26-month high in early October.

At home, the price of the staple was last fixed in March. After an emergency meeting with six major importers, the ministry announced that a 25kg bag would stay at US$14.00 wholesale and US$14.50 retail.

With import costs climbing, importers are likely to push for an increase. Yekeson’s formula of verified costs plus a reasonable margin may justify one. His weekly price list will then put any rise in public view, county by county. The Senate should ask him now whether US$14.50 can hold, and on what basis it would change.

An Inspectorate that barely registers

Yekeson promises inspectors will pursue “hoarding, collusion, false invoicing and short measures.” The ministry’s own figures suggest little enforcement capacity today.

At a budget hearing last week, he reported that the ministry had collected about US$4.12 million by September 30. Of that, inspectorate fees and fines brought in roughly US$48,700, about 1 percent. He acknowledged those collections could improve.

The pledge is also not new. In 2024, his predecessor Amin Modad rolled out a rebranded Inspectorate Division to keep vendors from selling rice above the government ceiling. The committee should ask how many inspectors the ministry has, how many cases it opened this year, and what money comes with “resourcing” them.

Small business: right diagnosis, no deadlines

On Liberian enterprise, Yekeson’s diagnosis matches what traders report. He has said that women make up 75 percent of traders reporting financial constraints.

His answers are sensible but undated:

* Procurement set-aside. The law already reserves a quarter of qualifying public procurement for Liberian-owned small businesses. He promises to publish compliance “agency by agency,” but gives no date.

* Credit. A credit guarantee programme will come “only with the requisite approvals and clear fiscal safeguards,” a signal that no money is yet set aside.

* Late payment. He will “engage” concessionaires and “report progress,” with no target for how quickly government and companies must pay.

* Business registration. Service centres exist in seven counties, with nationwide expansion planned for 2027. His “every county” pledge carries no date.

* Liberians-only sectors. He will enforce the reservation of rice and cement retail, fuel stations and sand supply through ownership checks. He did not say how many such businesses are now foreign-owned.

The 2029 goal to “produce more of what Liberia consumes” has no baseline or target. He has also warned that a stronger currency can cut what farmers and processors earn, a tension his import-substitution plan does not address.

Questions of record

Yekeson told senators he will disclose all relevant interests, comply with the Code of Conduct and recuse himself where conflicts arise. He did not say whether he still holds shares or roles in South Atlantic Capital Group or Panchariya Group West Africa, where he previously served as CFO and president, respectively.

His appointment has also revived older questions. Smart News Liberia reported that his name appeared in a 2013 Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission asset verification that raised questions about deposits totaling more than US$300,000. His statement did not address it.

What the Senate should hold him to

Yekeson’s statement is the work of someone who knows the market’s pressure points. The question for senators is whether they will confirm the diagnosis or demand the mechanisms.

Five commitments would turn the speech into a record that can be checked:

1. Weekly county-level prices for rice, fuel and cement, published by the 100-day mark.

2. A date for the rule requiring traders to post the Central Bank’s daily exchange rate.

3. Publication of the full fuel pricing formula alongside pump prices.

4. An agency-by-agency report on the 25 percent procurement set-aside, with a deadline.

5. Full disclosure of his remaining business interests before confirmation.

He has offered quarterly reports to the committee. If confirmed, the first should show progress on each.

World.title: Liberia: Economist Samuel Jackson Appeals to Court for Permission to Travel Abroad Amid Health Concerns
World.content:
Jackson (center), who is seeking court permission to travel abroad for medical treatment, remains barred from leaving Liberia. He was seen being assisted by two men at the courthouse.

MONROVIA — Liberian economist and political commentator Samuel Jackson has appealed to Criminal Court “A” Judge Onesimus Barwon for permission to travel abroad for specialized medical treatment, citing concerns about his deteriorating health as he faces charges in connection with the death of his wife.

By Victoria Wesseh

Jackson was seen struggling to walk on the grounds of the Temple of Justice in Monrovia on Thursday, October 22, prompting renewed attention to his reported health condition.



The economist is seeking medical leave to obtain treatment outside Liberia but remains barred from leaving the country as his legal proceedings continue.

Jackson is facing charges in connection with the March 2026 death of his wife, Ntombi Khumalo Jackson, a South African attorney who was found dead in their Monrovia home.

Jackson told authorities that he discovered his wife semi-conscious in their bedroom after returning home from a television talk show engagement.

Khumalo Jackson, who was born in Gauteng, South Africa, was the founder of NK Attorneys. Her death attracted widespread public attention, particularly after images allegedly showing bruises and other injuries on her body circulated on social media.

Reports indicated that she suffered severe head injuries and required emergency brain surgery.

The circumstances surrounding her death have since become the subject of legal proceedings involving her husband.

Jackson’s request for permission to travel abroad for medical treatment now presents the court with a matter requiring consideration alongside the conditions imposed on him as the case proceeds.

The court’s decision on his request was not immediately available.

World.title: Liberia: War Victims, Survivors Protest at Court Office, Capitol as House Chairman Pledges to Put Court Bill Before Plenary Tuesday
World.content:
Some of the protesters at the war crimes court office. Credit: Anthony Stephens/New Narratives.

Hundreds of war victims, survivors and justice advocates protested at the war crimes court office and the Capitol Building, demanding approval of legislation to establish the long-awaited court.

A disagreement erupted at the Capitol after a lawmaker said a legislative committee had decided to exclude economic crimes from the proposed court. Protesters objected, prompting another lawmaker to assure them that both categories of crimes would be covered.

The House Committee Chairman pledged to bring the matter before plenary Tuesday, as the government’s timetable for establishing the courts faces uncertainty.

By Anthony Stephens, senior justice correspondent with New Narratives

Hundreds of victims and survivors of Liberia’s civil wars, joined by justice advocates, protested Thursday outside the government office overseeing the establishment of a war crimes court, temporarily disrupting operations, before moving to the Capitol Building, where a senior lawmaker pledged to place the long-delayed legislation before the House plenary on Tuesday.

The peaceful demonstrations drew people with disabilities, rural women, elderly victims and survivors, young people, and traditional and religious leaders. For hours, protesters gathered outside the Office for the Establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court, holding placards demanding justice. One read: “REAL PEACE IS NOT THE SILENCE OF GUNS. REAL PEACE IS DISPENSING JUSTICE AND ENDING IMPUNITY. WE CALL ON THE EXECUTIVE AND LEGISLATURE TO GIVE THE PEOPLE JUSTICE & ACCOUNTABILITY NOW…”



“What’s going on wrong? We are suffering,” said Korpo Dennis, president of the Women in Peacebuilding Network, her voice cracking as she broke down in tears, burying her face in her lappa, a traditional cloth wrapped around her waist. Addressing Jallah Barbu, the office’s executive director, Dennis questioned why President Joseph Boakai had not raised the issue at the United Nations General Assembly, as she said he had promised. “He na come, we can hear nothing. We want answer today or else, we will sleep on this street.”

The protests underscored mounting frustration over Liberia’s failure to establish a court to prosecute atrocities committed during its civil wars, more than two decades after the fighting ended. Despite repeated government commitments and consultations, competing bills remain before lawmakers, leaving uncertain when those accused of wartime crimes will face prosecution.

Dennis’s organization was among the women’s peace groups widely credited with helping pressure Liberia’s warring factions to end the conflicts.

Barbu told protesters he remained confident that Boakai had not abandoned his commitment to establishing the court. Prevented from entering his office, along with other staff, he unsuccessfully attempted to reach House Speaker Richard Koon by telephone.

He then contacted James Verdier, the speaker’s chief of staff, who assured protesters that the legislation would be approved. Unsatisfied, the protesters moved to Capitol Hill to press lawmakers directly.

Kula Fofana, Boakai’s press secretary, did not respond to a request for comment on the protesters’ concerns.

“It has taken us too long,” said Jeremiah D. Cooper, a member of the Group of 77, an organization representing people with disabilities. “The same Liberian people who voted for you are the same Liberian people demanding that you pass certain documents in the interest of the country,” he added. “You people say you will not do it. Why?”

Jeremiah D. Cooper, one of the protesters.

But the gathering soon exposed a disagreement over whether the proposed court would prosecute both war crimes and economic crimes.

Prescilla A. Cooper, a Montserrado County representative and member of the House Committee on Claims and Petitions, told protesters that a joint legislative committee tasked with harmonizing the competing bills had agreed to proceed with legislation establishing a war crimes court, leaving economic crimes to be handled separately by the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission.

The protesters rejected her account, insisting that economic crimes allegedly committed during Liberia’s civil wars must also fall within the proposed court’s jurisdiction.

Justice advocates have long argued that including economic crimes would allow the court to order convicted warlords and other perpetrators, including institutions found responsible, to pay restitution to victims and communities harmed by their actions.

Prince Toles, chairman of the House Committee on Claims and Petitions, sought to reassure the protesters, saying he shared their position that the legislation should establish a War and Economic Crimes Court.

“We signed it in 2024 (the joint resolution). We signed it 5G. But this one, we will give it 20G,” Toles said, referring to the Legislature’s earlier support for establishing the court. “If people did not rob the system, all of us would have lived better. I want to tell you that we are with you.”

“We will bring this matter before plenary,” Toles said. “But if they ask us to bring a paper signed by the different stakeholders, I will just propose that you draft something for us temporarily. Bring it here tomorrow (Friday), then I will put it on the floor on Tuesday.”

Plenary, the full membership of either legislative chamber, is its highest decision-making body. Toles’s pledge does not guarantee a vote or passage Tuesday.

House leaders subsequently invited protest organizers to a meeting.

“We feel a little bit relieved that it will work,” Peterson Sonyah, executive director of the Liberia Massacre Survivors Association, said by phone afterward. “We are impressed with the discussion. We are planning to be there on Tuesday.”

The protests came as Liberia approaches a deadline in its plans to establish the courts.

Under a 36-page roadmap submitted to Boakai in July 2025 , the court office projected that the National Anti-Corruption Court would be operational by November 2026, followed by the War and Economic Crimes Court in November 2027.

With neither court’s establishing legislation approved, the timetable faces uncertainty. The roadmap also envisaged completing trials by 2031, after which the war crimes court would transition to a residual mechanism.

Liberia is also preparing to assume the rotating presidency of the United Nations Security Council in December, a moment justice advocates say will draw international attention to the country’s unfinished accountability efforts.

A FrontPage Africa/New Narratives survey of 1,150 people across 11 counties found that 91 percent supported establishing the court, while 89 percent said they would not vote for lawmakers opposing it.

The survey was not scientifically sampled. Only 4 percent of respondents reported awareness of lawmakers’ consultations on the proposed court.

The legislative process has been complicated by six competing proposals.

They include a War Crimes Court bill from the Liberian National Bar Association ; a separate proposal from civil society organizations working with the Independent National Commission on Human Rights ; and two bills introduced by Senate President Pro Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence and Senator Joseph Jallah , one proposing a War Crimes Court and another a Special Economic and Corruption Crimes Court.

The remaining two bills were prepared by the court office , proposing a War and Economic Crimes Court and a separate National Anti-Corruption Court. Boakai subsequently forwarded both proposals to the Legislature .

The senators’ proposals drew criticism from justice advocates , who warned that provisions concerning jurisdiction and appeals could weaken wartime accountability.

In June, more than 40 House members attended a two-day technical deliberation in Buchanan, Grand Bassa County , organized by the court office and its partners to examine the legislation.

Separately, the Senate Committee on Judiciary, Human Rights, Claims and Petitions began consultations on the competing bills , seeking to resolve differences over senior appointments, prosecutorial independence and appeals.

The committee also outlined plans to harmonize the proposals , with further consultations and hearings expected before the legislative session ended.

Neither chamber approved the legislation before lawmakers departed for their constituency break.

The Legislature was scheduled to return October 9, but a dispute over lawmakers’ benefits delayed the House’s reopening. Regular business resumed October 13.

For Sonyah and the other organizers, Tuesday will test the assurances they received. They intend to return to the Capitol to see whether the matter reaches plenary — and whether the proposed legislation retains both war crimes and economic crimes.

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by the U.N. Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the European Union. The funders had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Ashios Melu honoured posthumously
World.content:
29 years after his death, Zambia and Mighty Mufulira Wanderers legend Ashios Jordan Melu has been honoured posthumously for his outstanding contribution to sport and raising Zambia’s profile internationally.

Melu was honoured by President Hakainde Hichilema at the Investiture Ceremony on the occasion of the 62nd Independence Anniversary at State House.

He was recognised alongside boxer Patrick Chinyemba and Copper Princesses head coach Carol Kanyemba.

Melu captained Zambia from 1988 to 1992. In 1992 he turned to coaching as assistant coach at Wanderers before taking over as head coach.

In 1994, he was named Zambia national team assistant coach to Roald Poulsen. He then led Wanderers to back-to-back league championships in 1995 and 1996, giving the club its first league success since 1978.

Melu died in 1997.

Chinyemba was recognised for his achievements in amateur boxing and representation at major international competitions, including the Paris Olympic Games. Born on January 3, 2001, in Lusaka, he has won several senior national titles and competed in IBA and World Championship events.

Kanyemba, who leads the Under-17 women’s national team, the Copper Princesses, was honoured for her contribution to youth development and women’s football. Born on January 23, 1988, in Kateete, she has guided the team through regional and international competitions including FIFA Under-17 Women’s World Cup qualifiers.

Meanwhile, National Olympic Committee of Zambia President Alfred Foloko congratulated the trio, saying their achievements show talent, resilience and commitment that help raise Zambia’s profile internationally.

“We especially appreciate the focus on youth development, women’s football, and the lasting legacy of Zambian football. We also extend our sincere appreciation to President Hichilema for recognising and celebrating these sports personalities,” Foloko said.

World.title: Diplomatic Dean calls for Africa to Lead Its development
World.content:
The Dean of the Diplomatic Corps in Zambia Hawa Hassan Mohamed has called on African countries to take greater responsibility for their development, peace and prosperity, saying the continent must lead efforts to change perceptions about Africa.

Ms Mohamed said African countries needed to take ownership of their development agendas rather than depend on external actors to determine their priorities.

Speaking in an interview during Zambia’s 62nd Independence Anniversary celebrations, she said Africa had become more aware of global developments and was increasingly seeking to reshape narratives that had historically defined the continent.

She said Zambia’s development ambitions under the Grow Zambia agenda reflected the importance of countries taking charge of their own progress.

She described the agenda as one that Zambians should own and champion, stressing that the responsibility for achieving development goals rested primarily with the people themselves.

“It means that Zambia is going to grow. Zambia is going to do its own thing. The theme is going to be developing by themselves. It is something that we own, we are championing and we are going to do it,” she said.

Ms Mohamed also urged African countries to learn from one another by adopting successful practices from countries that had made progress in key areas of governance and development.

She cited elections as one area where countries could learn from one another, encouraging African nations to observe successful electoral processes and adopt positive practices that could strengthen democratic governance across the continent.

She pointed out that sharing experiences and replicating successful approaches could help African countries advance common development goals and strengthen cooperation.

And the United Kingdom (UK) reaffirmed its commitment to supporting Zambia’s development ambitions under the Grow Zambia agenda.

British Deputy High Commissioner to Zambia Simon ten Brinks-Jackson said the UK stood ready to continue supporting the country in achieving its development objectives.

He described the Grow Zambia agenda as forward-looking and optimistic, noting that the country had significant opportunities for growth and development.

“The Grow Zambia agenda is really forward-leaning, really optimistic, and the UK stands ready to continue supporting Zambia with those objectives,” the High Commissioner said.

The diplomat also congratulated the people of Zambia on the country’s 62nd Independence Anniversary, describing the occasion as special.

Freedom fighters also called on Zambians to safeguard the peace emphasizing that it was not easy to attain it.

Mr Stanely Mhlanga urged the young people to maintain Zambia’s peace if the country is to sustain its development.

Meanwhile, a youth, Pauline Bwalya, urged young people to remain peaceful, avoid abusive behaviour and contribute positively to national development as the country commemorates its 62nd Independence Day.

Ms Bwalya said Independence Day should remind citizens of the importance of preserving the freedom secured by those who fought for the country’s liberation.

Ms Bwalya encouraged young people to uphold peace, noting that their conduct was important to Zambia’s development and the country’s image internationally.

World.title: Muchinga PS calls for peace, unity
World.content:
Muchinga Province Permanent Secretary, Tuesday Bwalya has called on Zambians to uphold unity, peace, hard work and integrity as the country commemorates its 62nd Independence Anniversary.

‎

‎Dr Bwalya said Independence Day is an important reminder of the freedom the country enjoys and the collective responsibility of citizens to contribute to national development.

‎

‎He said this during the Independence Day flag-hoisting ceremony at Chinsali Municipal Council.

‎

‎Dr Bwalya said Zambia attained independence on October 24, 1964, following the courage and sacrifices of freedom fighters and founding leaders who fought for the country’s liberation.

‎

‎He said the nation should continue to honour those who contributed to the country’s independence by working towards a peaceful, united and prosperous Zambia.

‎

‎He also explained to the audience the meaning of all the colours on the Zambian flag.

‎

‎“Our flag tells our story. The green color reminds us of our land and natural resources, the red recalls the struggle for freedom, the black represents the people of Zambia, while the orange stands for our mineral wealth,” he said.

‎

‎Dr Bwalya added that the eagle on the national flag symbolises freedom and the country’s ability to rise above challenges.

‎

‎He said the national flag should serve as a reminder of the country’s motto, “One Zambia, One Nation,” which calls on citizens to promote unity and peaceful coexistence.

‎

‎“As we hoist the flag today, let us renew our commitment to unity, peace, hard work and integrity. Let us respect our laws, protect public property, care for our communities and give young people hope and opportunity,” Dr Bwalya said.

‎

‎He said independence should not only be regarded as a day of celebration but also as a responsibility for every citizen to contribute to building the nation.

‎

‎Dr Bwalya urged Zambians to serve the country with honour and ensure that their contributions laid a strong foundation for future generations.

‎

‎He said the 62nd Independence Anniversary provided an opportunity for citizens to reflect on the country’s journey, achievements and aspirations for the future.

‎

‎The flag-hoisting ceremony forms part of activities to commemorate Zambia’s 62 years of independence.

‎

‎This year’s independence is held under the theme, “Zambia @62: Our Journey, Our Growth, Our Future.”

World.title: Lavushimanda vaccinates 7,013 domestic animals against anthrax
World.content:
The Department of Fisheries and Livestock in Lavushimanda District, Muchinga Province has vaccinated 7,013 domestic animals against anthrax in the district.

‎

Livestock Production and Extension Officer Godfrey Singoyi said this is out of a total target of 9000 animals to be vaccinated against Anthrax this quarter representing 96.91 percent of the vaccination coverage.

‎

‎Mr Singoyi categorised the vaccinated animals as 4,616 cattle, 1,618 goats and 369 sheep.

‎

He was speaking yesterday during a district one health technical working group meeting held at the District Health Office.

‎

‎He explained that the office had earlier received 6000 doses of the anthrax vaccine while the other vaccines used were readily available at the department.

‎

‎Mr Singoyi said the anthrax vaccination exercise is still underway.

‎

‎”We are at over 90 percent in terms of vaccination of animals against anthrax,” he said.

‎

‎And speaking at the same meeting, Senior One Health Officer In Charge of Human Health from Zambia National Public health Institute (ZNPHI), Albertina Moraes urged the district one Health Technical working group to work as a team when attending to any Health issues.

‎

‎Ms Moraes says the Health Technical working group comprises different government departments, people from the business community and members of the community with the aim of planning and working together on various health issues.

‎

‎”You all need to be planning for activities together, working together and coordinating, even ensuring that you sign on the attendance register,” she said.

‎

‎Meanwhile, Thomas Maunda, a Metrologist from the Ministry of Green Economy (MGEE) also highlighted the importance of the District Health Technical working group in planning for disasters, attending to any risks that may arise in the district in order to find a solution.

‎

‎”This group is very important in the district hence the need for coordination among the departments that are in this group,” he said.

‎

‎The District Health Technical Working group Comprises of officers from various government departments including health, council, ZANIS, Livestock and Fisheries, Disaster Risk Management, the Chamber of Commerce as well as traditional leaders among others.

World.title: East PS advises Zambians to reject tribalism
World.content:
Eastern Province Permanent Secretary Paul Thole has called on Zambians to reject tribalism and politics of hate and safeguard national unity and peace as the country celebrates 62 years of independence.

Mr Thole said Zambia’s future depended on citizens embracing diversity, protecting the peace secured by freedom fighters and making choices that promote national development.

He was speaking during the hosting of the national flag at the 1940 Building in Chipata ahead of the country’s 62nd Independence anniversary.

Mr Thole said the Independence Day theme, “Zambia at 62: Our Journey, Our Growth, Our Future,” reminded citizens that the country’s progress depended on the choices they made today.

He urged Zambians to honour the sacrifices of freedom fighters by preserving the peace and freedom they secured for future generations.

Mr Thole also commended the people of Chipata for demonstrating tolerance, saying leadership should be based on merit rather than a person’s tribe, colour or religion.

He said the government, under President Hakainde Hichilema, was pursuing the Grow Zambia agenda to move the country from economic stability towards production-led economic growth.

Mr Thole said Eastern Province was contributing to the country’s food security, with the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) purchasing 264,000 metric tonnes of maize this year, compared with approximately 130,000 metric tonnes in the previous year.

He said the increase demonstrated the region’s growing production capacity and its potential to support neighbouring countries, including Malawi.

Mr Thole urged citizens to understand and work towards the country’s development targets in agriculture, mining, energy and tourism.

And Chipata District Commissioner, Elidah Banda paid tribute to freedom fighters for their sacrifices in securing Zambia’s independence.

Ms Banda said the national flag was not merely a piece of cloth but a symbol of freedom, unity, peace and national identity.

She urged citizens to reflect on the country’s journey to independence and uphold the values represented by the national flag.

Meanwhile, speaking on behalf of freedom fighters in Eastern Province, Thomas Majula called on young people to recognise the contribution of women to Zambia’s liberation struggle.

Mr Majula cited Julia Mulega, a marketeer in Lusaka who was known for mobilising women and participating in demonstrations during the colonial period.

He said her courage and determination demonstrated the important role women played in supporting the struggle for independence.

Mr Majula urged young people to appreciate and support women, saying their contribution to society should never be overlooked.

“Look after the women. They will look after you,” he said.

World.title: Kaoma hoists flag to mark 62nd independence anniversary
World.content:
Kaoma District has successfully hoisted the national flag in commemoration of this year’s Independence day under the theme ‘Zambia @62: our journey, our growth, our future’.Kaoma District Commissioner, Kashina Sheba led Senior government officials, organisation, institutions, Senior citizens and youths among others to witness the historic and colourful event held at Kaoma district administration premises.

Kaoma Pentecostal Assemblies of God Reverend Progress Chifuwe during his exaltation thanked God for safely leading Zambia through all the 62years from 1964 to date just like he led the Israelites from Egypt through the wilderness into the promised land.

He noted that through it all, the nation has grown economically, democratically and spiritually through the declaration of Zambia as a Christian nation, while enjoying peace.

Reading the scripture in both Deuteronomy 8 verse 2 and Psalms 33 verse 12, Reverend Chifuwe implored Kaoma residents to reflect on what God has done for them in all the 62 years and remember where they have come from, where they are and focus on where they are going as a country and appreciate God for his love and mercies.

“Pose and look back to where we are coming from as our Journey, where we are as our growth and where we’re going is our future. God has led Zambia through the wilderness for 62 years from 1964 to date just like he led the Israelites from Egypt into Canaan”.

“The peace, calmness, economic growth, and democracy show that as a nation we’re in the hands of God. So let us remember where we are coming from because forgetfulness is the killer of gratitude,” Reverend Chifuwe said.

Kaoma Town Council Chairperson, Kausheni Mupishi, Council Secretary, Kate Mukonde, Kaoma Council Director of Human Resource and Administration, Liswaniso Kabwela, District Operations Joint Committee members, Outgoing Kaoma District Administrative Officer (DAO), Mishengo Mishengo and the Acting DAO, Ilinanga Makoba were among the notable people at the event.

Former Kaoma District Commissioner, Liale Mubanga, United Party for National Development Kaoma District Chairperson, Andrew Kakumbi and other party members, Councilors as well as the general public were also in attendance.

The event was characterised by entertainment from Kaoma secondary school brass band, Luena Barracks brass band and Pop band respectively.

World.title: Nalumango urges Zambians to safeguard peace, unity
World.content:
Vice-President Mutale Nalumango has urged Zambians to safeguard the country’s peace and unity, describing them as the nation’s greatest assets.

Mrs Nalumango says peace and unity were essential for Zambia’s continued social and economic development and should be preserved under the national motto, One Zambia, One Nation.

She was speaking last evening when she led the ‘symbolic’ midnight flag-hoisting ceremony held at the Lusaka Showgrounds to mark the country’s 62nd Independence anniversary.

The ceremony, attended by government officials, traditional leaders, diplomats, deputy defence service chiefs and hundreds of Lusaka residents, commemorated Zambia’s historic transition to independence on October 24, 1964.

Mrs Nalumango said the midnight flag-hoisting tradition was an important national event that brought Zambians together regardless of their backgrounds, beliefs, religion or affiliations.

She called on citizens to honour the sacrifices of freedom fighters by actively participating in the country’s social and economic development.

Mrs Nalumango said this year’s theme, “Zambia at 62: Our Journey, Our Growth, Our Future,” provided an opportunity for citizens to reflect on the country’s achievements, acknowledge challenges and renew their commitment to building a prosperous nation for present and future generations.

She said the New Dawn administration, under President Hakainde Hichilema, had embarked on rebuilding the country through expanded access to free education, improved health services, infrastructure development, increased economic activity and opportunities across various sectors.

She said progress had been recorded in agriculture, mining, manufacturing, tourism, energy, information and communication technology, among other sectors.

She urged citizens to build on the achievements made so far and contribute to shaping a stronger and more prosperous Zambia.

And speaking at the same occasion, Ministry of Defence Permanent Secretary (PS) Maambo Hamaundu said the freedom secured by Zambia’s forefathers should never be taken for granted.

Mr Hamaundu commended men and women in uniform for their continued role in safeguarding the country’s peace, security and stability.

He said peace and security were essential for national order and economic and social development.

The PS urged Zambians to reflect on their individual responsibilities in shaping the country’s future, saying every citizen had a role to play in sustaining the gains of independence.

Meanwhile, 2026 Independence Defense Ceremony Organising Committee Chairperson, Likando Muyunda said the midnight flag-hoisting ceremony was intended to remind citizens of the historic events of the night of October 23 to 24, 1964.

World.title: Lives on landmines: Zim’s long road to a safer land
World.content:
Opinion

Vanessa Gonye · October 23, 2026

HE lost not one, but both legs to deadly landmines scattered across his community.

Such is the tragic story of Kenias Chihumo (83), who lives under Chief Chirambadeya in Mudzi district and has endured nearly four decades of life with a disability caused by landmine explosions.

According to Chihumo, his first accident occurred in 1988.

Thirteen years later, in 2001, he suffered a second explosion along the Mudze River in Mudzi, at the same location as the first incident.

Having lost both lower limbs, he now moves around on his knees.

“I was doing some farming in my garden, which is close to the river, where I would fetch water to use,” he said.

“That is when I stepped on it at the bank of the river.”

In 2001, he suffered a similar ordeal while farming along the same river, stepping on another landmine.

“In 2001, I encountered the same accident and was taken to Harare Central Hospital (now Sally Mugabe Central Hospital) for treatment,” he said.

Life was never the same for Chihumo, whose injuries left him without both legs.

An estimated three million anti-personnel landmines were laid between 1974 and 1979, creating dense minefields along Zimbabwe’s borders.

Since independence in 1980, between 1 500 and 1 700 people have reportedly been killed or injured, while more than 120 000 cattle have been lost.

Chihumo is among those whose lives have been profoundly affected by the country’s landmine legacy.

For survivors, the consequences extend far beyond the physical injuries, often bringing lasting emotional and financial hardship.

“My life has been suffering since I became disabled,” Chihumo said.

His elderly wife now takes on menial work, including farming and other odd jobs in the community, to ensure the family has something to eat at the end of the day.

Despite his circumstances, Chihumo puts on a brave face and appears to have come to terms with his fate, painful as it remains.

Another landmine survivor, Daniel Kutsakatika (39), of Jurimani village, said counselling had helped him cope with the abrupt changes to his life after losing a leg in an explosion.

Kutsakatika was on his way home from work when he stepped on a landmine.

Since that day, life has been difficult for the father of six, who must provide for his large family, which includes his two wives.

“I was coming from doing my job as a herdsman, holding my child,” he said.

“I didn’t feel anything at first, but just found myself on the ground.

“My companion started to panic and I told him not to worry, but to carry me home.”

Kutsakatika said he sought assistance at a nearby clinic before being referred to Parirenyatwa Group of Hospitals for further treatment.

His leg was subsequently amputated.

“From the incident to date, my life has never been the same.

“I am struggling to take care of my family.”

The ordeal left him traumatised, although he tries to reassure those around him that he is coping.

He broke down in tears midway through the interview, revealing the lasting emotional impact of the incident.

“I received counselling, which was really helpful and I have accepted the new life,” he said.

“Another challenge is that my artificial leg is quite worn out and it is making life difficult for me.

“It is my wish to get assistance to start a project so I may increase income for my family.”

Despite his struggles, Kutsakatika welcomed the ongoing de-mining exercise in the area, which is nearing completion.

He said the operation would help give residents a greater sense of security, as many continue to live in fear of becoming victims of landmine explosions.

For now, he said, the threat remains real, with landmines still scattered across the community.

Addressing a gathering during a high-level field visit to mine-affected communities under Project RECLAIM in Mudzi, United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) resident representative Ayodele Odusola said about 700 landmines had been discovered and destroyed in the district.

“Because of this partnership, we have real results to show since our work began in January 2026,” he said.

“Here in Mudzi, since April 2026, MAG has made over 80 000 square metres of land safe. Almost 700 landmines have been found and destroyed.

“In Rushinga, between February and October 2026, The HALO Trust has cleared nearly 93 000 square metres of land. It has found and destroyed over 1 800 landmines.”

Odusola said the combined area cleared in the two districts exceeded 173 000 square metres.

“That is about the size of 24 football pitches, now safe for families to farm, to graze their cattle and to walk on. Over 2 500 landmines that will never again take a life, a leg or a cow,” he said.

In a speech read on her behalf by Defence deputy minister Levi Mayihlome, Defence minister Oppah Muchinguri-Kashiri acknowledged that landmines continued to pose a threat to people living in border areas.

“The government recognises that landmines continue to threaten lives, restrict access to productive land and undermine livelihoods in affected communities,” she said.

“The government will therefore continue to mobilise resources to accelerate mine clearance and promote inclusive development.”

Since clearance operations began in February 2026, Project RECLAIM has made progress in both

districts.

By September 2026, the project had cleared 92 353 square metres in Rushinga district and destroyed 1 833 landmines, against a target of 122 500 square metres.

In Mudzi, the project aims to clear 110 000 square metres by completion.

Meanwhile, UNDP-funded mine-action operations have released 80 941 square metres of land and recovered and destroyed 694 anti-personnel mines.

The project is funded by the Government of Japan and UNDP. Japan committed US$2 946 582,32, while UNDP is contributing US$400 000 towards its implementation.

The project began in August 2025 and is scheduled to run until December 2028.

For communities in Mudzi and Rushinga, every square metre cleared represents more than a project statistic. It is land that families can use to grow food, graze cattle and travel with less fear.

For survivors such as Chihumo and Kutsakatika, de-mining cannot reverse the injuries they have s

uffered.

But it can help protect others from similar tragedies, restore access to productive land, support livelihoods and uphold the dignity of those living with the consequences of Zimbabwe’s landmine legacy.

World.title: Patients first: Why ZADHR supports the medical aid reforms
World.content:
Opinion

ZADHR · October 23, 2026

PAYING for medical aid should bring peace of mind, not the fear of being unable to afford treatment when illness strikes.

Yet for many Zimbabweans, making monthly contributions does not guarantee that their medical expenses will be fully covered.

When the hospital bill arrives, patients and their families may still be left struggling to meet the shortfall.

At the heart of this problem lies a fundamental question: should a medical aid society that collects members’ contributions to finance their healthcare also own and operate hospitals, pharmacies and other facilities from which healthcare is purchased?

When the same institution controls the funding and competes to provide the service, conflict of interest can arise, patient choice can be constrained and the interests of members risk being pushed aside.

The Zimbabwe Association of Doctors for Human Rights (ZADHR) supports the proposed reforms to separate the financing of healthcare from its provision.

This is not simply a debate about business ownership.

It is about accountability for members’ contributions, fairness in the healthcare market, the quality-of-care patients receive and the protection of the right to healthcare under section 76 of the Constitution of Zimbabwe.

Medical aid must put patients first.

The proposed reforms offer an opportunity to restore that principle by ensuring that medical aid societies focus on financing members’ healthcare, while independent providers compete to deliver the care patients need.

With appropriate safeguards and a carefully managed transition, Zimbabwe can move towards a system that places patients’ interests, dignity and access to good quality healthcare at its centre.

Where we are today

Medical aid covers a small and shrinking share of Zimbabweans.

Industry figures presented to Parliament in April put coverage at about 8% of the population, with more than 90% paying for care out of their own pockets.

Members typically contribute between US$55 and US$65 a month.

Over the past two decades, the largest societies have become much more than funders.

They have bought or built hospitals, clinics, pharmacies, laboratories, imaging centres, dental practices and ambulance services.

Researchers at EQUINET documented this as early as 2010.

They found that most acquisitions were existing facilities rather than adding new capacity to the health system.

Instead of containing costs, as promised, the move coincided with rising costs.

In practice, a single society can now sit on both sides of almost every step in a patient’s care.

It holds the money, writes the price list, approves or rejects claims and owns facilities that compete with the very providers it pays.

Independent doctors, hospitals and pharmacies must, therefore, negotiate their fees with, and wait to be paid by, a direct competitor.

This creates a structural conflict of interest, even where the people making decisions act in good faith.

Patients who cannot cover the gap often end up in already overstretched public hospitals.

The cost of this arrangement is, therefore, carried by the whole health system, not only by medical aid members.

Meanwhile, reimbursement rates in many schemes have not kept pace with the real cost of running a practice, which inflation, currency instability and imported equipment and consumables have all pushed up.

When a society pays less than care actually costs, the difference does not vanish.

It is passed on to the patient as a shortfall and too often the provider, not the payer, is held responsible.

What the reform proposes

The Health and Child Care ministry has proposed amending section 14 of the Medical Services (Medical Aid Societies) Regulations, 2000, SI 330/2000, as amended by (SI 35/2004 and SI 58/2025) the regulations that govern medical aid societies.

The amendment would bar societies from owning or operating healthcare facilities such as hospitals, clinics and pharmacies.

Societies would return to their core function: pooling members’ contributions and purchasing care on their behalf. Those that already own facilities would be required to divest.

The proposal has been before Parliament’s Portfolio Committee on Health, which heard submissions from the industry in April 2026.

Funders, led by the Association of Healthcare Funders of Zimbabwe and Cimas Health Group, have campaigned hard against it.

Civil society organisations, including the Community Working Group on Health, and many doctors have spoken in its favor.

Why ZADHR supports the reform

Medical aid exists to finance care, not to build business empires

Contributions are paid to protect members when they fall ill, and societies hold non-profit status for exactly that reason.

Keeping sensible reserves is responsible management.

Using members’ contributions as capital for commercial expansion, without giving those members any ownership or say, is something else entirely.

The conflict of interest is structural, not personal

A society that owns clinics has every incentive to steer members towards its own facilities, and to pay independent providers less.

It can approve claims quickly at its own pharmacy and slowly elsewhere or treat its own laboratory as the default.

EQUINET’s research found that only 11% of plans fully reimbursed services from providers outside the society’s own network.

That is not managed care; it is managed choice.

Patient choice and continuity of care suffer

Patients with chronic illnesses, pregnancies or cancer often need a doctor they trust over many years.

When a society nudges or forces members towards its own facilities, that relationship is broken.

Choice of provider is not a luxury. It is part of good, safe medicine.

Quality must be judged by outcomes, not throughput

A facility can treat large numbers of patients and still deliver poor care if consultations are rushed and staff are stretched thin.

When the payer owns the provider, no independent party checks whether members receive the standard of care their contributions pay for.

A purchaser that stands apart from providers can set and enforce standards across all of them, from waiting times and staffing to clinical results.

Fair competition protects patients Independent doctors, hospitals and pharmacies are being squeezed out, especially in smaller towns.

Fewer independent providers means fewer options, longer distances and, ultimately, higher prices.

Smaller medical aid societies, which do not own facilities, are also disadvantaged against vertically integrated rivals.

Claims of lower costs have never been independently verified

Integrated societies say their own facilities are cheaper.

If that is true, the evidence should be published and independently audited so that members, regulators and Parliament can judge it for themselves.

So far, it has not been. Because societies are spending money that belongs to their members, the burden of proof rests with them.

Shortfalls are a policy choice, not a law of nature

A scheme whose premiums rise with costs, but whose reimbursement rates lag behind them, will always leave members with a gap.

When that same scheme also earns revenue from its own facilities, the incentive to fix its rates weakens.

Removing the ownership link pushes societies to compete on what members value most: how fully and fairly they pay for care.

Good governance requires clear lines

The sector has suffered serious governance scandals, including revelations in 2014 of extraordinary executive pay at one of the largest societies.

Complex group structures, with subsidiaries spanning hospitals, pharmacies and property, make oversight harder for members and regulators alike.

A society that only funds care is far easier to supervise.

This is international best practice

Separating the purchaser of care from the provider is a widely used principle of health financing.

It is also the foundation on which Zimbabwe must build a fair National Health Insurance scheme.

Getting the private funding market right now prepares the ground for universal health coverage.

Answering the industry’s objections

The funders have warned of a “collapse cascade” if the reform passes. Their concerns deserve a serious answer.

“Without our facilities, tariffs and premiums will rise.”

Societies already have a powerful tool to control costs: the tariffs they negotiate and the claims they approve.

A strong, independent purchaser can bargain hard with every provider. It does not need to own the hospital to do so.

If integration truly lowered costs, the savings should already show in lower premiums and fewer shortfalls. Members do not see them.

“We built facilities because the market failed.”

Medicine shortages and tariff inflation are real problems.

The answer is better regulation, strategic purchasing and stronger public facilities, not turning funders into competitors.

A temporary fix for market failure has become a permanent conflict of interest.

“Kaiser Permanente and Bupa do it.”

These organisations operate in markets with strong, independent regulators, transparent accounts and enforceable consumer protections.

Zimbabwe has only just placed medical aid societies under the Insurance and Pensions Commission (IPEC), through section 2 of the Insurance and Pensions Commission Amendment Act of 2026 gazetted in April 2026, and that oversight is still being built.

Copying the business model before the safeguards are proven is a risk to members, not a reform.

“Jobs and services will be lost.”

Divestment does not mean closure. A clinic sold to independent doctors, a nursing group or an investor continues to employ staff and treat patients.

What changes is who owns it, and whether its owner also controls the purse.

A phased, supervised transition can protect both jobs and continuity of care.

ZADHR agrees with the industry on one point: the reform should be implemented carefully, with a sensible transition period and independent oversight.

What we ask of Parliament and the ministry

ZADHR urges Parliament and the Ministry of Health and Child Care to:

lPass the amendment prohibiting medical aid societies from owning or operating healthcare facilities.

lSet a clear, phased divestment timeline, with protection for staff and continuity of care for patients.

lMake IPEC’s new oversight count. The Insurance and Pensions Commission Amendment Act of 2026 places medical aid societies under IPEC under section 2.

lIPEC must be resourced to audit societies and their subsidiaries, enforce solvency and protect members, working hand in hand with the ministry on standards of care.

lRequire transparent reporting, including audited accounts, claims ratios and how reserves are invested, published annually for members.

lReview the tariff framework so that reimbursement reflects the real cost of care, ending the shortfall trap for patients.

lProtect members’ choice of provider, so that no member is penalised for seeing a doctor or facility of their choice.

Zimbabweans who pay into medical aid are entitled to know that their contributions are used to pay for their care, and for nothing else.

Separating the funding of care from its provision is a simple, well-established principle that protects that promise.

ZADHR urges Parliament to adopt it, and to return the patient to the centre of a system that exists to serve them.
