World.title: Sudan: Drone Strikes Killed At Least 306 People in Three Weeks
World.content:
UN human rights chief Volker Türk on Friday strongly condemned an escalation in drone strikes across Sudan this month, which killed at least 306 people and injured hundreds more in the first three weeks of October alone.

The strikes, attributed to both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), hit homes, markets, hospitals, displacement sites, power stations and water sources in Kordofan, Darfur, Blue Nile, Khartoum and other states, according to the UN human rights office (OHCHR).

"The increasing use of drones, already accounting for the majority of conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan this year, is deeply disturbing and is exacting a horrifying toll," Mr. Türk said.

Targeted by both sides



In a particularly disturbing trend, the office documented numerous strikes on displacement sites, where people who had already fled the fighting had sought shelter.

Between 6 and 10 October, alleged drone strikes attributed to military government forces on shelters for displaced people in Ghubeish and El Nuhud in West Kordofan killed at least 25 civilians, including women and children.

On 9 October, an alleged RSF drone struck a crowd of displaced people engaged in artisanal gold mining near a displacement site in Abu Shendi, Blue Nile, killing at least 31 people, most of them women and children.

On 18 October, at least 139 people were killed when a transportation truck was hit in a "double tap" repeat strike in Dibab, West Kordofan, an area controlled by the RSF militia.

Markets and hospitals have also been hit, including an RSF-attributed strike on Um Darfa hospital in Blue Nile on 11 October that seriously injured two health workers and left the facility non-operational.

"Scores of civilians have been killed, including internally displaced persons, and vital infrastructure and services have been eviscerated, driving further displacement and deepening the already severe humanitarian crisis," said OHCHR Spokesperson Seif Magango.

Deadly strike

Peacekeepers with the UN Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) this week visited communities affected by a drone attack on 19 October on Amiet Market and the Todach area in Abyei, the disputed oil-rich region between Sudan and South Sudan. The attack killed more than 80 people.

Close 

UNISFA troops were the first to reach the scene, where "every shop was burning", said Lieutenant Colonel Muhammad Farooq, commander of the Mission's Pakistani battalion.

The Mission deployed quick reaction and firefighting teams to stop the fire spreading and took more than 27 injured people to its hospital in Todach, according to Acting Force Commander Brigadier General Adebowale Ajabge.

Angelina Musa Diaw, a trader and mother of three, said she had lost everything. "No work, everything is gone," she said. "I am here with my children. But I need help."

Call for ceasefire

Mr. Türk called on the parties to respect their obligations under international humanitarian law (IHL), including by not directing attacks against civilians and civilian objects.

"Broader peace efforts must squarely address the continued influx of arms that is fuelling the conflict and press for an end to the transfer of arms that are used in manifest disregard of the IHL obligations protecting civilians," he said.

"I urge both parties to the conflict, and their affiliates, to commit to a ceasefire," the High Commissioner added, stressing that a negotiated settlement with human rights at its core, underpinned by accountability, is the only feasible pathway to sustainable peace in Sudan.

World.title: Kenya: 'Burden and Loss' Builds in DR Congo, As Kenya Strengthens Ebola Containment
World.content:
As Ebola continues to spread in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), more resources are needed to fight the disease and feed patients and families, UN agencies said on Friday.

"If we lift the foot off the pedal, the virus will resurge very quickly, will continue to spread to newly affected areas and pose a threat for the country, the region and the world at large," warned Dr. Catherine Smallwood, World Health Organization (WHO) incident manager in the DRC.

The country remains the epicentre of an outbreak of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease that was officially declared in mid-May. It began in the volatile eastern region and has now spread to eight provinces, the latest being Nord-Ubangi in the northwest.

There have been 9,765 cases to date and nearly half - 4,727 - have died. Additionally, 30,000 contacts are being monitored each day over a three-week period.



A smaller outbreak in Uganda was officially declared over in August, while cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and France.

Lives and livelihoods lost

In the DRC, "we're seeing an incredible permanent burden and loss of livelihoods in those families that are affected", said Dr. Smallwood, speaking from the eastern city of Bunia to journalists in Geneva.

At nearly six months in, the outbreak "is occurring in an area that is geographically vast and moving into ever hard to reach locations and remote locations", she noted. Some places can take several days to reach by boat or motorcycle and are inaccessible by car or plane.

The crisis continues to unfold amid ongoing conflict, hunger and displacement, and the World Food Programme (WFP) is working to ensure that families get enough to eat. The UN agency is also building Ebola treatment centres, among other operations.

Feeding hungry families

WFP's Representative in the DRC David Stevenson shared stories of the people who depend on its support.

One woman, Francine Birungi Amoti, lost a child to Ebola and is raising her six surviving children and a baby entrusted to her care. She is unable to attend to her fields due to violence.

"For Francine, food assistance means being able to feed the children in her care when reaching her fields could cost her life," he said, speaking from the capital Kinshasa.

"This is what a crisis on top of a crisis looks like: disease and bereavement, compounded by insecurity and hunger."

Concerns and challenges

Dr. Smallwood also pointed to another concern as the number of people dying from Ebola outside recognised treatment centres "remains a big flag of late detection of cases at the community level".

The past week has seen a decline in the number of people dying in the community or outside Ebola treatment centres which indicates that actions to increase early detection and quick referral to care have been working.

However, WHO understands that in some parts of eastern DRC, "patients are visiting between two to five different health facilities before they're referred to Ebola treatment centres", representing "a really, really big challenge".

Beds for patients

Dr. Smallwood said there have been significant improvements in the quality of care provided at Ebola treatment centres. WHO had set a target of 3,000 beds across affected areas and currently over 2,000 are available.

She also highlighted the positive fact that 2,600 people in the DRC have survived Ebola. Clinics are being opened where they can access care, including to monitor presence of the virus and any related conditions that may arise, as well as psychosocial support.

© WHO/Ardo Farah A healthcare worker in Kenya prepares Ebola response materials as part of a training exercise. Update from Kenya

There is also good news on the Ebola front in Kenya following the country's first case and fatality earlier this month - a Kenyan man who had been working in the DRC before flying back to Nairobi via Uganda.

More than 100 contacts were identified, some of whom will complete their 21-day quarantine on Sunday and will be heading home to their families.

Close 

WHO representative in Kenya Dr. Neema Rusibamayila Kimambo welcomed the development.

"I think their sacrifice has been important in ensuring that the community is protected and that we don't have community spread today," she told UN News.

Listen to the full interview here.

Support, not stigma

She stressed that these people should not be stigmatised as being released from quarantine does not mean that they had Ebola, only that they had contact with someone who did.

With Ebola now confirmed in four African countries, Dr. Kimambo underscored that governments must remain vigilant.

"Africa is very interconnected and nobody is safe until everyone is safe," she said. "So, as long as we have Ebola in DRC at the scale that it is, or in any other country, it means that we are not safe. Therefore, the key message is preparedness."

World.title: Kenya: Soil Mapping Aims to Boost Agricultural Production in Kenya
World.content:
A new Kenyan initiative is helping farmers better understand their soils in a bid to improve crop yields amid intensifying climate shocks.

The Soil Mapping for Resilient Agrifood systems (SoilFER) programme supports farmers to develop reliable soil information that will inform agricultural decisions such as which fertilizer to use and how much.

So far, more than 3,600 soil samples have been collected and mapped across 45 counties, contributing to a digital soil map designed to provide farmers with location-specific information about their land.



Select farmers also receive training to diagnose and fix soil degradation - earning the title "soil doctor" - who then go on to teach their peers.

SoilFER was launched through a partnership between the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) in Kabete, with financial support from the United States Department of State and Japan.

'Now we know better'

For Agness Munialo, a farmer from Kakamega county in western Kenya, learning about soil composition and fertility has changed how she thinks about farming.

"Farmers would use excessive chemicals, sometimes even more fertilizers in an attempt to get more yields. Now we know better," she said.

Ms. Munialo, a trained soil doctor who participated in the SoilFER programme, said the initiative was helping farmers, particularly in rural areas, better understand soil composition, pH levels and fertility.

According to Barrack Okoba, FAO-Kenya's national coordinator of the programme, making soil information accessible is essential to building resilience in agriculture.

"Part of resilience is to make sure that our information system is available and supporting farmers to build sustainable farm management," he said.

Through the support of FAO, KALRO has renovated three labs and equipped them with state-of-the-art technology to support analysis of soil samples collected across the country.

The samples are georeferenced, with the findings transmitted directly to farmers' mobile phones.

Gen Z in agriculture

The initiative is also attracting interest from young people exploring opportunities in agriculture.

Jackline Kioko, a KALRO intern who participated in the launch, said the information shared had given her a better understanding of how soil testing could inform decisions on her family's farm.

Close 

"I'd love to do farming more, now that I have the information that you can actually test your soils to know what nutrients it requires," she said.

Collaboration and information sharing

Kenya's Cabinet Secretary for Agriculture, Mutahi Kagwe called for stronger collaboration among agricultural institutions to promote coordinated decision-making, enhance information sharing, and ensure that soil health is integrated into the work of all relevant institutions.

"I want to urge Kenyans that before thinking about what to plant or the fertilizer to use, think about soil testing," he said.

The event also marked the launch of the Kenya Soil Partnership, the Kenya Soil Laboratory Network and the national rollout of the Global Soil Doctors Programme.

The SoilFER programme is currently being implemented in six other countries: Ghana, Guatemala, Honduras, Mozambique, Tunisia and Zambia.

World.title: Africa: 'Too Arrogant, Too Sure of Itself' France Confronts Its Legacy in Africa
World.content:
Fifteen years after France promised a new relationship with Africa, Paris is still struggling to reconcile its rejection of colonial-era interference with its desire to retain influence on the continent. RFI Africa specialist Christophe Boisbouvier argues in a new book that France can still build a partnership of equals - based on respect rather than arrogance or domination.

"Too arrogant, too sure of itself, France failed to see the anti-French wave coming," Boisbouvier says. His book, Françafrique Is Dead, Long Live Africa-France, examines the breakdown of France's old model of relations with the continent.

For decades after African countries gained independence, Paris maintained privileged relationships with friendly leaders and sought to protect its strategic interests - sometimes through military intervention.

The system, known as Françafrique, gradually became synonymous with a neo-colonial pattern of French influence and patronage.



Military retreat

French troops have been forced to withdraw from Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, where military governments have turned away from Paris and towards Moscow. France has also ended permanent military deployments in Chad, Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire through negotiations.

Some of the damage dates back to former president Nicolas Sarkozy's 2007 speech in Dakar, Boisbouvier argues, when Sarkozy said Africans had "not sufficiently entered history".

"That phrase did a great deal of damage to Franco-African relations, because many Africans saw in it - a terrible word - 'arrogance'," Boisbouvier says.

Even President Emmanuel Macron has sometimes displayed "an attitude of superiority that African countries have not understood" and increasingly refuse to accept.

But the balance of power is changing. Africa's combined economy is set to become larger than France's this year, with gross domestic product of around €3 trillion - what Boisbouvier describes as a "historic economic milestone".

"That's a historic date which shows that France can no longer be in a dominant position," he says. France must now build a relationship based on "respect and partnership, on an equal footing".

He cites the Africa-France summit in Nairobi in May as evidence of the potential for renewed economic cooperation, including with major African investors such as Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote.

At the Africa Forward summit, a different conversation about France

Intervention dilemma

Some of France's military interventions have proven helpful, and yet received little attention, Boisbouvier argues.

One came in September 2015. After the overthrow of Blaise Compaoré in Burkina Faso, supporters of the former president attempted a military coup against the transitional authorities led by Michel Kafando.

French forces, under then president François Hollande, provided rapid but crucial assistance to thwart the putsch.

"It was very precise assistance. It lasted a few minutes, but it was enough to make the coup fail," Boisbouvier says.

That intervention had remained secret until now. Boisbouvier suggests Burkinabe officials at the time may have asked France to keep it under wraps.

While that episode showed France intervening to help protect a democratic transition, the question of when Paris should weigh in militarily remains difficult.

In 2019, a French air strike against rebel forces advancing in northern Chad prompted criticism in France. Macron, fearful of being accused of neo-colonialism, came to regret it and decided France should no longer intervene in African political crises, Boisbouvier says.

That decision had grave consequences, he argues. Two years later, Chadian president Idriss Déby was killed while visiting troops fighting rebels.

'I'm incredibly proud of my record' on Africa, Macron tells RFI

Policy reversal

Macron appeared unequivocal in June 2025.

Asked in a televised interview whether the post-colonial system endured, he replied: "It stopped several years ago... Many people who claim that France is in decline are effectively saying, 'You should stage coups or put a stop to them when they happen', but we don't do that sort of thing any more."

Six months later, Macron did the opposite by intervening in Benin, Boisbouvier says.

In December 2025, Benin's army attempted to overthrow the country's president, Patrice Talon. France provided intelligence and logistical support, while Nigeria supplied military assistance, including air strikes and ground troops, at Benin's request.

"It was a French counter-subversion operation, involving French aircraft and Nigerian Super Tucano planes, alongside the decisive intervention of forces loyal to Talon," he says.

Benin authorities say coup attempt foiled, President Talon safe

For Boisbouvier, the operation showed that Paris had not abandoned military involvement in Africa but was prepared to act when it believed a partner government faced a threat - particularly one that risked strengthening Russian influence.

The apparent reversal reflects a French president still struggling to find a coherent policy on Africa - caught between a determination to distance himself from France's colonial past and a desire to retain influence when a friendly government is threatened, Boisbouvier argues.

The book also turns to Gabon, where General Brice Oligui Nguema seized power in August 2023, ousting Ali Bongo and ending the Bongo family's 56-year dynasty.

France was connected to the coup, Boisbouvier claims. He points to tensions over a possible Chinese naval base in Libreville, which Bongo supported but was opposed by both Macron and then US president Joe Biden.

While there is no proof of France's explicit involvement in organising or supporting the coup, "everything suggests that the French intelligence services were aware of the preparations for General Oligui Nguema's coup", Boisbouvier says.

Leaked files reveal Russia's blueprint to expand African Sahel alliance

Can France offer something different?

There is no question of France abandoning Africa altogether, Boisbouvier argues, pointing to opportunities for economic cooperation and says a relationship based on equality could be rebuilt with emerging powers such as Nigeria, Kenya and South Africa.

Close 

Senegal offers a possible model of a post-colonial shift in relations.

President Bassirou Diomaye Faye, elected in 2024 on a sovereignty-focused platform, forced France to withdraw from its last two military bases in Dakar in July 2025. But Senegal has left room for economic cooperation, which Boisbouvier says shows France can remain a partner without maintaining its former military dominance.

France also faces competition from powers whose influence has grown as its own has waned.

Russia has capitalised on anti-French sentiment, particularly in the Sahel, deploying Russian paramilitaries, now called Africa Corps, to prove it can better protect against jihadist threats than former colonial power France.

With no colonial past, Moscow initially benefited from what Boisbouvier calls a kind of "historical virginity". It also proved adept at using social media to promote its influence and peddle disinformation - something France was slow to recognise.

But he believes Moscow's advantages are diminishing, pointing to allegations of abuses by Russian forces and their partners in Mali, including the killing of hundreds of civilians in Moura in 2022.

Just days before the Russia-Africa summit on 28-29 October, France's strongest argument, he says, is now political rather than military.

"What France and the other European countries offer is nothing less than democracy and human rights."

This article was partly based on an interview in French by Arnaud Pontus.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: As Ebola Spreads to 8th DR Congo Province, Families Battle to Feed Themselves
World.content:
A health worker carries a stretcher into an Ebola treatment centre in the DR Congo.

Geneva — Hunger in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) is undermining efforts to combat Ebola as the deadly disease has expanded across borders and also to an eighth province of the huge central African country, the UN said on Friday.

Families facing Ebola in the DR Congo, which has a population of more than 105 million, can find that protecting themselves from the virus can also mean losing the means to feed their children, according to the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP).

“Today, the outbreak has spread to an eighth province, reaching communities already under immense pressure,” David Stevenson, the WFP's DRC country director, said during a UN press conference.

“As it spreads, hunger continues to undermine the measures needed to contain it.”



And earlier in the week, the World Health Organisation (WHO), on Oct. 20, said that Nigeria has confirmed one imported case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

It became the fifth country to detect the virus since the DRC declared an outbreak on May 15.

The spread of the disease comes as agencies fighting the escalating Ebola virus in the DRC constantly battle to win the trust of local communities, according to international groups in the field calling for the protection of health workers.

Stevenson said that the WFP has two critical roles: helping families seek care without sacrificing food and providing the logistics backbone that keeps the wider response moving.

“Without sustained support, we risk leaving families unable to follow health guidance when it matters most.”

The WFP official explained that in Ituri’s Mungbwalu, the epicentre of the outbreak, Francine Birungi Amoti has lost a child to Ebola.

“She is raising her six surviving children and another baby entrusted to her care. Violence has cut her off from her fields.

“She told me, ‘If you go, you may not even return alive, and I do not have money to buy food at the local market. So we stay at home, and WFP helps us enormously.’”

For Francine, food assistance means feeding the children in her care when reaching her fields could cost her life.

'INSECURITY AND HUNGER'

“This is what a crisis on top of a crisis looks like: disease and bereavement, compounded by insecurity and hunger,” said Stevenson.

He also cited the case in North-Kivu’s Butembo, where Isabelle Kyakimwa arrived at an Ebola treatment centre without strength.

“As she recovered, she told us: ‘Food is important for us as patients because it helps us regain the strength to keep going.’

Close 

Her words show what food assistance brings to a treatment centre: regular, safe, nutritious meals that support recovery, dignity, and continuity of care.

“Food does not treat Ebola. Medical teams do,” said Stevenson.

“But their work takes place amid severe food insecurity and continued violence that repeatedly displaces families, destroys livelihoods and complicates access to care.”

He said food assistance is vital to supporting patients through that care and that WFP needs $115 million over the next six months, including $79 million for hot meals and dry rations.

World.title: Kenya: Calls for Penalties Follow 12-Story Building Collapse
World.content:
A building under construction collapsed in the Eastleigh neighborhood of Nairobi.

Nairobi — Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has called for tougher penalties against rogue developers and the restoration of prosecutorial powers to county governments following the collapse of an incomplete 12-storey building in Eastleigh.

Sakaja said weak penalties for violating construction regulations undermine enforcement efforts and allow developers to compromise building safety, putting lives at risk.

Speaking as he led multi-agency rescue operations at the site along 1st Avenue, 9th Street, the Governor urged professional bodies representing architects, engineers and quantity surveyors to take action against developers who dismiss qualified experts after obtaining construction approvals.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He said some developers engage licensed professionals to secure approvals but subsequently remove them from projects and proceed with construction using unqualified personnel, undermining safeguards intended to ensure buildings meet approved designs and safety standards.

"We have formally written to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, and we hope our request will be considered. Counties must be empowered to take firm action against rogue developers who disregard building regulations and put lives at risk," Sakaja said.

The Governor questioned the deterrent effect of existing penalties, noting that some developers found guilty of violating construction regulations could face fines as low as Sh5,000.

"Even when such offenders are arrested and taken to court, the penalties can be as low as Sh5,000, which is not a sufficient deterrent," he said.

Sakaja argued that restoring prosecutorial powers to county governments would strengthen enforcement and enable authorities to take firmer action against developers who disregard approved construction plans and safety requirements.

He called on professional associations representing architects, engineers, quantity surveyors and builders to collaborate with county governments in identifying and investigating cases where qualified professionals are withdrawn from construction sites under questionable circumstances.

The Governor said the bodies should take appropriate disciplinary action against professionals found culpable, adding that experts responsible for building design, supervision and safety must be allowed to discharge their duties without interference.

Sakaja also reiterated the need for developers to obtain occupation certificates before putting buildings into use. He said structures must undergo the necessary inspections to establish that they are safe and fit for occupation.

According to the Governor, developers are required to secure county approvals, engage qualified professionals and sign indemnity forms committing them to comply with approved plans and construction standards.

However, he said some developers disregard these commitments after obtaining approvals, compromising the integrity of construction projects.

The calls for stronger enforcement came after an incomplete 12-storey building collapsed in Eastleigh, triggering a multi-agency search and rescue operation amid fears that people were trapped beneath the rubble.

The building was still under construction, with the ground floor occupied at the time of the collapse.

Nairobi City County emergency response teams were coordinating operations alongside the National Disaster Operations Centre, the Kenya Red Cross, the Kenya Defence Forces and other agencies.

Heavy machinery had been deployed to clear debris and create access to sections where victims could be trapped, as additional resources were mobilised to support the rescue effort.

Sakaja urged families and members of the public with information about missing persons to report to designated centres established by rescue teams at the scene.

Close 

Residents were also advised to share information through the county's emergency hotlines, 1508 and 1199.

"Our health teams are on standby to provide immediate medical attention and support rescue efforts as soon as victims are reached. We are doing everything possible to ensure the operation proceeds as quickly and safely as possible," he said.

The collapse has renewed scrutiny of building safety enforcement in Nairobi, particularly compliance with approved construction plans, the engagement of qualified professionals and inspections at different stages of development.

Sakaja said stronger legal powers, tougher penalties and closer collaboration between county governments and professional bodies were necessary to hold developers accountable and prevent similar incidents.

He maintained that restoring county prosecutorial powers would complement existing inspection and enforcement mechanisms by strengthening the ability of local authorities to pursue violations of construction regulations.

World.title: Rwanda: Kagame Defends Strict Dress Codes Amid Rwanda's Dressing Controversy
World.content:
Rwandan President Paul Kagame has defended cultural expectations on dressing, arguing that societies have their own standards of acceptable behaviour which should not be abandoned simply because other countries embrace different ways of life.

Speaking on Thursday while addressing more than 10,000 young Rwandans at BK Arena in Kigali during the "Meet The President" session, Kagame said dress codes should be understood within the context of the places people visit and the values of the society in which they live.

"If you are going to the beach, by the water, where people go to relax, there is a certain way you can dress and behave that may be different from other places. That is perfectly acceptable. But imagine someone coming here dressed as though they were at the beach. Would that work? Wouldn't you all turn around and wonder, what happened to this person?" Kagame asked.



His remarks come amid a growing debate in Rwanda over restrictions on women's dressing, following incidents in which women have faced scrutiny over their clothing in public spaces.

The debate intensified after a video circulated showing police officers forcefully handcuffing a young woman wearing a miniskirt at a bus park in Rubavu.

The Rwanda National Police subsequently cleared the woman of wrongdoing and detained the officers involved pending disciplinary review.

The incident also drew criticism from human rights advocates and public commentators, who argued that cultural values should not be used to justify police intimidation, harassment or arbitrary enforcement of dress standards against women.

Addressing the wider debate, Kagame said the expectations should apply to men as well, arguing that discussions about dressing are often unfairly directed at women.

"By the way, this is not just about women. Most of the time, these things are made to be about women, but the same applies to men. Even now, imagine we are sitting here, and a man suddenly walks in, as though he has just come from the gym, wearing shorts, with nothing on his upper body, and comes to sit among us. People would ask, what happened to this person? Did he forget where he was going?" he said.

Kagame argued that societies should be allowed to maintain their own social standards rather than adopt practices from other countries without considering whether they fit local values.

He said people's willingness to participate in a particular social setting could also depend on the expectations established by those organising it.

"Now, if we had all agreed to come dressed that way, then perhaps that is how it would be. But some people would not come. Isn't that so? Some would simply decide not to attend, saying, we are not going to be part of that," he said.

The Rwandan leader said communities have ways of regulating behaviour through shared expectations and self-regulation, adding that practices accepted elsewhere should not automatically be embraced by Rwandans.

"There is a way society regulates itself, including through self-regulation. But when you simply say, we have seen this elsewhere, so let us do the same here, and you bring it into our society, society may tell you, we have not reached that point yet. Perhaps we were moving in that direction, but we are not there yet," Kagame said.

He called for disagreements over cultural values to be handled through dialogue rather than hostility, saying people should be able to reach an understanding when differences emerge.

"That should not create any hostility. There should be a way of regulating these things so that people can come to an understanding," he said.

Kagame compared society's response to unfamiliar practices to the body's reaction to a foreign object, which it gradually attempts to remove.

"It is like a foreign body. I think those of you in the medical profession know this. When a foreign object, a fragment of something, enters the body, the body tends to reject it. It keeps pushing it out. Even when a thorn gets stuck in your skin, if you leave it there for some time, it begins to work its way out. Eventually, you find it near the surface and remove it. Society works in much the same way," he said.

He added that tensions can arise when individuals seek to introduce practices that conflict with the established values of a community, while other members of that society resist the changes.

"A healthy society, with its own way of functioning, when something unfamiliar is introduced into it, gradually, little by little, that society begins to push it away. There is then a struggle between someone trying to change society to fit something they have brought from elsewhere, and society itself saying, do not bring these things here, and pushing that person away. But there should be no conflict. That is how these things should work," Kagame said.

Close 

He urged young people to reflect on the values they want for themselves and the direction in which they want their society to develop.

"Young people like you should keep these things in mind. Think about them. Understand what it is that you want for yourselves," he said.

Kagame also called for open discussions about changing social norms, urging young Rwandans to question practices that are becoming more common but which they consider inconsistent with their culture or harmful to society.

"Even here, in our discussions, people should be able to raise these questions and say, there are things we have seen becoming increasingly accepted in our society, yet they are not part of our culture. They do not even bring us any benefit. Why should we accept them, especially when they are things that harm people? Why?" he asked.

World.title: Nigeria: Health Is Economic Infrastructure - Why Nigeria Must Invest in Health
World.content:
blog

Listen to this article 8 min The recently concluded World Health Summit in Berlin, themed "From Crisis to Resilience: Innovating for Health", reinforced a key message: health spending is an investment, not just an expense. Yet Nigeria's 2026 Appropriation Bill proposed ₦2.48 trillion for health out of ₦58.47 trillion, about 4.2% of the budget. That is less than a third of the 15% target African governments agreed to in the 2001 Abuja Declaration.

Closing this gap requires recognising health as an investment in economic growth, much like roads and power. Nigeria's growth ambitions depend on people being healthy enough to participate in the economy. Health should therefore be treated as economic infrastructure in the country's development priorities and budget decisions.

What the evidence actually supports



Egypt's experience illustrates the potential economic returns of health investment. At the summit session Funding the Future: Unlocking the Economic and Fiscal Returns of Health Innovation, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, Egypt's Minister of Health and Population, described a $240 million early-detection programme reaching 60 million people, followed by affordable generic treatment. It was projected to save $7 billion by 2030, a 688% return.

However, these are projections, not a confirmed result. For Nigeria, achieving comparable gains would require screening capacity and reliable medicine supplies that are not yet available at the same scale. Martin Seychell, Deputy Director-General at DG INTPA at the European Commission, cautioned that better outcomes depend on how the money is spent.

"We should not make the mistake of simply gauging and assessing efforts simply on the basis of how much money we are investing in health budgets. Because we know, of course, if you underinvest, you will not get good outcomes. But it doesn't follow that if you just increase the health budgets without a clear strategy, you will get better outcomes."

Nigeria's clearest return is household income

One of the clearest benefits for Nigeria is the funds families could keep if healthcare were more affordable. At the Health as an Investment: Preparing Systems & Societies for the 21st Century session, Dr Githinji Gitahi, Group CEO, Amref Health Africa singled out Nigeria when discussing the high out-of-pocket health expenditure, noting that what people pay out of pocket is "ridiculously higher than the government spends."

People pay about 71.9% of current health expenditure out of pocket. An analysis of the 2023/24 General Household Survey found that 45.5% of households faced catastrophic health spending, meaning health costs accounted for at least 10% of their household budget. These bills can force families to borrow, sell belongings or cut spending on food and education.

During the Strategic Health Economy session, Dr Ezekwesili recalled that evidence showing that malaria cost Africa about 2% of its GDP "changed the conversation" with ministers and described the disease as a "productivity tax on the economies." The Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare estimates that malaria reduces Nigeria's GDP by more than $1.1 billion each year, while Nigeria accounts for 27% of global cases.

At the same session, Dr Satoshi Ezoe, Japan's Assistant Minister for Global Health, explained that Japan reached universal health coverage in 1961 while still recovering from the Second World War, and argued that "we laid the foundation by making UHC, which led to socioeconomic development."

Nigeria is one of the first eight countries in the UHC Knowledge Hub, a Japanese initiative with the World Health Organization and the World Bank that brings health and finance ministries together to plan for universal coverage. Successful coverage should mean fewer families are pushed into hardship by medical bills and fewer workdays lost, not enrolment figures alone.

Who captures the value?

The economic case for health investment extends to building local industries and creating employment opportunities. Yet Africa captures little of the value from the health products it uses, as Dr Obiageli Ezekwesili, founder and chief executive officer of Human Capital Africa, told the summit during the session The Strategic Health Economy:

"[Africa's] capacity in terms of... global manufacturing... it's less than 5%. Then you look at... competitiveness... how much value does Africa gain from the health value chain -- also insignificant...

Nigeria aims to increase local production of essential health products to 70% by 2030. The Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain is supported by tax and duty waivers on pharmaceutical inputs and about $2 billion in financing commitments.

However, packaging imported products locally is not the same as making them locally. Manufacturers still rely on imported active pharmaceutical ingredients to produce medicines, leaving them exposed to foreign-exchange fluctuations and price volatility.

Local production also needs skilled workers, as does the wider health system. Nigeria has 95,456 registered doctors but only 60,551 with active practising licenses, while its 2024 National Policy on Health Workforce Migration requires wider implementation.

The role of policy in enabling health workers to deliver care also features in the summit session Health as an Investment: Preparing Systems & Societies for the 21st Century, where Dr Githinji Gitahi, Group CEO of Amref Health Africa, stressed its importance for community health workers.

Making investment accountable

Funding also must reach the services it is meant for. At the Health as an Investment: Preparing Systems & Societies for the 21st Century session, Dr Gitahi warned that prevention and vaccination budgets "are the first to be cut" when fiscal space tightens, because their results are less visible.

Nigeria shows the risk: in 2025, only ₦36 million of the ₦218 billion appropriated for federal health capital projects was released. For Nigeria, the value of health investment lies in the industries it builds and the workers it equips. Realising that value requires funding, procurement and regulation to support these goals.

Close 

The following steps could help put this into practice;

The Office of the Accountant-General and Budget Office should include health infrastructure in quarterly cash plans and publish how much funding is released.

The National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) and state schemes should automatically enrol eligible conditional cash transfer beneficiaries and publish whether enrolment reduces their out-of-pocket spending. In addition, the NHIA, the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA), and state governments could consider offering qualified Nigerian manufacturers multi-year purchasing agreements with clear standards for price, quality, and delivery. Reliable demand would make it easier for manufacturers to invest.

Incentives under the Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain (PVAC) and NAFDAC approval pathways should reward verified local production, including making ingredients and meeting quality standards. Annual reporting should show which products are replacing imports.

Health belongs in Nigeria's growth strategy for the same reason ports and power do: the economy depends on it. That case must be reflected in funding released on time, stronger local production and affordable, quality care. Nigeria needs to spend more on health, use the funds strategically and measure whether people and the economy are better off.

World.title: 135 people arrested across France as police find potential weapons on protestors, official says
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

French authorities have so far arrested 135 people Saturday as nationwide protests resumed, France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told reporters.

Most of the arrests were prompted after police officers preemptively searched protesters, Reuters reported. Those taken into custody allegedly had items that could be used as weapons, including fireworks and ball bearings.

Nuñez did not specify where the arrests were made. In Paris, where tens of thousands of people are marching, police said they have conducted more than 3,000 checks and arrested 65 people, the BBC reported.

"Violent individuals have no place in the marches," the Paris Police Department said in a social media post. "The objective is clear: to prevent troublemakers from joining the procession, and to ensure the safety of the demonstrators."

AMERICANS WARNED ABOUT PARIS TRAVEL AFTER VIOLENCE, LOOTING AND TEAR GAS-FILLED STREETS

Central Paris resembled a city under lockdown, as shopkeepers boarded up storefronts, museums closed and more than 20 metro stations suspended service.

In other cities — including Clermont-Ferrand, Grenoble, Lille and Nice — police have resorted to firing tear gas to break up unruly crowds, Reuters reported.

Also in Nice, police used a water cannon to disperse a group of demonstrators who refused to pull back. And in Marseille and Lyon, there have been clashes between police officers and hooded youths.

FRANCE’S TEEN RIOTS TAKE EXPLOSIVE NEW TURN AS GOVERNMENT POINTS FINGER AT HARD LEFT

Some 70,000 police officers have been deployed across France to clamp down on agitators and prevent the kind of unrest seen during recent demonstrations, when cars were torched and the city hall building in Limoges was set on fire.

Last weekend, more than 2,700 people were arrested during protests that later turned into riots and looting sprees.

The nationwide marches were meant to reflect broader dissatisfaction with the French government, with protesters taking to the streets to air a range of different grievances.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The protests began weeks earlier and were led by high school and university students. They were frustrated with teacher shortages and poor conditions at schools, including overcrowded classrooms and dilapidated buildings.

The movement gained momentum when major labor unions joined the demonstrations, broadening the protests to include opposition to the government's austerity policies and concerns over wages, pensions and the overall cost of living.

World.title: French CEO warns 'purely chaotic' riots prove the country has reached the 'dead end of socialism'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

France has reached the "dead end of socialism" as violent protests spread across the country, a French artificial intelligence entrepreneur said Friday.

Speaking on "The Faulkner Focus," Brivael Le Pogam blamed decades of left-wing policies for what he described as growing unrest and declining public services in France.

"Right now we are just seeing the dead end of socialism," Le Pogam, CEO and co-founder of Argil AI, said.

FRENCH AI CEO WARNS AMERICANS AGAINST VOTING DEMOCRAT SAYING 'YOU DON'T WANT TO BE FRANCE'

"It's super sad, and it's purely chaotic right now. And I think, so, basically there is a lot of different causes, but mainly for me, it's the consequences of socialism," he added.

The demonstrations began with students expressing frustration over conditions at their schools and the quality of education. Protests have since spread across France, with some turning violent and leading to looting and thousands of arrests.

On Saturday, thousands marched in Orléans, southwest of Paris, to protest what they described as fascism, while other demonstrators gathered in the capital. French authorities said they planned to deploy 70,000 police officers ahead of additional demonstrations to prevent a repeat of the destruction and looting seen the previous weekend.

PHOTOS SHOW AFTERMATH OF RIOTS AS MASKED GROUPS CLASH WITH POLICE ACROSS FRANCE

Le Pogam said that despite France's universal healthcare system, patients in some parts of the country face lengthy waits to see a doctor or receive certain medical services.

"We are paying through taxes, through the salaries for that. But years by years, there is some zone in France where you need to wait, for example, one year to get a doctor," he said.

Le Pogam argued that government control has also contributed to declining standards in education and other public institutions.

"Basically like the education, everything touched by the states, it's just crumbled and becoming bad and bad year by year," he added.

FIFTY ANTIFA GROUPS IN FRANCE JOIN VAST NETWORK TO ENSURE CHAOS IN WEEKEND PROTESTS

French President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday that the government would move to prohibit what he called "illegitimate" protests. He also accused "ultra-left groups" of fueling the unrest, saying their goal was to "bring down the Republic."

President Donald Trump also expressed concern about the unrest and questioned whether the NFL should proceed with Sunday's scheduled regular-season game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints at Stade de France in Saint-Denis, just outside Paris.

"I would have said the NFL could have probably postponed that match if you want to know. Because France is really in trouble," Trump told reporters Friday. "That's what happens when you go left. That's what happens when you allow unlimited numbers of people into your country from very unfriendly countries."

Le Pogam also criticized the government's response to the demonstrations, arguing that authorities have a responsibility to protect the public.

"The crazy thing is the government say to the people to protect themselves and for me, it's crazy," he said. "It's literally the — it's the fate of the states to protect people, and we are seeing that everywhere."

World.title: Jalen Hurts puts spotlight on blood thinners: 5 mistakes that could put patients at risk
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts' diagnosis of blood clots in both lungs has put blood thinners in the spotlight.

Hurts is receiving treatment with the medication and is expected to miss the remainder of the 2026 season, according to the NFL.

Even young, physically active people can develop dangerous blood clots, especially when risk factors such as an injury, long travel or recent surgery combine. "Being in shape lowers your risk, but it doesn’t make you immune," said Dr. Joseph V. Lombardi, chief physician executive at AtlantiCare.

CHRISTINA APPLEGATE'S MS MISDIAGNOSIS AFTER 5 YEARS OF TREATMENT EXPOSES ALARMING MEDICAL REALITY

Hurts’ case also highlights the precautions patients taking blood thinners may need to follow.

The medication can help prevent dangerous clots from growing or forming but can also make it harder for the body to stop bleeding after an injury — a concern for athletes playing high-contact sports or anyone who falls or gets hurt.

"Taking [blood thinners] consistently, understanding potential interactions, and recognizing warning signs can greatly reduce the risk of complications," Dr. Yazan Abou-Ismail, a hematologist and thrombosis expert at the University of Utah, told Fox News Digital.

STACKING SUPPLEMENTS WITHOUT KEY TEST CAN DO MORE HARM THAN GOOD, EXPERT WARNS

Here are five mistakes patients should avoid:

1. Stopping treatment without medical guidance

While some patients only need blood thinners for a limited time, others may need them long term. When a clot has a clear cause, such as an injury, treatment often lasts about three months, Lombardi told Fox News Digital.

The duration depends on factors including the reason for treatment and whether a patient has had previous clots, Abou-Ismail added. Stopping too soon can raise the risk of another clot, while continuing longer than prescribed may increase bleeding risk.

SILENT INFLAMMATION COULD BE DAMAGING YOUR BODY — AND 5 HABITS MAY HELP KEEP IT IN CHECK

Patients should not stop or extend treatment without speaking with their doctor.

2. Skipping or doubling doses

Missing doses repeatedly can weaken a medication's protection against clots, Abou-Ismail said, but what to do after a missed dose depends on the specific drug.

Patients should follow the instructions for the prescription or call their pharmacist or doctor — not automatically take an extra dose to make up for a missed one.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

3. Adding medications or supplements without checking

Aspirin and NSAIDs including ibuprofen can increase bleeding risk when taken with blood thinners, Abou-Ismail said. Some prescription drugs and supplements, including fish oil and turmeric, can also affect bleeding or medication levels.

Patients should ask a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything new, even if it is sold over the counter.

4. Brushing off signs of serious bleeding

Some bruising or minor bleeding may occur but persistent nosebleeds, blood in the urine or unexplained increases in bruising warrant a call to a health care provider, Abou-Ismail said.

CLICK HERE TO 

Uncontrolled bleeding, vomiting blood, black or tarry stools, a sudden severe headache or new confusion, vision changes or trouble speaking require urgent care.

After a significant head injury, patients should seek medical evaluation, even if they initially feel fine, experts note.

5. Taking part in high-risk activities

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

A hard hit or fall can lead to serious bleeding in patients taking a blood thinner, which is why Hurts cannot play football during treatment.

Patients should ask their doctor which activities are safe for them. Some may be able to continue exercising but contact sports and other activities with a high risk of injury warrant extra caution.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Blood thinners do not dissolve an existing clot, Lombardi cautioned. They help prevent it from growing while the body clears it over time. The right treatment and precautions vary, so patients should contact their care team with questions about doses, side effects or activity.

World.title: Bush dynasty delivers another blow to GOP in Texas Senate battle as family member breaks ranks
World.content:

Another member of the Bush family dynasty, Neil Bush, is throwing his weight behind Texas Democratic Senate hopeful James Talarico, saying he voted against a political style he believes has "damaged our country."

World.title: Your credit can look normal while someone steals your identity
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

You check your credit score, see nothing unusual and assume your identity is safe. But what if someone has already stolen your personal information and your credit report shows absolutely nothing? That's entirely possible.

Credit monitoring can help detect certain types of identity theft, particularly fraud involving new credit accounts. However, criminals can also target your existing bank accounts, retirement savings, government benefits and phone number without triggering a traditional credit alert. As a result, a clean credit report can give you a false sense of security. Here's what credit monitoring can catch, what it might miss and how to better protect yourself.

Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Join us Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com.

IDENTITY THEFT PROTECTION IS CHANGING: WHAT TO LOOK FOR

What credit monitoring actually watches

Credit monitoring tracks changes to your credit file. Depending on the service, it can alert you to suspicious activity involving your credit history.

Common alerts include:

New credit accounts: A lender reports a newly opened account.

Hard credit inquiries: Someone applies for credit using your information.

Credit score changes: Your score changes because of activity reported to a credit bureau.

Collections activity: A collection account appears on your credit report.

These alerts can help you discover new account fraud before the damage grows. However, credit monitoring depends on information that lenders and other companies report to credit bureaus. Therefore, it cannot reliably detect identity theft that occurs entirely outside the credit reporting system.

Six ways criminals can target you without triggering credit monitoring

Criminals have several ways to misuse your information, steal money or make you more vulnerable to fraud without triggering a traditional credit monitoring alert. Here are six situations worth watching for.

1. Existing bank account takeover

A criminal gains access to your existing checking account, savings account, retirement account or payment app. Because the account already exists, the takeover may never appear on your credit report. Instead, you might first discover the theft through an unfamiliar transaction or a notification from your financial institution.

2. Government benefits and tax fraud

Someone uses your Social Security number to file a fraudulent tax return or claim government benefits. You may receive an IRS notice about a tax return you never filed. Alternatively, you could discover unemployment benefits claimed in your name. Neither situation necessarily changes your credit score.

3. Medical identity theft

A thief uses your health insurance information to receive medical care, prescriptions or equipment. You might then receive bills for services you never used. Even worse, someone else's medical information could end up in your records. Traditional credit monitoring generally will not detect the misuse itself, although unpaid debts could eventually create other financial complications.

4. SIM swap and phone account fraud

Criminals may convince your mobile carrier to transfer your phone number to a SIM card or device they control. Once they have your number, they may intercept certain verification codes and attempt to access your accounts. A sudden loss of cellular service could be an early warning sign, especially if you did not request a change.

5. Scams involving direct payments

A scammer tricks you into authorizing a wire transfer, sending money through a payment app or purchasing gift cards. Because you initiated the payment, even under false pretenses, traditional credit monitoring may have no indication that anything happened. Your financial institution might have separate fraud detection systems, but those protections vary.

6. Personal information exposed through data brokers

Your name, phone number, address and other personal details may appear on people-search websites or data broker databases. Criminals can use that information to create convincing phishing messages or impersonation scams. Although the exposure itself does not necessarily mean someone has stolen your identity, it can make you a more attractive target. The Federal Trade Commission identifies unauthorized bank withdrawals, unfamiliar medical bills and fraudulent tax filings among the warning signs of identity theft.

SOMEONE COULD HAVE OPENED AN ACCOUNT IN YOUR NAME. CHECK NOW

Why checking your credit score isn't enough

A credit score provides a snapshot of your creditworthiness based on information in your credit file. It does not show every account you own, or every place someone might use your personal information. For example, someone could access your retirement account while your credit score remains unchanged.

Similarly, criminals might use your phone number to get into an existing account without ever applying for credit. That's why it's important to review your actual credit reports rather than relying on your score alone. Even then, you'll need to check your other accounts separately.

How to spot identity theft your credit report can't catch

Fortunately, you can look for suspicious activity without paying for an expensive monitoring service. Start with these six habits.

1. Review your financial accounts regularly

Check your bank statements, investment accounts, retirement accounts and payment apps for unfamiliar transactions. Also, enable transaction and security alerts whenever your financial institutions offer them.

2. Watch for suspicious tax activity

Pay attention to IRS notices about returns you did not file or income from employers you don't recognize. You can also review your federal tax account through the official IRS website at irs.gov/ . You can also request a free six-digit Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN) from the IRS. This helps prevent someone else from filing a fraudulent federal tax return using your Social Security number. The IRS issues a new IP PIN each year.

3. Check your Social Security earnings record

Review your earnings history periodically to see whether it matches your actual employment. You can access your information through your my Social Security account at ssa.gov/myaccount. Unexpected earnings may require further investigation.

4. Review medical bills and insurance statements

Look for unfamiliar medical appointments, prescriptions, procedures or insurance claims. If something looks suspicious, contact your health insurance company or medical provider directly.

5. Protect your mobile phone account

Ask your carrier about account PINs, port-out protection and SIM swap safeguards. Additionally, consider using an authenticator app or security key instead of text-message verification when available.

6. Check where your personal information appears online

Search for your name, phone number and address to identify information exposed through people-search websites. You can request removal from individual sites or consider a reputable data removal service.

Pro tip: Choose one day each month to review your accounts and important records. You can combine it with a bill-payment routine to make the habit easier to maintain.

How identity theft protection services can help

Credit monitoring remains useful, but it cannot catch every type of identity theft. Some identity theft protection services offer broader monitoring that can help identify suspicious activity involving financial accounts, personal information and online accounts. However, the features and level of protection depend on the provider and plan you choose.

What to look for in identity theft protection

Credit monitoring: Alerts about new credit accounts, suspicious inquiries and changes to your credit reports.

Financial account monitoring: Notifications about potentially suspicious activity involving eligible bank accounts, investment accounts and retirement savings.

Dark web monitoring: Alerts when certain personal information, such as email addresses or passwords, appears in known data breaches or monitored dark web sources.

Phone takeover protection: Monitoring for signs that someone may be trying to transfer your phone number or take control of your mobile account.

Identity restoration assistance: Access to specialists who can help you navigate the recovery process if someone steals your identity.

Scam reimbursement: Some plans provide coverage for eligible financial losses, although limits, exclusions and eligibility requirements vary.

Data broker removal: Certain services help remove your personal information from participating people-search websites and data brokers.

Before signing up, compare the features, coverage limits and costs. Pay attention to which financial accounts qualify for monitoring and whether the service offers restoration assistance if identity theft occurs. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com

Remember: No identity theft protection service can prevent every scam or detect every instance of fraud. These services work best alongside strong passwords, multifactor authentication, account alerts and regular reviews of your financial statements.

What to do if you discover identity theft

If you suspect someone is using your information, act quickly. You do not need to wait for a credit monitoring alert.

Contact the affected institution. Call your bank, retirement plan administrator, mobile carrier or insurance company using its official contact information. Ask about securing or freezing affected accounts.

Change compromised passwords. Update your login credentials and enable multifactor authentication. Avoid relying on text-message verification if your phone number may be compromised.

Report identity theft to the FTC. Visit IdentityTheft.gov to file a report and receive a personalized recovery plan.

Contact the appropriate government agency. For suspected tax fraud, contact the IRS. For Social Security-related fraud, contact the Social Security Administration.

Consider freezing your credit. A free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion can make it harder for someone to open new credit accounts using your identity.

Keep detailed records. Save suspicious messages, account statements, confirmation numbers and notes from conversations with institutions.

You can also review your credit reports at AnnualCreditReport.com. The FTC confirms that free weekly online reports are available from the three nationwide credit bureaus.

Kurt's key takeaways

I always encourage people to keep an eye on their credit, but I wouldn't rely on a credit score to tell me whether my identity is safe. Someone could be accessing an existing financial account or misusing personal information without causing any immediate change to that score. That's why I recommend checking financial statements, turning on account alerts and taking advantage of additional safeguards when they're available. Identity theft protection services can provide another layer of monitoring, but you still need to pay attention to activity in your accounts.

When was the last time you checked your bank accounts, medical statements or phone account for signs of identity theft rather than relying on your credit score? Let us know in the comments below. Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

World.title: Why the over 56.5 is the play as Houston visits undefeated Utah in Big 12 action
World.content:
There are just two ranked matchups today, and one of those was between two SEC big shots, and then this one between two Big 12 teams. The Big 12 hasn’t gotten a ton of love this season, but there are four teams in the top 14 of the national rankings. You could make an argument that this is the best conference in college football. It wouldn’t be a great argument, but you could make it.

Tonight we have Houston taking on Utah in one of the best matchups of the day.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The Houston Cougars come into the game with a 3-1 record and as the 14th-ranked team in the country. Their lone loss this year was against Texas Tech in a very close road game. They lost the game 28-26, clearly putting up a strong fight. It hasn’t been completely smooth sailing for the team, though. They’ve won the past four weeks, beating Georgia Southern by 14 points, then UCF by 10 the following week.

In the past two weeks, the team has taken down Kansas State and Oklahoma State. Against Kansas State, they won by 19 points on the road. Against the Cowboys, they won by just three. In fairness to Houston, they entered the fourth quarter with an 11-point lead over Oklahoma State. The Cowboys put up 14 points in the quarter, but a Houston touchdown gave them a lead Oklahoma State could never get passed.

THE SEC MIGHT HAVE MORE HEADLINERS, BUT THE BIG 12 HAS THE MOST UNDERRATED MATCHUP OF WEEK 4

The Utah Utes, the worst-named team in football, are 6-0 and the 10th-ranked team in the country. This will be the toughest game they’ve played to date, and it might be one they were already focused. Last week they took on Colorado on the road, but won 27-24. I think Utah might’ve already been thinking about this game, because the Buffaloes aren’t even close to being as good as the Utes. Sometimes teams just have bad games, but that’s okay.

Utah has also beaten Kansas, Iowa State, Utah State, Arkansas, and Idaho this season. The only game that was within one score was the Colorado game. Their next closest game was against Iowa State, also a road game, where they still won by 14 points. At home this season, they’ve won by an average of 33.8 points.

Their team is built around quarterback Devon Dampier. He has completed about 69% of passes this season with 15 touchdowns and four interceptions. He has also run for another three scores this season. He does a bit of everything for the team, and Houston will have their hands full trying to stop him.

HOUSTON RALLIES FOR COMEBACK VICTORY OVER UCF IN FRONT OF A PAINFULLY SPARSE HOME CROWD

This game features two really good offenses. Connor Weigman from the Cougars is one of the better quarterbacks in the league. He has 20 touchdown passes this season in seven games. Dampier might be slowed down a bit, but I doubt he can be stopped altogether. I expect the two teams to both challenge all three levels repeatedly. I’m going to take the over 56.5 in this game.

World.title: Exclusive: DOJ reviewing Portland Thorns incident showing women’s sports supporters struck, forcibly removed
World.content:
The U.S. Department of Justice is reviewing a confrontation at a professional women's soccer match in Portland, Oregon after video captured women’s sports supporters forcibly escorted out by stadium security after being struck with a flagpole by other spectators projecting pro-transgender messaging.

"The Justice Department is aware of these reports and will review the matter thoroughly. Where the facts and the law warrant action, the Department will not hesitate to act," a department spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

A DOJ official separately said, "Based on what is known so far, the conduct described appears to raise viewpoint discrimination and First Amendment questions rather than sex discrimination. The Department is reviewing it."

ACTIVISTS EJECTED FROM SOCCER MATCH AFTER 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' BANNER IGNITES PHYSICAL CLASH WITH PRO-TRANS FANS

The Portland Police Bureau has also addressed the incident, saying two potential crimes have been reported.

"Off duty PPB officers are routinely hired to work at professional games and other events at various venues in Portland, and there were several at the Thorns game last night. PPB officers were not involved in any removals. They were called in when some individuals were refusing to leave and laying down, blocking an exit. When asked by police officers, the individuals agreed to leave. Outside, in an effort to promote public safety, officers did separate two groups with opposing viewpoints for a short time," Sergeant Kevin Allen told Fox News Digital.

"Two potential crimes were reported, case numbers 26-309064 (alleged harassment) 26-309306 (alleged vandalism). No one reported any injuries to police, and no injuries were visible. No immediate arrests were made or citations issued. The incidents are under investigation. Officers were wearing and activated BWCs according to PPB policy."

The confrontation unfolded Friday during Portland’s match against the North Carolina Courage at Providence Park. Approximately 20 spectators kept their XX-XY Athletics shirts covered through the first half, then revealed them and unfurled a large "Save Women’s Sports" banner as the second half began.

The organizers included activist Amy Sousa and commentator Brandi Kruse, who previously helped organize rallies supporting WNBA player Sophie Cunningham.

WNBA FACES GROWING SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM MOVEMENT AS NEW RALLIES ARE SET FOR FEVER GAMES IN OREGON, MINNESOTA

Footage documented members of the group being struck with flagpoles carrying transgender flags, confronted with profanity and physically removed by security.

Sousa told OutKick that she and other attendees filed police reports afterward.

"We were attacked by fans. We were hit with flags," she said.

Security restrained Kruse’s arm behind her back while escorting her through the stands. She questioned why her group was being removed after being attacked.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SUPPORTERS OPEN UP ON ENCOUNTER WITH SECURITY, PRO-TRANS FANS IN LATEST WNBA CULTURE CLASH

OutKick reporter Matt Calkins also had his phone knocked from his hand and beer poured on his neck while documenting the confrontation. A security guard pulled his credential from around his neck during an interview with Sousa, returning it seconds later.

Security director Jim McCausland said he did not have time to speak.

The Thorns' home stadium of Providence Park is owned by the City of Portland and operated by Peregrine Sports, LLC, according to the city. The Thorns are owned separately by RAJ Sports. Portland’s Spectator Venues Program oversees the city’s interests in the stadium and its relationship with the operator.

Viewpoint discrimination generally involves the government restricting expression because of the particular opinion expressed. The Supreme Court ordinarily prohibits such restrictions, according to Congress's Constitution Annotated.

Federal law also allows criminal prosecution under 18 U.S.C. § 242 when someone acting under color of law willfully deprives another person of a federally protected right.

The DOJ could examine whether city officials helped set or enforce the decisions to remove the fans because of their views. If officials, or private staff acting with them, willfully violated spectators’ constitutional rights, federal criminal charges could follow. The stadium’s public ownership alone does not establish a violation; the government’s involvement in the removals would be a key question.

The DOJ has not identified that statute as the basis for its review or announced charges in this matter.
