World.title: Proposed Law to Curb Powers of Hague-Based Court Returned to Kosovo Assembly
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Supporters of former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leader and former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci take part in a march in support of him in Pristina, Kosovo, prior to the verdict, September 12, 2026. EPA/GEORGI LICOVSKI

Kosovo President Justina Shiroka Pula sent the amended Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC) bill back to parliament on Thursday for review on the request of the Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK) which had proposed the bill, less than three weeks after its controversial approval.

The law, which aims to curtail the jurisdiction of the Hague-based court, came after weeks of street protests led by Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) veterans, who rallied under the slogan “Not in my name” – a reference to the KSC judge’s choice of words, “In the name of the people of Kosovo”, when he read the verdict.

“The president received a formal proposal from the parliamentary group of the Democratic Party of Kosovo – the sponsor of the legislation – to allow the assembly to reconsider the law, specifically the provisions concerning the jurisdiction and mandate of the Specialist Chambers,” read a statement from the president’s office on Thursday.

“The president has reiterated her opposition to any attempt to distort the historical truth of Kosovo, to cast doubt on the liberationist nature of the war, or to equate the people who fought for freedom and survival with the regime that oppressed them,” the statement read.

The initial bill was passed after four former KLA leaders were convicted by the KSC for the war crimes of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder, committed between April 1998 and June 1999.

Hashim Thaci and Jakup Krasniqi were sentenced to 25 years in prison each and Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi received 18 and 13 years, respectively, with credit for time served in detention from November 2020. The verdict can be appealed and their lawyers are working to challenge the conviction.

Given the uncertainty over whether the KSC will indict anyone else, the effect of the bill is uncertain, but the message it sent was clear, and the European Union was unhappy.

“The Law […] goes against Kosovo’s international obligations towards the EU,” read a statement from the EU after the law was initially approved. The EU finances most of the court’s operations.

In a speech at the Berlin Process Summit in Montenegro on Thursday, European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said that “weeks and months of defining moments” lie ahead for the Western Balkans and reminded Kosovo of its obligations under international law.

On Thursday, Perparim Gruda, a MP from PDK who was involved in drafting the recent KSC bill wrote on Facebook that “there is no error in the law amending the Law on the Specialist Chambers.”

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers is a hybrid court, part of Kosovo’s judiciary but located in The Hague and staffed by internationals. The court was established in 2015 under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies. Hashim Thaci was one of the main Kosovar supporters of the establishment of the court.

Since the conviction of the former KLA leaders over a month ago, criticism of the KSC has continued unabated in Kosovo. On October 14, Kosovo’s Ombudsperson, Naim Qelaj, held an event in Pristina to demand external oversight of the KSC.

Qelaj claimed that the court “has not been subject to democratic monitoring and control by the institutions of the Republic of Kosovo, creating a lack of transparency and accountability towards the citizens and institutions of Kosovo”.

He said it should report to the Kosovo authorities and that the Ombudsperson institution should be able to have access to its work.

KSC spokesperson Angela Griep told BIRN that “according to the legal framework of the Specialist Chambers, the Kosovo Ombudsperson does not have any responsibility with respect to the Specialist Chambers. This responsibility falls exclusively with the Ombudsperson of the Specialist Chambers in accordance with the Kosovo Constitution”.

World.title: One Dead, Crew Members Missing After Ship Sinks off Romania
World.content:
A Romanian navy squad during NATO naval drill ‘Sea Shield 24’ on the Black Sea, off the coast of Constanta, Romania, 16 April 2024. Photo: EPA/ROBERT GHEMENT

Romanian maritime authorities launched a rescue operation on Friday morning about 24 kilometres off the coast after a vessel was reportedly struck by a drone.

Rescuers are continuing to search for three missing crew members, according to preliminary reports.

The circumstances of the incident remain unclear, including the origin of the drone and whether the vessel was deliberately targeted.

President Nicusor Dan reacted swiftly to the incident, saying that it “is another event in the process of escalation that Russia is pursuing in the Black Sea region.”

The sinking follows an incident on October 15 when two other commercial ships were hit overnight while anchored in the Black Sea near the mouth of the Danube-Black Sea Canal, a major shipping route used to transport Ukrainian goods. Ukraine’s Black Sea ports have been a frequent target of Russian attacks.

Similar incidents have also occurred in Bulgarian territorial waters, where drone strikes have reportedly left at least 23 sailors dead or missing.

The escalating tensions in the Black Sea have prompted NATO to announce increased surveillance in the region following recent attacks on commercial vessels.

Meanwhile, Romania has proposed that it join Bulgaria and Turkey, the other two NATO member states bordering the Black Sea, in establishing a joint military command to be led by the three countries on a rotational basis.

World.title: Alleged Police Violence Against Minors Alarms Albania
World.content:
In a video shared on Monday evening, a group of police officers can be seen rushing towards several young people and beating them with batons. Amid the blows, one of them can be heard shouting that he is only 13 years old.

BIRN was unable to independently verify the ages of the young people in the video, but similar footage showing police in Tirana using violence against protesters, including minors, has circulated widely in the media and on social media over the past week.

The footage has raised concerns about how the State Police is treating children and teenagers involved in the wave of protests against Prime Minister Edi Rama’s government.

World.title: Serbia Braces for Most Uncertain Elections in 14 Years
World.content:
On Sunday, Serbia is bracing for what could be its most uncertain and high-stakes elections in 14 years, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, facing a challenge that has emerged out of a two-year student-led protest movement.

Since 2012, Aleksandar Vucic and his party SNS have largely dominated the political and electoral landscape. This time, however, the election outcome is far less predictable, political analysts say, as the student movement has reshaped the opposition landscape and mobilised supporters well beyond the established parties.

“These are the first elections in a long time whose outcome is entirely uncertain,” Nebojsa Vladisavljevic, a professor at the Faculty of Political Sciences in Belgrade, told BIRN.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Czech Culture Ministry Cuts Funding for Velvet Revolution Anniversary
World.content:
Former Hungarian central bank chief detained; govt tries to solve budget dilemma

Hungary’s former central bank governor, Gyorgy Matolcsy, was detained on Wednesday on suspicion of economic fraud causing substantial financial losses and the use of forged documents. Under Matolcsy, the Hungarian National Bank spent lavishly on refurbishment projects and established several foundations that channelled money into dubious foreign investments and projects that seemed to benefit family and friends. Several hundred billion forints are alleged to have been diverted from the central bank during his tenure or lost through investments. Media estimates put the total losses at 400-500 billion forints (1.0-1.4 billion euros). The current governor, Mihaly Varga, a former finance minister, and his team had submitted more than 30,000 pages of documents to the special investigative committee on central bank affairs by the end of September. Matolcsy’s detention signals the new government and prosecutors are getting serious about making key figures in the previous administration accountable for financial losses incurred during their 16 years in power. Matolcsy, once former PM Viktor Orban’s cherished economy guru, became governor of the central bank in 2013 after serving as economy minister in 2010-2014. Matolcsy’s term ended in 2025. His son and people in his business circle were reportedly among the main beneficiaries of lavish renovations to the central bank building.

Hungary’s new government tabled its first draft budget, causing disappointment in various quarters. The finance minister warned that budget discipline is necessary to prepare the country for joining the euro, planned for 2030-2032. In the draft budget for 2027, the government has pledged to cut the deficit from the current 7.0 per cent of GDP to 4.9 per cent by the end of next year and to 2.9 per cent for the end of its term in office in 2030. Inflation is forecast at 3.0 per cent and GDP growth at 2.4 per cent. Both Finance Minister Andras Karman and PM Peter Magyar acknowledged that there is a need for further wage increases in several sectors, but those could only happen “step by step”. As for immediate measures, the government fulfilled its electoral promise of doubling childcare to 24,000 forints (66 euros) a month per child and raising the minimum pension from January 2027. The draft budget would increase corporate taxes for multinationals, aligning with the global minimum tax regulations, from the current 9 per cent to 11.25 per cent. The government is introducing a special wealth tax for assets over 1 billion forints, and will further tax energy companies and banks. Major investments are pledged for health care, transport and energy, mostly funded by the unblocking of frozen EU funds. Magyar argued in his two-hour speech to parliament that cutting the deficit is essential, pointing to France and Romania as examples of governments unable to halt the spiral in spending. “Powerful, major economies – including European economies – are struggling in a debt trap, with the burden of interest payments choking their economies,” he said. Most controversial is the promised 1.5-trillion-forint cut in public sector funding. The police said they were disappointed by the 15 per cent wage increase and teachers voiced concerns about the 25 per cent increase pledged by the government from 2027. Workers in the cultural sector staged a small protest against their 10 per cent rise. “There are also sectors where there are no wages increases at all,” Magyar pointed out to those complaining, while asking for more societal solidarity.

World.title: What’s Going on With the Potential Šibenik Airport?
World.content:
October the 24th, 2026 – The idea of a future Šibenik Airport sounds feasible and very reasonable, but it seems like there’s been more than a few spanners thrown in the works…

The feasibility study and the revision of the conceptual design were supposed to be completed by the end of July this year, but almost three months later there is no public confirmation that the documents have been finished. As SibenikIN reports, in the meantime, the issue of the planned airport’s impact on the habitats of protected bird species has also been raised.

At a joint thematic session of the parliamentary committees for tourism and for maritime affairs, transport and infrastructure, held on Thursday the 22nd of October, the operations of Croatian airports, investments, their financial sustainability and future development were discussed. Representatives of the competent ministries, airports and the aviation sector took part in the discussion, and among the topics were the seasonality of traffic, the development of regional airports and the need for better transport connections.

However, the official parliamentary report fails to mention the Heart of Dalmatia airport project at Pokrovnik, in which Croatia holds a majority ownership stake. Although this does not rule out the possibility that the project was mentioned in passing during the session, it was not singled out among the development topics in the official summary.

the documentation should have been completed by july

Back in June this year, local portal ŠibenikIN reported on the status of the planned airport project at Pokrovnik. At that time, Šibenik Deputy Mayor Danijel Mileta, referring to a report by the company Zračna luka Srce Dalmacije that had been submitted to the City as one of the co-owners, confirmed that the feasibility study and the revision of the conceptual design with technical details were in preparation. According to the announcements at the time, both documents were supposed to be completed by the end of July 2026.

However, almost three months after the announced deadline expired, no publicly published confirmation has been found that the documents have been finished and handed over to the client. Such information is also not available on the company’s official website. At the same time, on 30 December 2025 the preparation of the environmental impact study and the main acceptability assessment of the intervention for the ecological network was contracted, with an 18-month deadline, i.e. approximately until mid-2027. According to the information obtained from the month of June, a geodetic elaborate, a climatological study and a project for a meteorological station had already been prepared, while the procedure for obtaining special conditions for the station itself was still ongoing.

protected bird habitats could become a serious problem…

In addition to the questions of deadlines and documentation, an additional obstacle has appeared that could affect the future of the project. As ŠibenikIN wrote in July, in the process of amending the Spatial Plan of Šibenik-Knin County the question of the planned airport’s impact on the habitats of protected bird species was raised.

Particularly highlighted were the calandra lark, the short-toed lark and the stone-curlew, whose habitats could be threatened by the construction and use of the airport. In the spatial-planning documentation it was warned that, due to nature-protection requirements, it might be necessary to re-examine the location or the category of the planned airport. Such a warning doesn’t mean that the ambitious Šibenik Airport project has been rejected or that construction at Pokrovnik has been banned. However, it opens the question of whether the existing conceptual design will be acceptable from the point of view of nature protection and whether additional changes will be required. It isn’t yet known whether these warnings have affected the preparation of the documentation that was supposed to be finished in July.

the state is the project’s majority owner

The Heart of Dalmatia airport project is being developed by the company of the same name, in which the Republic of Croatia holds a 55 percent ownership stake, while the remaining 45 percent belongs to Šibenik-Knin County and five cities. Josip Skelin was appointed director of the company back in May 2025.

Interestingly, State Secretary of the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure Tomislav Mihotić, who earlier participated on behalf of the state in the establishment of the company for the development of the Šibenik Airport, also took part in today’s parliamentary session on the future of Croatian airports. The Pokrovnik project has for years been presented as a possible contribution to transport connectivity and tourist development of this part of Dalmatia, but before any possible realisation a series of professional, spatial, environmental and financial questions still need to be resolved.

After the expiry of the July deadline for the key documentation, questions now remain open as to whether the feasibility study and the revision of the conceptual design have been completed, how much money has so far been spent on the project, what its current status is in the state transport plans, and whether nature-protection requirements will lead to a change in the planned location or category of the airport.

World.title: After Decades of Decay, Rijeka Torpedo Launch Station Will Rise Again
World.content:
October the 24th, 2026 – Following years of decay, the famous Rijeka torpedo launch station will be given back its full glory and turned into a tourist site.

Rijeka has an exceptionally rich industrial history, and one of its most important monuments is located on the western part of the city waterfront, in the former Torpedo factory complex. As Ivana Vasarevic writes for Putni Kofer, right next to the sea, stands an unusual reinforced-concrete structure – the historic torpedo launch station. This is the exact place where weapons intended for navies around the world were once tested. After very many years of deterioration, this building, protected as a cultural asset of Croatia, will finally receive the restoration it deserves. The current plans also include transforming the entire surrounding area into a new tourist attraction.

turning the clock back to the 1860s…

Commons/Muzej Rijeka

Sea salt, waves and weather over the decades seriously damaged the ramp, so the conservation department as early as 2019 ordered urgent protection measures. Fortunately, it was decided that the launch station would not be demolished and replaced by a replica, but that the original structure would be preserved. Works should begin in the last quarter of 2026 and be completed during 2027.

The answer as to precisely why this structure is so historically significant takes us 160 years into the past, when an invention that changed naval warfare was born in Rijeka. During the early 1860s, Rijeka native Giovanni Luppis was developing the idea of a defensive weapon with which enemy ships could be stopped before they approached land. He called it the “coast saver”, but he lacked the technical knowledge and funds for its realisation.

rijeka torpedos were sought after around the world

He presented the idea to Robert Whitehead, a British engineer and the former manager of the Rijeka Technical Institute. He then developed a torpedo resembling a metal fish that moved independently under the surface of the sea. The first usable torpedo was successfully tested in Rijeka in 1866, and nine years later the Institute became the R. Whitehead & Co. factory, the first torpedo factory in the world.

Rijeka torpedoes soon became sought after around the world. They were ordered by Great Britain, France, Italy, Germany, Sweden, Japan, Russia and many other countries. The factory expanded its business, opened plants abroad, and production in Rijeka continued until 1966. Of course, before delivery to customers the torpedoes had to undergo a series of demanding tests. That is precisely what the launch stations were used for, from which trial launches were carried out and the behaviour of the torpedoes in the sea was monitored.

The first launch ramps were wooden structures from the 19th century, and over time they were replaced by a more solid reinforced-concrete station. According to data from the Museum of the City of Rijeka, it was built in 1930, and four years later a section intended for testing torpedoes launched from aircraft was added. Thus the station served for simulating the launch of torpedoes from ships as well as from the air: Rijeka, after all, did not yet have its own airport at that time.

Although production ceased long ago, the ramp still reminds us of the time when Rijeka was an international centre of technological innovation. Its importance goes beyond local frameworks because it testifies to the development of an invention that changed world naval history. In addition to the restoration of the launch station, plans also include the arrangement of the Torpedo Visitor Centre. As the portal Fiuman recently reported, it would exhibit full-size torpedoes, their parts and technical elements, while a special virtual room would bring the history of this Rijeka invention closer through multimedia content.

transforming history into a tourist site

As for the architectural solution, it is conceived as a combination of industrial heritage and contemporary design. The façades of the centre should be adorned with archival photographs and technical drawings of torpedoes, while steel elements would in shape recall the plating of a submarine. Along the waterfront a promenade with a beautiful view of Kvarner and the launch station is planned, a viewpoint reached by stone steps, as well as a small square and the surrounding public areas.

World.title: Capped Prices Introduced for Pula Advent This Year
World.content:
October the 24th, 2026 – Good news for lovers of festive cheer as capped prices will be introduced for certain food and drink items sold at Pula Advent this year.

The City of Pula has decided to limit the prices of the most popular products at Advent stalls in order to make them more affordable. A city decision has set maximum amounts for part of the hospitality offer during the upcoming Advent. Index reports that rather unsurprisingly, this decision has been welcomed by all.

a new (capped) price list for pula advent

Under the new rules, the price of a hot dog, hamburger and bakalar (dried cod) will be limited to five euros. Mulled wine, hot chocolate and cocoa may cost a maximum of three euros, while the maximum price for tea and water will be two euros. The sweet offer, which includes fritule (fritters), pancakes and Christmas cookies, is also limited to three euros per portion. Deputy Mayor of Pula Siniša Gordić explained how the system will work. “It is about one product that caterers must have on offer, as stated in the public call. For the entire rest of the offer, if they want to have something additional, they can set the prices themselves if there is interest,” Gordić said. He added that a minimum quantity or portion has also been defined for the products with limited prices.

Danijel Britvić, who has been taking part in Pula Advent for years, considers the idea good, but warns that the quality of ingredients affects the final price. “Hot dogs are 80-gram items, an ordinary frankfurter that I already had for five euros in a large bun. We have a 100-gram sausage and it cannot cost five euros, but six or seven. I will have the same prices as last year, but I will also include a hot dog at the set price in the offer,” Britvić said.

What is new in Pula has already been a proven model in Poreč. There, part of the offer has been sold at limited prices for years, which has proven to be a successful practice. “We’ve adjusted those prices over the years according to market conditions, but always so that they remain within a framework that allows each of us to go out with friends to Advent, treat everyone to a drink and eat something, without it being too great a financial burden and so that they come back again,” said Ajna Temimović from the City of Poreč.

The first test of the new decision by the Pula city administration will be visible soon, as the public call for the lease of Advent stalls ends at the end of October.

World.title: Anušić: Ukraine is Showing the Bravery Croatia Did in the 1990s
World.content:
October the 24th, 2026 – Speaking in Vukovar, Defence Minister Ivan Anušić has stated that Ukraine is currently going showing the bravery Croatia did back during the 1990s.

Defence Minister Ivan Anušić spoke in Vukovar about how Croatia must continue to help Ukraine because its defeat or the imposition of an unjust peace could lead to a new war on the borders of the European Union.

“Such heroism, sacrifice and respect for one’s homeland is what we also saw in our Homeland War back in 1991. That is why we must continue to help the Ukrainian people who, unfortunately, are going through the same wartime fate we experienced in the 1990s. Because if Ukraine loses this war or if it’s forced into an unjust peace, we’ll once again have war on our own borders,” Anušić said, according to a statement from the Ministry of Defence (MORH). Index reports that the minister made the remarks at the premiere of the documentary film “Glory to the Heroes”, which tells the story of two Ukrainians of different political convictions who fought and died for the independence of their country.

After the premiere, Anušić took part in a panel discussion on the Homeland War and the war in Ukraine. Alongside him were Croatian defenders Fanika Janko and Ivan Lukić Zolja, as well as the documentary’s director Alceo Marti. The conversation was moderated by Goran Rotim.

Anušić stressed that Croatia, because of its own wartime experience, particularly understands what the Ukrainian people are going through today. “There are a great many parallels between our Homeland War and the war in Ukraine. The Croatian people, who themselves lived through the sufferings of war, have a special understanding for the Ukrainian people. Just as Vukovar in 1991 put up heroic resistance against a superior Greater Serbian aggressor and became a symbol of Croatian freedom, so Ukraine today is heroically fighting against Russian aggression and keeping the war away from the borders of the European Union,” Anušić said.

He added that Vukovar, because of its defence in 1991 and the suffering it endured during the Homeland War, is a particularly appropriate place for the premiere of a film about Ukrainian defenders. Speaking about the two Ukrainians whose destinies are shown in the documentary, Anušić emphasised that, despite their different political views, they defended their country together.

“One of your interlocutors in the film says that war brings out the worst in people, but it also brings out the best. Two young men who were politically on different sides, when the freedom of Ukraine was at stake, then had only one side – their common struggle for Ukraine,” the minister concluded. He added that similar stories of courage, sacrifice and unity can also be found among Croatian defenders from the Homeland War.

World.title: Four Croatian Aminess Campsites Win Prestigious ADAC Superplatz Award
World.content:
October the 23rd, 2026 – Four Croatian Aminess campsites have taken home the prestigious ADAC Superplatz award, further spotlighting the progress camping in Croatia has experienced.

The latest prestigious ADAC Superplatz award has been given to Aminess Style Camping Atea Resort on the island of Krk. Poslovni reports that the latest prestigious ADAC Superplatz award has been awarded to Aminess Style Camping Atea Resort on the island of Krk, as part of the jubilee 20th Croatian Camping Congress, thereby joining the camping resorts Maravea and Sirena in Novigrad and Avalona on the island of Pag, which already carry this label.

The latest awards come at a time when Croatian camping is further strengthening its already enviable international position. Croatia is increasingly profiling itself as one of the highest-quality European camping destinations, and Aminess, with its investments, innovations and high management standards, is confirming its position among the leading Croatian companies in the premium camping segment.

“Four campsites with the ADAC Superplatz label are confirmation of the quality of Aminess’s camping offer and its position at the very top of Croatian camping, but also an incentive for further investment in its development. We are particularly proud of Atea Camping Resort, in whose development we invested 32 million euros last year. Such awards show that investments, knowledge and the dedication of employees bring concrete results. Our ambition is to actively raise European camping standards by developing products that, in terms of quality, facilities and guest experience, compete with the best in Europe. Croatian camping is at the very top in Europe, and Aminess wants to actively contribute to its further development and strengthening of competitiveness,” said Mladen Knežević, President of the Management Board of Aminess.

The renovation of Aminess Atea Resort, worth a hefty 32 million euros, was completed in 2025, transforming the campsite into a five-star premium resort. The renovation included raising the quality of accommodation, arranging pitches and modern accommodation units, developing additional facilities for guests and introducing modern digital solutions. Special emphasis was placed on preserving the natural environment and increasing the share of green areas, while reducing accommodation capacities in order to provide guests with greater privacy, comfort and a higher-quality holiday experience. Achieving the highest quality standards, including the criteria for ADAC Superplatz, was one of the key goals of this investment.

ADAC Superplatz is otherwise one of the most prestigious awards in the entire European camping industry and is awarded by the German automobile club ADAC on the basis of very strict quality criteria. The award is therefore an important indicator of excellence, but also additional confirmation of the competitiveness of Croatian campsites on the demanding European market.

World.title: Croatian Studio Mipmap Developing Digital Version of HEAT Board Game
World.content:
October the 23rd, 2026 – The Croatian studio MipMap is currently developing the digital version of the award-winning and wildly popular HEAT board game.

The Croatian studio MipMap has joined forces with Asmodee, whose portfolio includes some of the world’s best-known board games. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the Croatian independent video game development studio Mipmap Digital, in cooperation with the international company Asmodee (whose portfolio includes some of the world’s most famous board games such as CATAN, Ticket to Ride and Dobble) is developing the official digital adaptation of the award-winning board game HEAT: Pedal to the Metal, published by Days of Wonder. The digital version of the game will be available on Steam as well as on devices running iOS and Android.

putting a digital spin on a 60s wonder

Set in the golden age of motor racing back during the 1960s, HEAT: Pedal to the Metal is a board game by Asger Granerud and Daniel Pedersen in which victory depends not only on speed, but also on timely decisions and judging how much the engine can be pushed. Players use cards to manage speed, successfully negotiate corners and compete against friends, computer-controlled opponents and players from around the world.

One of the main challenges for the talented Croatian development team was to transfer the experience of playing HEAT at the table onto screens of different sizes. The digital adaptation features three-dimensional depictions of four tracks located in the USA, France, Great Britain and Italy. Players will be able to race against computer-controlled opponents known as Legends, organise local races with friends, take part in championships that include garage upgrades, sponsorships and different weather and track conditions. Cross-platform play will also be available, along with private rooms and automatic player matching. The Legends expansion will be included free of charge from day one, and additional official expansions are planned after launch.

The cooperation between Mipmap Digital and Asmodee began with a simple conversation at the SPIEL Essen 2024 fair. The Croatian studio approached Asmodee representatives with the idea of a digital adaptation of HEAT, and the first meeting gradually grew into a collaboration with Days of Wonder on the development of the game. One of the main challenges for the development team was to transfer the experience of playing HEAT at the table onto screens of different sizes. The digital adaptation remains faithful to the rules and visual identity of the original game, while using the possibilities of the digital format for clearer presentation of information, camera focus on key moments of the race and automation of certain parts of the game.

a major partnership

“Two years ago, we went to SPIEL 2024 hoping to start a conversation about the possibility of a digital adaptation of HEAT. Returning to this year’s fair, now that the game is in development, is therefore particularly significant for us. HEAT has a very distinctive identity, both visually and in the way it is played, and we have worked closely with Days of Wonder to transfer everything that makes this game special into the digital version,” said Joško Mikuličić, director and co-founder of Mipmap Digital.

“We’re extremely pleased to be working with Croatia’s Mipmap. An exciting and distinctive board game like HEAT deserves the best possible digital adaptation. We’re more than sure that Mipmap, owing to its experience and passion for HEAT, will create an outstanding digital experience for players and further enrich the experience of playing this board game,” said Christian Dunn, Head of Interactive Content Licensing at Asmodee.

who are mipmap?

Mipmap Digital is otherwise independent Croatian video game development studio specialising in digital adaptations of board games. The studio was born out of a shared love of games and the well-known problem of board game enthusiasts: finding the time, place and company for joint play. Drawing on experience in video game development, the team decided to make favourite board games more accessible in digital form while retaining their distinctive characteristics.

Mipmap Digital’s portfolio includes digital adaptations of the board games Roll Player, Point Salad and Canvas, while HEAT: Pedal to the Metal is currently in development. Asmodee is one of the world’s leading companies in the board game industry, dedicated to connecting people through games and stories. With over 2,200 employees worldwide, the company has one of the largest portfolios of board games.

World.title: Negotiations Continue Between Zagreb Airport and Wizz Air
World.content:
October the 23rd, 2026 – Negotiations are continuing between Zagreb Airport and Wizz Air, with the popular airline citing cost issues being the primary remaining obstacle.

During September, 455,530 passengers passed through the airport, while the growth rate for the first nine months of the year fell to just 1.1 percent. As is somewhat seasonally appropriate, the capital’s airport recorded its third consecutive monthly drop in passenger numbers; in September traffic fell by 3.3 percent, continuing the slowdown that began back in July. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that during that month, 455,530 passengers passed through the airport, while the growth rate for the first nine months of the year shrank to only 1.1 percent. The latest figures come at a time when Croatia Airlines is reducing capacity during the process of renewing its fleet.

new routes and a new incentive scheme

Passenger numbers at the airport are expected to fall again in October, followed by a gradual recovery in November, while December, according to estimates, should remain at last year’s levels, reports Ex-Yu Aviation News. Zagreb Airport has attracted four new routes this year, including those to Warsaw (Modlin), Tel Aviv and Beijing (via Bucharest). By comparison, six new routes were introduced in 2025 and ten back in 2024. During 2026, the airport also lost four routes, three of which were operated by Croatia Airlines. Several factors have influenced the slowdown in growth: rising fuel prices, which make airlines more cautious about launching new routes; the stall in the expansion of Croatia Airlines’ network; and the increase in almost all basic airport charges and fees at Zagreb Airport.

Zagreb Airport is trying to return to stronger growth and has launched a new incentive scheme for which airlines can apply until the 31st of December. This new model significantly lowers the threshold for obtaining incentives compared with the previous system – in which the wildly popular Ryanair was the only beneficiary, and carriers were required to achieve at least 35,000 passengers per year. This change is expected to make the system more accessible, especially for smaller markets and airlines considering routes with lower passenger volumes. Another key difference concerns the duration and flexibility of the programme.

ongoing negotiations with wizz air

The previous model was designed for a five-year period, while the new one is limited to four years but introduces mechanisms that reward better results in the initial phase. Carriers that exceed the figure of 100,000 or 150,000 passengers in the first five years of operations can secure the continuation of incentives without the obligation to meet annual thresholds. As part of its new growth incentive model, Zagreb Airport is excluding certain destinations from the list of eligible ones, as they are considered either sufficiently developed or strategically less important within this programme.

Despite interest in Zagreb, Wizz Air announced this summer that costs associated with the airport remain the main obstacle to establishing a base in Croatia’s capital. Nevertheless, they have not ruled out the possibility of introducing flights to Zagreb and confirmed that negotiations are ongoing. Zagreb Airport ended last year with a record of almost 4.7 million passengers, an increase of 9.2 percent compared with 2024. Based on currently reported capacities on scheduled routes, Zagreb Airport is expected to record an overall capacity increase of 1.8 percent in November.

This is mainly contributed by Ryanair, which will offer just over 17,000 additional seats, as well as the new Air China route and capacity increases by Austrian Airlines, KLM and Air Serbia. For December, stagnation is currently forecast, with around 100 fewer seats than in the same month last year. Capacity reductions at Croatia Airlines, Lufthansa and Qatar Airways are the main factors negatively affecting growth during the last month of the year.

World.title: Hajduk Beats Thun 1-0 to End 32-Year Wait for European Away Win
World.content:
Hajduk made it two wins from two in the Conference League league phase on Thursday night, beating Thun 1-0 in Switzerland. Dalisson scored the only goal in the 17th minute. Gonzalo Garcia’s side dominated the first half but had to withstand heavy pressure after the break, in a match that featured remarkable misses at both ends.

The result ended a long wait. Hajduk’s last away win in the group or league phase of a European competition came on September 28, 1994, when Aljoša Asanović’s 88th-minute goal earned a 1-0 win over Steaua in Bucharest in the Champions League. Following their 2-1 win over Ajax in the opening round, Hajduk now have a maximum of six points from two matches.

Lineups

Thun (4-4-2): Steffen; Fehr, Bürki, Bamert, Mambwa; Reichmuth, Roth, Kait, Maier; Labeau, Dursun

Hajduk (4-2-3-1): Silić; Acapandié, Hadžikadunić, Marešić, Hrgović; Del Moral, Fayad; Bamba, Dalisson, Šotiček; Šego

Match report

Hajduk set the tone from the start. Bamba went down under a challenge from Mambwa in the Thun box in the 2nd minute without getting a decision, and needed treatment on his ankle. A minute later, Šego tested Steffen, who saved comfortably.

Hrgović broke superbly down the left in the 10th minute, but his pass for Šego was cut out. By the 13th minute, Hajduk had two-thirds of the possession and were pressing Thun high up the pitch, and four minutes later that pressure paid off. Nico Maier gave the ball away in midfield, and Dalisson carried it to the edge of the box. His first shot was blocked, but the ball came straight back to him, and the Brazilian flicked it into the net with the outside of his boot for 1-0.

Thun should have equalized in the 24th minute. Brighton Labeau got away from Acapandié and fired low inside the box, but Silić saved, and Furkan Dursun dragged the rebound wide from 16 meters. Mambwa blazed over from more than 20 meters in the 30th minute.

Thun saw more of the ball after falling behind, but Hajduk’s pressing kept them from settling, and the chances kept coming for them. Šotiček’s effort from around 20 meters in the 33rd minute was heading just inside the post until Steffen tipped it behind. From the resulting corner, Hrgović was free on the left of the box, but he fired well over. Fayad then shot straight at Steffen from 17 meters, and in the 37th minute Bamba struck the post directly from a corner.

Hrgović blocked a Fehr shot in the 44th minute. Two minutes were added, and Hajduk went in 1-0 up at the half, a lead that could easily have been bigger.

Neither side made changes at the break, but the balance shifted quickly. Del Moral was booked in the 47th minute for stopping a Mambwa run, and Thun began to push Hajduk back. Fehr curled wide of the right post from the edge of the box in the 54th minute. Labeau’s turn and shot was blocked two minutes later, and Roth was booked for pulling back Dalisson to stop a counter. Reichmuth then shot straight at Silić in the 58th minute.

Marešić was booked in the 64th minute. A minute later, Del Moral headed a Fehr free kick clear just ahead of Bürki, and Labeau sent a shot over from around ten meters after a corner.

Hajduk had a golden chance to double their lead in the 68th minute, when Olivier Mambwa shoved Bamba in the box, and Gillett pointed to the spot. Šego stepped up but struck a weak penalty down the middle, an easy save for Steffen.

Melnjak then replaced Šotiček for Hajduk. Reichmuth was booked in the 73rd minute for a foul on Del Moral.

Then came the miss of the night. In the 75th minute, Labeau broke down the right and squared the ball to Noah Christoffersson, who somehow put it wide of an empty net from close range.

García brought on Livaja and Dendoncker for Šego and Del Moral in the 78th minute, while Thun replaced Labeau and Roth with Braschi and Derbaci, and later Reichmuth with Lengen. Martin and Van Hoorenbeeck replaced Bamba and Fayad in the 84th minute. Livaja won a free kick two minutes later and then headed wide from the resulting cross.

Four minutes of stoppage time were added, and Hajduk nearly sealed it on the break in the 92nd minute, when Dalisson tried to lob from distance and hit the crossbar. Hajduk held on for a 1-0 win and a significant step towards the knockout phase of the Conference League.

World.title: Justice chancellor: Wild boar cannot be made to suffer when training hunting dogs
World.content:
The Ministry of Regional Affairs and the Ministry of Climate should establish clear legal rules for training hunting dogs using live wild boars to ensure animal welfare and legal clarity, the Chancellor of Justice's Office says.

Four years ago in May, the regional affairs minister issued a regulation on measures to prevent and control African swine fever, introducing an exemption under which the ban on keeping pigs outdoors does not apply to wild boars kept for training hunting dogs.

The Estonian Union for the Protection of Animals asked the chancellor of justice to examine whether the regulation complies with the Animal Protection Act. The organization also pointed out that the law provides no legal basis for using wild boars kept in artificial environments to train hunting dogs and that no detailed requirements have been established for such training.

Deputy Chancellor of Justice-Adviser Olari Koppel said the ban on keeping pigs outdoors is a biosecurity measure and that the minister has the authority to introduce exemptions, provided they comply with EU law and do not undermine animal disease prevention. Koppel therefore sees no reason to believe that the exemption for training hunting dogs violates these conditions.

However, he noted that the regulation only provides an exemption from the ban on keeping pigs outdoors. It does not provide a legal basis for using wild boars to train hunting dogs or authorize activities prohibited under the Animal Protection Act.

"The absence of a specific legal provision does not, however, mean that such an activity is prohibited, provided other applicable rules are followed," Koppel said, adding that it must be possible to conduct training without endangering the animal's welfare.

The law does not establish a specific legal basis or detailed requirements for training hunting dogs using live wild boars. The activity is primarily governed by the Nature Conservation Act and the general animal welfare requirements arising from it.

Under the Animal Protection Act, animals must not be subjected to suffering or pain. According to Koppel, if hunting dog training cannot be conducted without causing such harm, the executive branch cannot make the activity permissible through regulations, guidelines or administrative practices.

"In that case, only the Riigikogu can decide through legislation whether the objective of the training and the benefits it provides justify making an exception to the prohibition established by law," Koppel said.

Koppel said the lack of clarity in the regulations is a problem. To address it, the Ministry of Regional Affairs and the Ministry of Climate should establish the conditions for training hunting dogs in legislation rather than merely in guidelines or explanatory memorandums. This would ensure compliance with animal welfare requirements and provide legal clarity.

World.title: Isamaa party promises to close the climate ministry and create scandals committee
World.content:
Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu said at the party's council meeting in Tallinn that the campaign for Estonia's parliamentary elections has begun and is intensifying.

"Those same three parties that, under SALK's leadership, have established a politics of lies under both Kaja Kallas' and Kristen Michal's governments are now maneuvering to escape political punishment and put up camouflage nets," Reinsalu said, referring to the coalition Reform Party and Eesti 200, as well as the opposition Social Democrats.

According to the Isamaa chairman, Eesti 200 is being pressured to withdraw from the elections so that its remaining voters will instead bolster the Reform Party and the Social Democrats.

"So much for political accountability," Reinsalu said. "With the prime minister's speech to the party council, the Reform Party has launched a new wave of fearmongering and lies. This is being dressed up in a marketing campaign whose underlying message is that, yes, we have failed, but we will do better in the future."

"The Reform Party is featuring a beloved actor in its campaign, while the Social Democrats have adopted a different tactic, attempting to conceal their complicity in the Kallas-Michal government by maneuvering to put forward the secretary general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as their candidate for prime minister. This maneuver will not succeed!" the Isamaa chairman said.

Reinsalu summed up Isamaa's political plans following the 2027 Riigikogu elections with the words "Let the citizens decide."

The party plans to give citizens the right to initiate early elections, following the Latvian model, and to establish a commission of inquiry into scandals after the elections. Lying before the commission would be a criminal offense.

In the area of defense, the party plans to close the border with Russia.

Isamaa also pledged to introduce a supplementary budget that would cut spending.

"Cost-cutting starts at the top: parliamentary and ministerial salaries, closing the Ministry of Climate and a critical review of foundations and subsidies," the party pledged.

On taxes, Isamaa promised to abolish the motor vehicle tax and reduce value-added tax on basic foodstuffs (meat, fish, milk, fruit, vegetables and bread) to 13 percent starting July 1, 2027.

The party also promised to end what it described as the harassment of businesses. "The Climate Act will be thrown in the trash. Investment certainty and a stable operating environment will be restored for the resource-based economy."

The party pledged to carry out an artificial intelligence revolution with the same boldness that Estonia once demonstrated in building its digital state. "The goal is genuine productivity growth, exports and simpler government operations. Sovereignty risks will be taken into account."

Isamaa promised to protect fundamental freedoms and repeal unnecessary restrictions.

The party also pledged to ease the burden of raising children on families and protect teachers' incomes.

In the energy sector, the party will emphasize oil shale. "The energy sector will be provided with dispatchable generation capacity, domestic resources (including oil shale) and affordable prices. Efforts to render oil shale-based energy production unviable will be halted."

The party also promised stricter requirements for the use of Estonian in public spaces, a conservative immigration policy and the restoration of regional balance.

Parliamentary elections will take place in March 2027.

World.title: Passenger ferry traffic on Narva River in danger of being discontinued
World.content:
Passenger ferry service launched on the Narva River five years ago is at risk of shutting down as the riverboat Caroline has proved too large for the Port of Narva.

The riverboat Caroline made its final trip of the season from Narva to Narva-Jõesuu in late September. The vessel is currently docked at the Port of Sillamäe, but it remains unclear where it will go next or where it will spend the winter.

The Estonian Transport Administration discovered that Narva's river port is not authorized to accommodate vessels of Caroline's size.

"The Transport Administration conducted a port inspection and found that Caroline is not a small vessel, but the port is registered as a small craft harbor. The port must change its registration. The harbormaster must also hold a license to operate larger vessels rather than just a small craft operator's license," said Kert Süsmalainen, head of the Transport Administration's waterways and ports department.

According to the Transport Administration, the fact that Caroline had previously used the Port of Narva without any problems was due to an oversight by the port operator. Five years ago, the vessel's length was measured at the waterline. However, Caroline's actual length exceeds the permitted limit by 120 centimeters.

Narva River. Source: Jenny Va / ERR

The City of Narva is trying to resolve the issue quickly. The port's registration has already been amended and there are plans to establish a passenger waiting area. However, finding a qualified harbormaster for the passenger port could prove challenging.

"It's clear that there are no people with those qualifications in Narva. Language proficiency is another obstacle. Our concern, of course, is that if a harbormaster is hired solely because of our vessel, their entire annual salary costs will likely be passed on to us through port fees. That, in turn, raises the question of whether we can make the numbers work," said Caroline owner Kaspar Eisel.

Operating Caroline on the Narva River is becoming increasingly challenging financially. While the riverboat carried around 10,000 passengers per season in its early years, that number fell to just under 3,000 this summer.

Whether Caroline will operate on the Narva River next summer and under what conditions, will be determined through negotiations with the management of Narva's river port.

World.title: Estonian courts overloaded with prison inmate complaints
World.content:
Estonian prisoners are prolific filers of complaints, placing a significant burden on the courts. Prisoner complaints account for more than a quarter of all administrative court cases.

In 2025, prisoners filed a total of 908 complaints with the Tallinn and Tartu administrative courts, accounting for 27 percent of all administrative court cases. More than 680 complaints have been filed in the first nine months of this year.

The courts are preparing for an increase in complaints and their workload, involving both Swedish and Estonian prisoners.

"If around 600 prisoners are brought to Estonia and they file complaints at a similar rate to Estonian prisoners, we could expect approximately 300 complaints a year," said Kaupo Kruusvee, chairman of Tallinn Administrative Court.

He noted that the first complaints have already been filed by Estonian prisoners who believe that inmates transferred from Sweden enjoy better conditions.

Attorney Katarina Talumäe did not rule out the possibility that some of these complaints could be justified.

"One of the most significant long-term consequences of the prison rental agreement could actually be a positive impact, in some respects, on how Estonia's existing prison system operates," she added.

The courts will decide whether and under what circumstances the complaints are justified. According to court data, approximately 1.5 percent of prisoners' complaints have been upheld so far.

Prisoners challenge a wide range of issues, from living conditions to access to medical care.

Swedish prisoners have also raised their concerns with the chancellor of justice. They are dissatisfied with living conditions and see the language barrier as another problem.

Talumäe noted that foreign prisoners have also raised concerns about maintaining contact with family members and other loved ones in Sweden.

"This could result in additional, disproportionate costs for prisoners. Questions about whether certain restrictions are proportionate could ultimately lead to cases being brought before the administrative courts," she said.

According to Merle Ulst, director of Tartu Prison, the complaints are to be expected.

"We are examining the chancellor of justice's findings very carefully and will provide a response to the chancellor in early December," Ulst said.

Talumäe said that many complaints already consume court resources unnecessarily. However, there are currently no effective ways to limit the number of complaints.

"To my knowledge, the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs also has information on the number of disputes and we have suggested looking into how other countries handle the situation," Kruusvee said.

"There is also information suggesting that prisoners in neighboring countries do not turn to the courts nearly as frequently. It might be worth analyzing why this practice is so much more widespread in Estonia," he added.

World.title: Expert: SDE waiting in the wings as disappointment with other parties mounts
World.content:
The Social Democrats' recent rise in the polls may reflect voters growing disillusioned with their preferred parties, while Isamaa's declining support could be linked to a lack of fresh ideas, a political analyst says.

Why have the Social Democrats gained ground?

One important factor that has remained unchanged for many years is that the Social Democrats are the second choice for quite a few people. They have another favorite party, but the Social Democrats would be their next choice.

Perhaps we are now in a situation where a large number of people no longer see their first choice as a good option. That could just as easily change again as we get closer to the elections.

So is that first choice the liberal Reform Party, meaning the liberal Social Democratic Party is winning over its voters?

Quite possibly. We do try to distinguish between parties based on which are liberal and which are not, but I think that distinction is no longer as clear as it was years ago. We have seen parties pursue policies that are very difficult to reconcile with their former image.

That may be one reason why people feel their first choice is not particularly appealing right now. Looking at the changes in Emor's polling, they have been quite sharp. We probably need a little more time to see whether this is a lasting shift.

Riina Solman (Isamaa) says the Social Democrats will run out of steam by March, but what is behind Isamaa's decline? Have they run out of steam themselves, with no new ideas or new faces?

Perhaps to some extent. But maybe this is simply an interim period with a little less news, because they really haven't introduced any new issues. As for new faces, though, that doesn't mean they haven't reached agreements with people that we know nothing about.

We didn't know the Social Democrats had reached an agreement with Jonatan Vseviov either. Such decisions are usually announced at a tactically opportune moment. We may yet see new names emerge from other parties as well, which could change the situation again.

Is Jonatan Vseviov a good candidate for prime minister? Will he boost the Social Democrats' support?

Why wouldn't he be? The fact is that we know relatively little about him at the moment and people who don't follow politics on a daily basis know even less. Those who do follow politics are probably familiar with his views on security, defense and foreign policy. But when someone becomes a candidate for prime minister, they have to take positions on a very wide range of issues and we still know very little about where he stands on those.

How much time is left to generate excitement with electoral candidate lists? The lists will soon have to be finalized, campaigns will have to get underway and the battles over places on the lists will have to be settled.

Perhaps some of those battles have already been settled. The final fine-tuning of the lists may continue for a while, but I believe the top spots in some electoral districts have already been decided. There may simply be some names we don't know yet. Only a couple of parties have launched campaigns on a larger scale, so we've really only seen the opening moves so far.

The last election seemed to be a contest between two parties, with voters having to choose between them. Will the message of this election be about who can attack the Reform Party the hardest?

That will certainly be part of it.

Isamaa is undoubtedly counting on economic issues, although that is becoming a little more complicated.

The current budget debates in the Riigikogu already show that the Reform Party has concrete figures and facts demonstrating that the situation is improving. Admittedly, the deficit and government debt remain issues. But I think virtually every party currently represented in the Riigikogu has contributed substantially to that. They have all had a chance to govern and have happily added to the debt, so that may be a difficult issue to campaign on.

We may also see security issues return to the forefront, but I just hope they don't become a major political battleground.

World.title: Energy firms: Higher network fees could deter battery storage investment
World.content:
Six energy firms warn that higher network fees for battery storage from 2027 could deter investment in Estonia. Elering says discounts would shift costs to other customers.

Battery storage allows electricity to be saved for later use or sold back to the grid when prices are high. But renewable energy companies say changes to transmission system operator (TSO) Elering's transmission fee structure will make battery storage significantly more expensive in Estonia.

Mihkel Annus, head of regulatory affairs at Enery Estonia, said the changes could deter investment.

"Battery storage helps lower electricity prices for consumers, and everyone ultimately benefits from more storage being deployed in Estonia," Annus said, noting that thanks to Lithuania's network fee structure, using batteries is several times cheaper there.

He warned that higher costs here at home could mean that "investments the system needs and consumers benefit from will naturally bypass Estonia."

Elering CEO Kalle Kilk said the changes are not specifically aimed at battery owners. Instead, they reflect a broader restructuring of fees, shifting the balance between capacity charges and electricity transmission charges.

Battery owners are exempt from the latter, but the costs associated with their use of the grid remain.

Elering CEO: This is the fairer approach

Kilk said Elering had to choose between making other customers cover those costs or redistributing charges so each customer pays for the costs they incur.

"I think this is the fairer approach," he said, adding that the Competition Authority has already approved the new structure as well.

Energy companies have also raised their concerns with the Ministry of Climate. Energy and Environment Minister Erkki Keldo (Reform) said he understood the need for more battery parks to lower electricity prices and reduce price spikes, but Elering also needs to cover its costs and invest in the grid.

"I'll look into whether we can strike a balance that allows Elering to collect its network fees and invest in the grid without making new battery parks too uncompetitive," he said.

World.title: Only around a hundred of Tallinn's 1,200 bus stops have electronic displays
World.content:
Only around 10 percent of the capital's public transport stops have electronic real-time information displays and while the city plans to install more, it has no intention of equipping every stop with one.

Tallinn has approximately 1,200 public transport stops, including temporary stops used, for example, during roadworks when normal traffic arrangements change and public transport is diverted.

Around 100 of these stops have electronic information displays, some of which are older LED real-time information boards and others more modern LCD real-time displays. Although Tallinn is gradually installing more of them, the number is not expected to increase by dozens each year, nor does the city intend to install displays at every stop.

Tallinn's Transport Department told ERR that the network of information boards and displays is being expanded gradually, based on how frequently stops are used and the technical options available.

"LCD displays come at a considerable cost, so the aim is not to provide information to passengers through displays at every stop. The priority is stops with higher passenger numbers. If equipment costs fall or more affordable solutions become available in the future, this approach can be reconsidered. Smartphone-based solutions can help reach all passengers at every location," department spokesperson Roberta Valtenberg said.

The Transport Department itself analyzes which stops should receive displays.

A single LCD display currently costs €1,950, with installation costing an additional €250. VAT is added to these amounts.

This year, real-time displays have been installed at stops around the Haabersti roundabout as part of upgrades to bus shelters. During the reconstruction of Lauteri tänav this summer, a new shelter and real-time display were installed at the Hotell Olümpia stop. A display is currently being installed at the Nisu stop.

Funding has been allocated for the purchase and installation of another 13 displays this year, Valtenberg said. How much funding will be available for displays next year is not yet known.

"In addition to funding, the ability to install displays depends on the availability of the necessary infrastructure, particularly electricity connections and whether shelters are ready. As a result, the pace of installation is determined not only by the budget but also by the technical readiness of the stops," she said.

Therefore, in addition to the most important criterion — that a stop serves a large number of passengers and routes — other key considerations include whether it already has an electricity connection and whether new shelters are planned.

"The aim is to carry out the work in a logical sequence and avoid unnecessary excavation and subsequent reconstruction," Valtenberg said.

Electronic information display at a Tallinn bus stop. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

World.title: Archival studies shed light on sunken steamer's fate in Estonian waters
World.content:
The wreck of the cargo steamship Success, which sank in Estonian waters in 1885, is among 15 shipwrecks newly placed under state protection to preserve Estonia's underwater cultural heritage.

More than 100 underwater heritage sites in Estonia's maritime areas are under state protection. Another 15 shipwrecks have now been added to the list. According to underwater archaeologist Maili Roio, conditions in the Baltic Sea have helped preserve shipwrecks, but that alone is not enough.

"We're actually in a very good position here on the Baltic Sea because the sea itself does an excellent job of preserving our shipwrecks. However, our maritime areas are being used increasingly intensively and for a growing range of purposes. The state must therefore ensure that underwater cultural heritage is taken into account when planning activities," Roio explained on ETV morning show "Terevisioon."

The newly protected sites include the wrecks of 12 sailing ships, the destroyer S31, a steamship and the cargo steamship Success. Four are located in internal waters, nine in territorial waters and two in Estonia's exclusive economic zone. All the wrecks are sufficiently well preserved to serve as important archaeological sources of historical information.

Placing a shipwreck under protection does not mean that the surrounding maritime area can no longer be used. However, certain restrictions apply in designated areas and must be taken into account. When a wreck and its immediate surroundings are protected and a buffer zone has been established, planned activities must take into account the need to preserve the wreck. For example, wind turbines should be installed far enough away from a wreck to ensure that construction work does not damage or destroy it.

Although the 15 newly protected wrecks represent a significant addition, Roio said they are just a drop in the ocean. The Estonian Transport Administration conducts seabed surveys every year, uncovering new wrecks in the process. However, not every wreck is automatically granted protection.

"We can't simply place a wreck under protection as soon as it's been located. We need preliminary information from the seabed: what kind of wreck it is, how well it has been preserved and what information it might contain," Roio said.

One of the newly protected wrecks lies at a depth of more than 60 meters. It caught the attention of underwater archaeologists because of its shape and dimensions. The wreck resembled a willow leaf: It was relatively narrow and elongated, suggesting that it could be an older vessel.

According to preliminary estimates, the wreck dates from the 16th or 17th century. Researchers examined footage captured by an underwater remotely operated vehicle, allowing them to study parts of the ship without immediately undertaking more complex underwater archaeological work.

Roio said the footage shows only a small portion of the wreck. Two masts are visible, indicating that it was a two-masted sailing ship. However, the parts of the wreck visible on the seabed do not provide a complete picture of its condition.

The wreck of the steamer Success. Source: Ivar Treffner/Estonian Maritime Museum

Further research is needed to establish the wreck's precise age and origin. There is currently no definitive information about the ship's history or whether it can be linked to written historical records.

The depth also makes research more challenging. Archaeological excavations are more difficult at depths exceeding 60 meters, although they could help determine what other archaeological material the wreck contains.

Another newly protected wreck is more recent and better preserved than the first. It is a sailing ship dating from the 17th or 18th century, with parts of its structure rising several meters above the seabed. Both its anchor windlass and a large gaff boom are visible. In this case, researchers were able to go beyond examining the wreck on the seabed and connect the discovery with earlier archival research.

According to Roio, underwater archaeologists worked with the National Archives of Estonia to gather information about sunken vessels. Information found in archival records helped establish the history of one wreck, identifying it as the cargo steamship Success.

The ship was traveling from Kronstadt to London when it sank in Estonian waters in July 1885. It had previously run aground in the Gulf of Finland and sustained damage. To get the vessel moving again, some of its cargo was thrown overboard. Roio said the cargo steamship's wreck is well preserved, although it has sustained some damage.

Roio described the 19th century as a fascinating period of transition in shipbuilding and maritime navigation. The introduction of steamships transformed shipping, but steam-powered vessels continued to use sails. Masts are also visible on this wreck, offering insight into how different maritime technologies coexisted.

"This transitional period is really fascinating. At the same time, the ship still has those beautiful lines characteristic of sailing vessels. It must have been a very beautiful ship," Roio said.

According to Roio, the Estonian Maritime Museum initially suspected, based on sonar images and the dimensions of the wrecks, that they might be warships. Only additional information gathered from the seabed can establish what the vessels actually were.

A third example is the wreck of a 19th-century sailing ship that still has its figurehead, a decorative feature attached to the bow. The survival of such details is remarkable because they are often among the first parts to break off or suffer damage from trawling.

Roio said trawling has long been one of the main activities responsible for damaging shipwrecks in Estonian waters. It is therefore particularly unusual to find a vessel with such details still intact, as they provide valuable clues about the ship's original appearance and construction.

Placing shipwrecks under state protection also helps Estonia fulfill its obligations under UNESCO's 2001 Convention on the Protection of the Underwater Cultural Heritage.

The wreck of steamer Success. Source: Ivar Treffner/Estonian Maritime Museum
