World.title: 'Shouldn't have to wear a flak jacket': Haines spoke of risks to MPs before attack
World.content:
As the nation recoiled this week at the brutality of the physical attack on Independent MP Helen Haines, a small but terrible poignancy pulsed beyond public view.

For the past year, Haines has been a key Australian advocate of a groundbreaking project to map the physical and mental health risks to which public representatives are exposed in their line of work.

The study — understood to be the largest ever undertaken into Australian MPs' mental health and apprehensions around physical safety — canvassed the experiences of 288 current and five former representatives from federal, state and local government over the past year.

Conducted by the Berlin-based Better Politics Foundation, the report titled Fit To Lead is still in draft form, due for release next month.

But the sentiment coursing through the survey responses is powerfully encapsulated by a single anonymous MP's quote in the report's introduction, penned by the foundation's Australian-born co-CEO, Kimberly McArthur.

"We don't want to make politics comfortable, but we do want it to be safe," the MP says.

"You shouldn't have to wear a flak jacket, physical or emotional, to do the job."

These words belong to Helen Haines. Her office this week authorised the ABC to attribute them to her, hoping that the critically injured MP's own words could be heard among the tumult this week.

“Helen is a non-combatant,” says one parliamentary veteran, a political opponent. “For her to be attacked in this way is just unthinkable.” (ABC News: Dallas Freedman)

Female MPs fear for safety

McArthur, who now lives in Berlin, and colleagues were horrified to hear of the attack on Haines. She is a listed "champion" of and key collaborator on the study.

"What happened to Helen is shocking," McArthur says.

"But I am sorry to say that those of us who work with politicians in Australia have feared an attack like this was coming for some time."

McArthur says half of the study's female respondents reported fears for the safety of "self or family or team" had a significant or substantial effect on their wellbeing.

"When the job becomes this dangerous, the harm does not stay with the individual," she says.

"Nearly 40 per cent told us their own wellbeing had at some point stopped them speaking out on issues they believe are important. It drives good people out of public life, and it quietly tells the next generation of leaders not to bother putting up their hand. That is not just unfair to them. It is a problem for all of us."

Kimberly McArthur, Co-CEO of Berlin-based Better Politics Foundation. (LInkedIn)

The Fit To Lead study will be released in Australia next month by Alastair Campbell, the high-profile British podcaster, author and former adviser to Tony Blair who has written extensively on mental health and politics.

On Wednesday, Campbell spoke about Haines on his podcast The Rest Is Politics. Campbell said Australia had always enjoyed a reputation as a safe place to be a public figure, but this was changing.

The Fit To Lead report established Australian politicians now experience "more depression and anxiety than people who work in the emergency services" he said.

Bob Hawke, picture here at a citizenship ceremony in 1985, later said the safe climate for politicians in Australia "distinguished our country". (National Archives of Australia)

Life is changing for MPs

The late Bob Hawke, interviewed on the ABC's Kitchen Cabinet in 2014, recalled with delight an occasion when — waiting with a high-level delegation of American visitors outside the MCG for a bus to take them back to their accommodation — he was greeted by a carload of young men who rolled down the windows and yelled: "G'day Hawkie! Hawkie! You're the best!"

"And I sad, 'Well if I'm that good, how about giving me a lift to town?'," the former prime minister recalled.

"And they said 'sure' so I just piled into their car," he said. The journey was unremarkable — Hawke was delivered to the hotel unscathed, having spent the trip chatting with his fans and calling their mums.

"The Americans couldn't believe it," Hawke said.

"It does distinguish our country. I mean, that could never happen — certainly in the United States where you're just surrounded by security and so on. One of the great marks of this country [is] you can do that and people would have a laugh, but it wouldn't be regarded as unsafe."

But life is changing for Australian MPs.

Nearly a decade after that Hawke interview, a six-episode season of Kitchen Cabinet featured two guests who were unable to film in their own homes because of serious threats on their lives.

Threats up fourfold before Helen Haines attack The attack on Helen Haines comes amid a rise in threats of political violence.

Both were female. Both were Indigenous — then cabinet minister Linda Burney and the independent senator Lidia Thorpe, who has faced consistent and alarming threats over her time in the parliament and has spent periods being unable to live in her own home.

In the past five years, the annual rate of threats against high office holders and federal MPs recorded by the Australian Federal Police has increased from 300 to more than 1000.

Online and social media threats are a significant driver; one senior Coalition figure estimated this week that she referred a dozen threats a week to the Australian Federal Police.

In the days since Haines sustained her terrible injuries, the threat level for public figures has not markedly dissipated. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Threat level hasn't dissipated

The shocking attack on Haines, for which police are yet to advance a motive although a man has been charged, has been described variously as a "wake-up call" and as a "turning point" for the Australian polity.

"Helen is a non-combatant," says one parliamentary veteran, a political opponent. "She's Switzerland. For her to be attacked in this way is just unthinkable."

But in the days since Haines sustained her terrible injuries, the threat level for public figures has not markedly dissipated.

Small Business Minister Anne Aly, who earlier this month disclosed that she received 19 death threats in one week after an opposition MP told parliament she and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese should be "stoned in the marketplace", says the temperature of online debate had — if anything — intensified since Haines was attacked.

“Intuitively you’d assume that the terrible thing that happened to Helen would have calmed things down,” she says.

"What's immediately happened is people jumping to conclusions — which is never a sensible thing to do — to lay blame, to identify the perpetrator: is he one of us, or one of them?"

On Thursday, Aly's electorate office received a letter declaring a bullet would be "too good" for her. It was accompanied by a package of Bibles, in what Aly and staff interpreted as a statement about her faith (Aly is the first Muslim woman to serve in federal parliament).

On Wednesday, a man was arrested in Perth for behaving in a threatening manner at the electorate office of state Labor MP Hannah Beazley, while allegedly carrying nunchucks.

In Brisbane on the same day, Communications Minister Anika Wells was obliged to close her electorate office after a woman carrying a replica firearm threatened the woman staffing the reception desk.

Wells is one of the many MPs who have grappled with death threats and online abuse; a Bankstown man was last year charged and fined for stalking the Brisbane MP.

Minister for Small Business Anne Aly says decreasing safety for MPs is not as simple as blaming social media. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Aly, who was an internationally renowned authority on terrorism and radicalisation before entering parliament, is no stranger to heightened threat environments.

But her experience as a parliamentarian has thrown into sharp relief the research she's done on radicalisation, and the trajectory that can push an individual from seeking information online to "lurking" among extremists to taking active and violent steps.

But she says it's not as simple as blaming social media.

"We're missing pieces of the conversation here," she says. "There's a substantial mental health factor. Particularly with men in their forties and fifties."

Several years ago, Aly was in her office when a man entered, armed with a knife. Aly and a staff member remained in the office to try and talk the man down, directing others to lock the door and summon police.

"That case involved mental health issues," she says.

Another threat — in which a correspondent advised Aly "would be shot" at a specific car park she regularly used — made it to court.

Deputy Nationals leader Darren Chester, who has held the regional Victorian seat of Gippsland for nearly 20 years, suspects the rate of online threats against MPs is under-reported.

"We evaluate them ourselves as to whether they're worth forwarding to the AFP, and of course we're not really qualified to do that," he says.

"It's much easier now for people with a grievance to get in touch with an MP. And you can do it 24 hours — you can fire off an email with three scotches under your belt where once you might have had to wait until morning to write a letter and maybe think again."

Chester is also listed as a champion of the Better Politics study. He cautions against a knee-jerk response to the Haines tragedy.

"You don't formulate drought policy when you're in the middle of a drought, and if you're making decisions about security in the middle of a crisis you run the risk of making bad decisions," he says.

"If you change your behaviour to the point where you're travelling around in motorcades, then you become aloof from your community, and the scumbags have won, and our democracy suffers."

Annabel Crabb and the National Party's Darren Chester during filming of Kitchen Cabinet. (ABC TV)

When online abuse gets physical

Chester says the face-to-face interactions with his constituents are vastly different from online ones.

"Nobody has ever said to my face the kinds of things that are said on social media," he says.

McArthur agrees social media is a significant driver of fear and apprehension among elected representatives.

"Traditional and social media personalities have an enormous role to play in holding power to account —which democracy needs — and in curbing the kind of pile-on and rhetoric that strips people of their basic safety and dignity," she says.

"The police have a role in taking threats against elected officials seriously, because harassment does not always stay online. And the public, that is all of us, has a role too. Before the next angry message is sent, it is worth remembering that these are human beings doing a frighteningly hard job on our behalf."

The tipping point between online abuse and physical aggression is hard to predict or judge, but ASIO director general Mike Burgess has warned repeatedly over the course of his term that extreme rhetoric and supercharged debate increases the chance of real-world violence.

And while the attack on Haines has widely been described as a “wake-up call”, the terror attack at Bondi last year already stands as a shocking demonstration of the way ideology can burst into violence.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

For serving MPs, who are obliged to be visible in their electorates as part of their jobs, protective measures can involve restricting advance notice of where they are planning to appear, posting photographs only after they've left a location.

But for local government candidates, disclosing private contact details can be part of the deal.

In states like NSW, WA and Tasmania, local government candidates are obliged by law to authorise campaign materials with their personal addresses. In other states including Queensland and Victoria, PO boxes can be used as an address, but a recent NSW branch conference of the Australian Local Government Women's Association heard the requirement to publicise a personal street address was a major disincentive for female candidates.

Delegates shared stories of receiving abusive calls late at night, aggrieved constituents coming to their homes and family members experiencing harassment.

A recent study of NSW women in local government, titled Not On My Council and authored by academic and Cumberland City councillor Diane Colman, found 61 per cent of women councillors experienced bullying, harassment or intimidation.

Despite the grim statistics at every government level, McArthur says the representatives surveyed are far from giving up.

"The overwhelming majority told us they would still encourage others to run for office," she says.

"The least we can do is make it a job worth standing for."

World.title: Women report stalkers abusing exercise apps to harass them
World.content:
It happened on an International Women's Day ride: a group of women cyclists had stopped at a cafe in Melbourne's north-east, refuelling midway through their route.

Bianca Pickett, a 51-year-old who works in IT, was sitting opposite an 18-year-old woman, Amy*, who gasped as she checked her phone.

"Amy said, 'Oh my god, this man has been messaging me on Strava for a couple of weeks; he just said he saw me on the road, and he's going to come and say hi.'" Pickett said.

Strava is the most popular fitness app that uses GPS-based activity tracking. It is also a social networking platform, allowing people to follow and message others, and see each other's running or cycling routes.

Many runners and cyclists plan their routes on apps, and then share them. (Getty Images: Ihor Biliavskyi)

Pickett asked Amy for his name, before shuddering; he was well-known for this kind of predatory behaviour.

"He ingratiates himself to younger women," Pickett said.

"He tries to isolate them, so he sends them messages, then tries to go on a ride with you, then befriends you. I hate to think what else has happened."

Amy, she said, was "terrified" when he arrived at the cafe. Pickett reassured her she would handle the situation, and told him it was a women's only ride.

While he begrudgingly left, Pickett said the man continued to follow the women on his bike, all the way back to Melbourne.

"I kept seeing him on corners, and thought, 'what is he doing?' I just wanted an International Women's Day ride that felt safe and lovely for everyone," she said.

Pickett said she and others had complained about the man to various cycling clubs previously, to no avail. But on this occasion, and with a new, female president in charge, he was finally banned from his latest club.

Loading Instagram content

"Prior to that several male presidents had been like, 'Oh, he's a good guy, he's always down at crits helping and supporting', so I always got shut down," Pickett said.

Some women, she added, were too embarrassed to complain if they had responded to his messages before realising his intent.

While grateful that action was finally taken, Pickett is alarmed by instances of men abusing the tracking features of exercise apps to stalk women.

Apps make it 'easy' to determine someone's location

Pickett has a long list of men she blocked after they attempted to harass or stalk her online.

"Some men will ask questions like 'So what apartment block are you living in? What's your route tomorrow? What racing are you doing next? So [basically], 'how do I determine where I can stalk you?'" she said.

Pickett argued that some exercise apps make it "easy" to determine someone's location.

"If you don't have privacy settings on you can figure out exactly where someone lives," she said.

"It happens to women all the time".

Apps like Strava are widely used to record, analyse and share exercise sessions. (Getty Images: Justin Paget)

Karen Bevan, CEO of Full Stop Australia, an organisation which supports people affected by sexual, domestic or family violence, said cyber stalking was an issue developers must take responsibility for.

"Too often, staying safe on these apps depends on people finding and changing settings they may not know exist," she said.

"This puts the burden in the wrong place — the harm comes from design choices and companies are the ones who should fix them.

"Platforms need to act first; most privacy settings should be switched on at sign-up, activity start and end points hidden automatically, messages from strangers off unless a user opts-in, and [there should be] quick, meaningful responses to complaints."

In a statement, a Strava spokesperson said the platform takes the safety and privacy of its global community very seriously.

"Our fully adjustable suite of privacy controls enables people to choose what they share and with whom. Key protections are on by default, including Messaging set to 'Friends Only', and the first and last 200 metres of activity maps are automatically hidden.

"We do not tolerate harassment, similar conduct or any other violation of our Community Standards. Our Trust and Safety team proactively monitors for violations, and carefully reviews any reports made by our community, taking appropriate action as needed."

Women want to run without being tracked

Melburnian Melanie Caple, 38, said the issue was not limited to cycling, either.

Caple is an app developer, mural artist and long-time runner who revels in the freedom of hitting the track alone.

Melanie Caple designed an app that allows runners to set an estimated end time. (Supplied: Melanie Caple)

"Running is the one thing that has meant I kind of feel OK in and about the world," she said.

Growing up in country Victoria, she moved to London at the age of 20, and said she regularly ran solo without thinking about letting anyone know where she was.

As she has got older, however — and with incidents like Samantha Murphy's alleged murder on a morning run — she has felt more pressure to let her family know where she is, and that she is safe.

With a wry sense of humour, she and her sister often exchange texts before runs with the hashtag #dontgetmurdered, followed by kisses.

Caple, however, drew the line at sharing her location while running.

Like Pickett, she has heard stories of women being cyber stalked.

Caple was also previously in an abusive relationship and said using GPS tracking mimicked being stalked.

"You want your family to feel assured that you're taking responsibility for your safety, but I didn't want to feel like I had to justify my freedom and independence in the world," she said.

Caple does, however, appreciate what draws most users to exercise apps: the chance to track her progress over time, and feel pride in her achievements, such as increasing the length of her runs, or completing them in shorter times.

As a result, Caple designed her own app — called SoloRunClubxx — which allows users to track their workouts without notifying anyone of their whereabouts.

However, the app also includes a safety feature which allows the user to set an estimated end time for their run and asks them at that point in time if they have finished their run safely.

They can either respond saying they have finished, or are still running. It is only if they do not respond that a loved one is notified with their location.

Melanie Caple often texts her sister before she sets out on a run. (Supplied: Melanie Caple)

Tech companies must 'keep pace with the law'

Caple has been buoyed by community feedback to the app, citing one example where a pregnant woman fell on her route, and was taken by ambulance to hospital. Her sister was notified of her location in the emergency department after she failed to report that she was safe.

Caple said the app was designed for extraordinary instances like these, so that women and gender diverse people can otherwise feel free of surveillance.

"I wanted to work out a way that, if something was going to happen to me on a run, in that worst case scenario, someone would know without me having to sacrifice my privacy and freedom," she said.

Bevan, from Full Stop Australia, also runs regularly, and said "everyone deserves freedom" while exercising.

Women regularly run in groups for an added layer of safety. (Getty Images: standret)

"I want what every runner wants: to run in peace, to run how I want, when I want, without looking over my shoulder," she said.

"Gender-based violence is about misusing power, and restricting someone's freedom to move is part of that."

She said the law recognises tracking as stalking, and the onus is on technology companies to "keep pace with the law".

"Location technology should be designed so it can't easily be turned into a tool of surveillance and control," Bevan said.

*Amy is a pseudonym used to protect her identity.

World.title: Ghosts of past reports linger for NT child protection review
World.content:
Poring over the 62 pages of the Independent Review into the Conduct of the Department of Children and Families report and its 45 recommendations, a multitude of systemic issues for the Northern Territory are made clear.

Underneath all of these complex challenges remains a key issue: accountability.

It's a question that threads through a growing mountain of reports and their hundreds of recommendations made over many decades, detailing failures in reducing harm for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians.

The NT government has committed to acting on all recommendations as a first step.

But the question remains: who has responsibility for making the changes to ensure children are kept safe?

Which leads to a further question.

What are the consequences if change does not happen?

Without an answer to these questions, communities are stuck with the status quo, or worse, having the wrong response applied without adequate means to correct course.

Katie Kiss is pushing for "implementation that delivers lasting change". (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Social Justice Commissioner Katie Kiss has acknowledged the NT government's response, emphasising the need for "implementation that delivers lasting change".

Commissioner Kiss also remarked that "the NT government still has not implemented the recommendations of the 2017 Royal Commission into child protection".

Currently, the consequences of inaction and inappropriate responses are evident in the Closing the Gap measures that remain locked in place, or widening on many counts.

Youth crime, child removal, family and domestic violence patterns across Australia point to significant, systemic flaws in the way those with authority exercise their power.

This was made heartbreakingly clear in the alleged murder of Kumanjayi Little Baby.

WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of her family.

Tackling the problem at the root

The review's co-authors singled out the immediate need for an audit into current safety plans. This will ensure the appropriate people are given safety roles for the protection of children in the NT.

In the case of Kumanjayi Little Baby, the review found that one person in her family's safety network had a "long criminal history of violence, including five counts of threaten to kill".

Media reports and comments made in NT parliament have named this person as the man now charged with Kumanjayi Little Baby's murder.

Information such as this is of critical importance, so that all steps taken by authorised officers are based on relevant and appropriate processes.

Kumanjayi Little Baby went missing from an Alice Springs town camp earlier this year. (Supplied: NT Police)

But the co-authors were also determined to say that "the review does not suggest that a prior conviction, of itself, necessarily renders a person unsuitable" for a protective role.

Developing a clear mechanism for assessing the risk — the nature of which type of conviction represents a relevant threat — will be essential.

For a community with high rates of interaction with police, the justice system and incarceration, understanding the implications of this step is significant.

As is recognising the highly mobile and overcrowded nature of many households in communities across the NT.

These considerations sit within a broader landscape that presents myriad challenges for the most vulnerable.

We see children born into families facing significant disadvantage and dysfunction, where even the most basic needs, such as finding a home or shelter and having a means of getting there, are hard to access and becoming more so.

This month has seen the 400-bed YiSSA short-stay accommodation centre closed in Darwin, while the Bush Bus service, which operates between remote communities and Alice Springs, has had funding cut.

Fears women and children bearing brunt of shelter closure Darwin's largest short-stay accommodation facility YiSSA is shutting its doors today, with hundreds of residents being told to move 100 kilometres away to a tiny outback town.

Dealing with this is hard enough.

But, as the review also revealed, "the current practice places significant responsibility on the non-offending parent to protect the child" — a burden the parent carries while their own safety is in jeopardy.

National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People, Sue-Anne Hunter, puts the onus on the Department of Children and Families.

"The question that needed answering was what the department did with what it knew. Responsibility for violence sits with the people who use it. Responsibility for the response sits with the department. It should never sit with a victim."

It's a view echoed by Muriel Bamblett, the chair of SNAICC, the peak body for community-controlled Indigenous children's services. She highlights the work of violence reduction programs in Victoria that tackle the problem at the root.

"You need behaviour change. You need to be able to work with those communities around preventing violence," she said.

"In Victoria, we've got violence reduction now […] It has to take a public health approach."

Rushed remedies

There is much to consider around community and child safety and, with lives in the balance, it is worth looking at the record set so far.

One case stands out: the Northern Territory Emergency Response, or NT Intervention.

When the Howard government suspended Australia's Racial Discrimination Act on June 21, 2007, military units were deployed to discrete Aboriginal communities.

The decision came after the release of the Ampe Akelyernemane Meke Mekarle "Little Children Are Sacred" report, led by Pat Anderson and Rex Wild QC.

Tasked with inquiring into the protection of Aboriginal children from sexual abuse, the co-chairs delivered a comprehensive 316-page report with 97 recommendations.

Clear guidance was provided: "In the first recommendation, we have specifically referred to the critical importance of governments committing to genuine consultation with Aboriginal people in designing initiatives for Aboriginal communities, whether these be remote, regional or urban settings."

NT child safety review authors say changes imminent The authors of the report that found extensive failings in the NT child protection system say recommendations should be acted on within six months.

That never happened. The legislation was rushed through in two months.

Ten years later, Anderson described the NT Intervention response as a "betrayal" that had led to "further abuse of Aboriginal people. That's what the intervention was".

The NT Intervention framework ended in July 2022 but stands as a stark reminder of the long-lasting impacts that can emerge when change is made without proper consideration of the recommendations.

This is something certainly worth remembering as the wheels turn once again on resolving this most enduring set of challenges.

World.title: Kiwi expats could prove crucial in New Zealand's 'knife edge' election
World.content:
With the upcoming New Zealand election on a "knife edge", expats like Brisbane woman Mary-Leigh Scheerhoorn could help shape the result.

A permanent resident of Australia, she is one of about 126,000 New Zealanders living overseas who are registered to vote ahead of the general election on November 7.

Kiwi expats account for more than 3 per cent of registered voters at this election, with nearly two-thirds of them in Australia.

Ms Scheerhoorn, a clinical nutritionist who has lived in Australia for 24 years, said she was voting to influence the country she hoped to return to one day.

As a Māori woman, she said she had a strong connection to New Zealand and was "drawn back to be with my people and my culture".

Voting is not compulsory in New Zealand, but at the 2023 election more than 77,000 of the up to 1 million Kiwis living overseas voted.

According to Electoral Commission figures, about 33,000 more overseas voters have registered than for the 2023 election.

Election a 'dead heat'

New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, who leads the National Party, is seeking a second term after defeating the Labour Party's Chris Hipkins in 2023.

The incumbent government — a right coalition of the National Party, New Zealand First and ACT Party — is up against a left bloc of the Labour Party, Green Party and Te Pāti Māori (Māori Party).

NZ voters search for reasons to stay The everyday stakes of New Zealand’s election.

Tom Jamieson, a senior lecturer in political science at Te Herenga Waka-Victoria University of Wellington, said polling suggested both the major parties, National and Labour, were generally in the high 20s.

However, a 1News-Verian poll released on Tuesday had National pushing ahead by five points.

Nonetheless, Mr Jamieson said there was a "dead heat" between the two blocs and the election looked to be on a "knife edge".

"A 1 per cent or a 2 per cent swing could decide the election," Dr Jamieson told the ABC.

"So I think it's probably in all of their interests to court the overseas vote as much as possible."

Christopher Luxon's National Party has been neck-and-neck with the Labour Party in the polls. (Reuters: David Rowland)

He said the non-aligned Opportunity Party could be a "kingmaker" if it won more than 5 per cent of the party vote — the threshold required to enter parliament without winning an electorate seat under the country's electoral system.

However, he said a lot depended on the turnout.

Dr Jamieson said New Zealand expats usually voted for minor parties, in part because they had historically worked harder to secure the votes of Kiwis overseas than the major parties.

He said the expat vote had also tended to "track left", with the Green and Te Pāti Māori parties receiving strong support from overseas voters at the 2023 election.

"The kinds of people who live overseas may relate more to their environmental stewardship and advocacy for Māori," he added.

Expat voting intentions

Ms Scheerhoorn said she was hoping for a new New Zealand government.

She said she was dismayed by the government's handling of issues relating to the Treaty of Waitangi/Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the nation's founding agreement with Māori people, and the removal of Māori language from some books that teach young children to read to avoid "confusion".

"This has felt like an open attack on the culture, which I think is very much the fabric of New Zealand," she said.

She said a future move home had made her consider things like the cost of living, housing and health care.

"If we want to go back and live in New Zealand … are there jobs available? What's the earning capacity? What's the tax situation look like?" she said.

Mary-Leigh and Darren Scheerhoorn planned on voting at New Zealand's 2026 general election from Australia. (Supplied)

She said she was very strongly drawn to the Green Party at this election and had voted for them previously.

Ron Deane, who moved to Australia from Rotorua three years ago, was also leaning towards voting for a minor party.

The Brisbane-based truck driver came over after struggling to find work in New Zealand and had similar concerns about the treaty, the cost of living and affordable housing.

He was voting because his friends and family in New Zealand were "feeling the pinch", often forced to make decisions about buying food and paying rent.

"Although I live in Australia, New Zealand is still home. I care about its future and believe it's important to have a say in the decisions that affect our people, culture and future generations," he said.

Ron Deane was analysing the remainder of the New Zealand election campaign before deciding who to vote for. (Supplied)

The 44-year-old said he was still deciding who he would vote for.

About 120,000 more New Zealand citizens left in the three years to August 2026 than returned, according to Stats NZ estimates.

Many like Jethro George moved to Australia in that time.

He said Australia's higher wages, cheaper house prices and lower cost of living were significant factors in the move.

"The roles I applied for in Australia paid almost double what I was on in New Zealand, with less responsibilities," he told the ABC from his home in Perth.

"Couple that with lower living costs and a relocation package, it was hard to say no."

Jethro George moved to Western Australia in 2024 with his family. (Supplied)

Mr George, a 35-year-old mental health worker who also owned his own consultancy business, said he was a swing voter.

He used to work in New Zealand on housing, homelessness and poverty-related issues.

All were key policy concerns for him along with the cost-of-living crisis, which he saw first-hand on a trip to New Zealand earlier this year.

However, he was frustrated by parties that "just attack each other" rather than suggest solutions and was not yet convinced by the policies of any party, major or minor.

"There isn't the strength that you would want to see in leadership," he said.

Parties court overseas voters

Kiwi expat Tracey Lee, a strategist and former sociologist, created the non-partisan campaign Every Kiwi Vote Counts in 2020, which aims to boost the number of overseas voters.

"Those [expat] votes and perspectives can change what goes forward," she told the ABC from her home in London.

Ms Lee helped organise a virtual town hall in early October so party leaders could speak to expat voters around the world.

Why young people are leaving New Zealand Max was earning more as a dishwasher in Australia than in his profession back home in New Zealand. He is among a record number of people leaving the country.

Jethro George said a big challenge for expats was holding on to their connection to New Zealand and seeing "the value of the vote".

"I think our votes count and they matter … the challenge is just really identifying and understanding where to put that," he said.

He wanted to see "a New Zealand that's thriving" and hoped to return there one day because he missed his family, friends and the culture.

It was difficult to see a return now, though, he said, based on where the country sat politically and economically.

"I want to live in a country where families can do more than just get by, and where contributing to the wellbeing of others doesn't come at the expense of your own family's time and financial security," he said.

World.title: 'Did we do well today?': This is what it takes to keep an independent restaurant open
World.content:
The work is relentless and the earnings unpredictable: So what keeps an independent restaurant owner in the game?

It's a Thursday morning and Bridget Raffal, co-owner of Claret Club, a restaurant and bar tucked into an old terrace on the edges of Sydney's CBD, is bracing for the worst.

One of the kitchen's two heat lamps has broken. Without it the venue's two chefs will struggle to keep food warm until a waiter can ferry their carefully prepared plates of risotto and quince and walnut clafoutis to customers.

"At first we thought it was just a broken bulb so we ordered one — a very expensive bulb," says Bridget, looking like she doesn't know whether to laugh or cry. "Now we think we have to replace it"

The bar's regular handyman, Christian, is on the phone and begins explaining Bridget's options. Her facial expression suggests none of them are great.

"I just want the best and cheapest," she says after she hangs up the call. "That's always what everything comes down to here — do we try for a quick fix or a long-term solution?"

Harry Hunter and Bridget Raffal are co-owners of Claret Club in Sydney's Darlinghurst. ( )

Hospitality has never been an easy job, known for long hours, low margins and high personal risk. But in 2026 the industry is in extreme crisis, facing a tornado of unfavourable conditions. According to CreditorWatch, one in eight restaurants and cafes closed between July 2025 and July 2026, almost double the average of other sectors. Analysts blame inflation, cost-of-living pressures, skyrocketing costs and damaging policy decisions.

A generation ago, average net profit for a restaurant or cafe was around 10 per cent, says John Hart, national president of industry peak body Restaurant and Catering Australia (RCA). By the end of 2025, that had shrunk to 2.5 per cent. Now, with minimum wage increases and costs such as the recent policy shift that means restaurants must absorb card bank fees, profit has dwindled to almost nothing for many operators.

"Twenty or 30 years ago I warned this would be what I called a 'culinary Armageddon'," Hart says.

Rising food and wage costs are partly to blame, but Bridget and her partner and co-owner Harry Hunter say their biggest issue is cost-of-living pressures, which reduce customer attendance and spend.

"We run a tight ship," Bridget says. "We just need more people through the doors."

Harry stands at the front of the restaurant watching passers by on Stanley Street. ( )

Independent venues, where the staff know your name and your drink order, where you can drop by for a meal and a chat after a long day at work, and where every inch of atmosphere is created by intuition and imagination, rather than AI — have never felt more important to the fabric of our cities and towns.

"'Commensality' — the idea of eating together to reinforce kinship links — is part of what brings a group together," says Teresa Davis, associate professor of marketing at the School of Business Analytics and Marketing and co-founder of the Australian Food, Society and Culture Network at the University of Sydney. "It builds and reinforces the social fabric."

Independent places like Claret Club do this particularly well. Their intimacy means customers connect not just with each other but with the people who bring the food and wine to the table.

Today, when the world swirls with uncertainty, upheaval and unrest, independent restaurants feel like a lifeline.

As a place to unwind and find community, independent restaurants can feel like a lifeline. ( )

"The experiences of being able to hang out with your friends, being able to escape from whatever it is for a little bit … being around people that you don't know, being treated well — all of that feels more essential than it ever has to me before," New York Times food reporter Brett Anderson recently told The Daily podcast.

The ABC spent two days and nights at Claret Club, an independently-run venue in Sydney's Darlinghurst, to witness exactly how much grit and grind it takes to stay open in today's crushing climate, and how much we stand to lose if places like it disappear altogether.

11:40am

The heat lamp issue has been set aside. Chefs Andy Buchanan and Fernando Vargas will have to make do with the remaining lamp for tonight's service, and the waiters and food runners will need to work twice as fast as usual.

Sous-chef Fernando Vargas and head chef Andy Buchanan prep for dinner. ( )

Bridget and Harry have begun discussing marketing and social media. There's a wine event upstairs tonight, and another scheduled next week with tickets still available.

"Should I do a last-minute social media push on it?" Bridget wonders.

"I'll write an EDM on Sunday and send it out on Monday," offers Harry, fluent in the shorthand for Electronic Direct Mail, something few restaurateurs would have thought about a generation ago.

"I thought it would be nice if we could have Sunday off together?" suggests Bridget.

Sundays are the one day the couple tries to spend away from Claret Club and their other venue, the wine bar Where's Nick in Marrickville. They have a regular ritual of gathering with friends for a quiz at another wine bar, or cooking something special at home, music on and glass of wine in hand.

Harry shakes his head. "I have to be here for a photo shoot anyway so I may as well do it then." A small flutter of disappointment flickers over Bridget's face.

Bridget says she'll post about the Plat du Bar special the team changes every week: a single-plate dinner and glass of wine that can be eaten at the bar.

"They're a good boost for mid-week sales and they're also culturally important for us," she says. "Solo diners come in for it which we love. People are on their way home from work and instead of going home and standing in front of the fridge and eating a piece of cheese and feeling sad, this is our way to say, 'Come in, let us take care of you'."

But, she adds, "the marketing girl hasn't always been so diligent at remembering to make the posts."

Who is the marketing girl? "Ha! Me. I'm the marketing girl!"

Bridget is in charge of the restaurant's social media and has to work hard to keep customer's coming through the door. ( )

The 'marketing girl' has to work harder than ever to keep the customers coming through the door as people tighten their belts.

"If people weren't desperately struggling to pay their rent and mortgages they'd be able to afford to go out and support restaurants and our city would be more vibrant because of it," Bridget says.

There is also plenty of competition for the money people do have, particularly when hundreds of restaurants are accessible at people's fingertips from the sanctuary of a sofa at home. The food delivery industry — platforms like Uber Eats and DoorDash — is worth 1.8 billion according to IbisWorld data. DoorDash research shows nearly three-quarters of Australian consumers think of ordering delivery as "an act of self-care", something to comfort themselves after a big week or to celebrate a special occasion, which is exactly the role that a restaurant like Claret Club is trying to play.

Midday

A new problem. Bridget takes a call about a leak in the restaurant's roof. There's also a leak in the roof at Where's Nick. Both are the landlords' responsibility but it's still up to Bridget to coordinate the repairs. She calls her team at Where's Nick to ask if the Claret Club can borrow their stand mixer.

"Our bread maker fell off the bench and getting it fixed is better than trying to get a new one," Bridget says.

1:00pm

Claret Club isn't open for lunch on Thursdays, but outside, Stanley Street is starting to get busy with the lunch time trade. The white tablecloth tables across the road at Bill and Toni's have a scattering of customers ordering red-sauce spaghetti and tiramisu. Junko, who runs the Japanese restaurant next door to Claret Club (they share a swag of festoon lights across their adjoining terraces) pops in to say hello. Christian the builder arrives, to nut out the heat lamp conundrum. Everyone greets him with hugs.

"It's a real little village here," says Bridget. "Bill and Toni's have sent people our way. The pub guys [The Lord Roberts, opposite] are great, the Bones Ramen guys are friends. There's a WhatsApp group where we all share information about the best plumber, the best ice supplier. Our ice maker broke and — thousands of dollars later — we still don't have an ice maker. So, we borrowed one from a neighbour."

The Lord Roberts pub across the road from Claret Club helped out when the restaurant's own ice machine broke. ( )

That, she says, is one of the loveliest things about running a truly small, independent restaurant business. Everyone's hanging in there together.

Stanley Street has a long history of togetherness. It was one of Sydney's first true Italian precincts. Family-run Beppi's — famous for its hand-harvested mussels and veal saltimbocca — opened 70 years ago this year (and still stands today). If Beppi's was out of your price range, by the early 1970s you could head to Bill and Toni's, for huge plates of cheap spaghetti and cups of cordial.

Back then, Darlinghurst was a low socio-economic area, dominated by boarding houses. Today it's full of chic, renovated terraces, and residents with money to spend. The Claret Club team simply wish more of them would walk through their doors.

3:10pm

Harry gathers the team in the small alcove next to the kitchen for a blind wine tasting. It's something they do regularly, as he and Bridget want the team to be able to talk with customers about new bottles.

Everyone scribbles notes as they swill dolcettos and gamays, describing what they taste.

The staff take notes as they taste a new selection of wine. ( )

Bridget has a deep knowledge of wine which she uses to select bottles to cellar. ( )

Claret Club has a strict policy about wine distributors trying to book themselves in for time with Bridget or Harry in the hopes of getting their wares onto the list.

"We do not take tasting appointments if you haven't been into the venue and spent money with us," says Bridget. "It's about taking the time to get to know us, and to think about how their wines will fit in. Emails are not a relationship."

3:50pm

Ten minutes until doors open, and Harry is still finishing the wine tasting. Someone presses play on tonight's playlist and a dramatic Italian version of Take My Breath Away from Top Gun fills the room.

"Harry loves a playlist," says Bridget. "We call this one 'Italian bangers'."

4:40pm

Guests have slowly begun arriving in the downstairs bar, but there are still plenty of spare seats.

Guests are arriving but there is room for more. ( )

6:00pm

An older couple steps inside. They stand at the entrance, looking slightly perplexed, and Bridget approaches right away. Her body language radiates warmth as she directs them to a table and points out the wine list scrawled on the mirror. She realises they are French, and switches to French herself so they feel even more comfortable.

It's impressive to witness how 'on' a restaurant host needs to be, from the moment the first customer arrives until the last leaves. At every interaction Bridget's face is curious and interested, her body leans forward and every reply comes with smiles and wide-open arm gestures. It's easy to think a restaurant professional is merely passing on information about food and drink, but a good one makes you feel you're the best thing to have walked through the doors that night.

Bridget has worked in hospitality all over the world and puts every part of herself into making guests feel welcome.

Bridget has hospitality in her bones.

"I grew up in a house that was totally centred on food and wine," she says. "The dinner table was where all the conversations happened. We never had a TV in the kitchen or anywhere near the dining table. Food was how we all came together."

She worked as a barista from the age of 16, then as both a chef and front-of-house, everywhere from France (hence her ability to speak French) to the Netherlands. In Amsterdam, Bridget's favourite moments were always spent around the dinner table with friends.

"You'd buy a bottle of three-euro Montepulciano from the supermarket and if it was a really special occasion, you'd splash out on a five-euro," she says, laughing. "The point was shopping for great food, having a glass of wine in your hand and making a meal with friends."

This, she says, is the sort of atmosphere she and Harry (who previously worked at Bentley Group and Dinner by Heston) wanted to recreate with their own venue.

"We wanted to run a place that reflects the values we care about, particularly treating our staff with respect, so they feel valued and protected. We couldn't do that if we worked for other people."

But autonomy can come with costs. Not only does endless worry over revenue and long hours make for stressful work, but it can be difficult for hospitality workers to take care of their physical and mental health. Bridget tries to make it to the gym three times a week to clear her head.

"We also try to do team beers maybe once a week, as a bit of a download and for connection," she says, but she steers clear of the heavy-drinking culture that is common to the industry. "I have a huge workload and focus is pretty important to me. I can't afford to be hungover."

7:50pm

The wine dinner upstairs is in full swing, and Matt Prokop and restaurant manager Utsav Shah are run off their feet to serve 22 guests. The missing heat lamp means they have to get the meals upstairs extra quickly before food goes cold. Downstairs is still quiet.

A group of 22 enjoys a meal with wine pairings explained by a sommelier. ( )

Bridget hides herself into a nook, just outside of the customers' line of sight, and tries to catch up on paperwork.

"I hate getting a laptop out during service — it's been drilled into me that you don't do that. But we are here for such long hours, if I don't do it now I'll never be able to do it."

Harry rushes past with wine bottles but pauses to drop a kiss on the top of Bridget's head. It's a small, private moment, one of the rare chances they have to connect in their long days.

Claret Club co-owners Harry Hunter and Bridget Raffal are also a couple. It's important to find little moments to share together during a busy workday. ( )

9:04pm

The wine dinner guests have moved on to their main courses. Claret Club food has old-fashioned elegance to it: fish pies, rich with cream and potato. Beef rib braised in Barolo, served on polenta.

"It has a simplicity, and references to Elizabeth David," Bridget says, noting the iconic British cookbook author.

Claret Club's food is inspired by iconic British cookbook author Elizabeth David. ( )

Bridget and Harry join the waitstaff in running plates of food to diners. ( )

The wine dinner guests seem thrilled. Many remember Chef Andy from Melbourne's upscale Dinner By Heston (now closed), and several drop by to thank him for the meal.

This, says Bridget, is a big part of the reason they do what they do. "Our customers are often well-travelled and when they rave about our food we think, okay. This is it. What we're doing is working."

When the guests stop by to thank Claret Club chef Andy it must mean the restaurant is doing something right. ( )

10:00pm

The kitchen team is beginning to wipe down benchtops and sweep the floors. Sommelier Matt had planned to knock off early but two customers appear at the door. He goes immediately to greet and seat them.

"We want to build a reputation for being open later at night, for being somewhere you can come at any time," Matt explains later.

"Our thing is, 'last guest out the door and we're done' — whatever time that is."

Claret Club sommelier Matt Prokop says the restaurant's attitude is to stay open until the last guest wants to leave. ( )

After being seated the two men change their minds. It seems they wanted more of a pub atmosphere than a wine bar where they're practically the only customers. Matt directs them to The Lord Roberts over the road.

"That's okay, we don't have to be for everyone," he says.

10:40pm

The chefs have left and Bridget has pulled the doors of the venue closed, but a few stragglers from the wine dinner are still hanging out at the bar. Harry and the remaining staff give their guests the same level of attention as when they first arrived: they're excitedly discussing the wines they drank and what they enjoyed.

After a long day Bridget pulls closed the restaurant doors. ( )

11:40pm

The last guest has left, and Bridget pours a glass of Barolo for herself, and hands a beer to Harry. They drink as they bring in tables from outside and clear the linen from the tables inside.

After the last guest leaves there's a moment to pause before pack up begins. ( )

"Are you ready to go home?" Harry asks Bridget.

"Yep, I think it's about time. That's a nice early finish," she says, "Twenty to midnight."

But then a friend and fellow hospo worker turns up at the door and suggests they all go for a drink. Matt brightens and everyone else agrees.

"You need a bit of time to decompress otherwise it's just this dystopian feeling of sleep, work, sleep, work," Matt says.

Together they head to a local bar.

Claret Club sommelier manager Matt Prokop catching up after service with former employee Eva: "You need a bit of time to decompress". ( )

Midnight

The team has ordered giant steins of lager. They share war stories about the night — who ordered what, who did or didn't like a dish.

There's no sense of hierarchy and everyone chats freely, with no indication that the owners are more important than the workers. A long day is a long day, for everyone involved.

"Did you see that guy who drank all his wines at the wine dinner, and then leant over and drank all of his neighbour's wines as well?" chuckles Matt.

Harry does a quick calculation about the wine dinner revenue.

"It was a lot of effort for not a lot of money. The tickets were under $200 for all those wines. So, we brought in about $3,000.

"Cozzie livs," he finishes with a sigh, ruing the cost of living in that distinctly Australian way.

Cozzie livs be damned. Matt and Harry agree that there's time for "just one more beer".

At 1:10am, they call it a night.

The restaurant landscape changes constantly, as it must if it hopes to survive.

It wasn't long ago that it was relatively rare to eat outside the home in Australia. Migrant communities in the mid-20th century ran small shops, trattorias and cafes, and by the 1980s restaurants of all kinds became more common, including American fast food.

Since COVID, the hospitality industry has arguably experienced more upheaval than ever before. Food ordered in-venue still makes up the largest revenue stream but data from point-of-sale software platform Lightspeed shows it's fallen from 31 per cent in 2024 to 20 per cent in 2025, as takeaway, delivery and catering take a larger share.

Younger demographics, with less money to spend, are looking for social interaction with a smaller price tag, such as relatively cheap frozen yoghurt and ice cream parlours.

Then there are the policy and societal problems that kneecap the sector: wage rises, capped migration, inflation and unfavourable tax pressures, which industry body the Australian Restaurant & Cafe Association (ARCA) says are causing carnage.

It suffered a recent blow: the Reserve Bank banned businesses from adding card surcharges to customers' bills. That cost is likely to be passed to customers as higher prices.

The last thing Bridget wants to do is make Claret Club less accessible, but she also knows they won't be able to absorb the costs.

Revenue challenges mean Bridget and Harry can't hire extra people to share the burdens they shoulder themselves.

"Our jobs are full-time hosts, reservations, operations, bookkeeping," says Bridget. "We write two wine lists, do HR for both venues. Combined it's around nine or 10 full-time jobs. We can't keep working like this. A good week for me is 60 or 65 hours. But it can easily be 90."

In Canberra, another restaurateur Louis Couttoupes was forced to close his independent venue, Onzieme, in May this year. Unlike at Claret Club, he says filling seats was never a problem.

"Because Canberra has such a big public service workforce ... people's incomes are more reliable and predictable," he says.

Instead, Onzieme was felled by the pressures of finding and retaining qualified staff, without them being poached by larger restaurant groups acting "as this vacuum cleaner for staff because they can offer more money", he says.

Those left in the pool tended to be wildly underqualified for the roles Louis needed to fill. "I got to the point where my lease was up and I looked ahead at the next five years and thought, 'I can't see this getting any better'."

So what happens to a city's soul if the only hospitality venues that remain are large groups, with focus-tested menus and cookie-cutter concepts? The sorts of places Bridget calls 'Disneyland' restaurants?

For starters, there is likely to be far more homogenisation, as restaurants look to buy in 'value-added' food products: items that are cheaper, easy to prepare, pre-packaged and exactly the same as those served by the restaurant next door.

"We've all seen the explosion in restaurants where everything is steak frites, seafood pasta," says RCA's John Hart. "We can all practically recite the menus."

Couttoupes offers a grim warning. The big groups will dominate, and the little guys will vanish altogether. "Small businesses are more connected to their staff, customers, suppliers and producers," he says. "If you lose them, then with it goes diversity, creativity and passion."

This idea of creativity, however, is where a venue like Claret Club may eventually eke out a small advantage.

Chef Andy still orders in beautiful red mullet, rather than easy-to-source, pre-cut barramundi or Murray cod. The restaurant's truffle supplier drives over the Blue Mountains with a haul especially for them.

Sous-chef Fernando prepares beautiful red mullet. No pre-cut barramundi at Claret Club. ( )

Bridget uses her expert sommelier skills to buy and cellar bottles when they're young, which means she can hold onto them and sell them at a minimal mark-up compared to others who buy at peak price. This, says John Hart, is what diners will increasingly seek out as the 'Disneyfication' of restaurants becomes more prominent.

"The ones that take ingredients and provide a dining experience that's something very special," he says, are the sorts of places we will yearn to go.

As long as the market conditions allow these independent restaurants to survive, that is.

Friday 10:30am

It's an earlier start today in anticipation of a busier Friday, and a lunchtime opening.

Harry and Matt are setting up, while sous chef Fernando is making bread with the stand mixer borrowed from Claret Club's sister venue.

Harry sets up tables along Stanley Street. ( )

Bread is made from scratch with equipment borrowed from Claret Club's sister restaurant. ( )

11:35am

Bridget arrives looking fresh despite the 1am finish.

"Hi love," she says to Harry. Even though the couple live together, they've barely seen each other that morning.

"There's not a lot of opportunity in the week to have any connection," she says. "We make a point to remember to be nice to each other."

Marketing ideas are always churning in both Harry's and Bridget's brains.

Harry has an idea for an art-house cinema on the restaurant rooftop over summer.

Bridget looks pained. "I'm so in the weeds, Harry. When am I going to be able to think about that?"

Midday

Doors are open and a few office workers are having small meals on the sunny tables outside. But the venue is nowhere near full.

Claret Club's upstairs dining room is a beautiful space but where are the guests? ( )

3:00pm

By mid-afternoon, Andy uses the time to test out new recipes, bringing a tuna and blood orange dish to Bridget and Harry for a taste test. The orange segments could be cut finer, but the flavour is spot-on. Bridget uses the spare moments to iron tablecloths.

Bridget and Harry taste Andy's dish and offer feedback. ( )

4:22pm

Nervy about the number of guests, Bridget puts up an Instagram post advertising their $10 martini happy hour that began at 4pm.

Within 30 minutes a group of four — Bridget and Harry's friends who have an office nearby — have come in and ordered a round.

Sommelier Matt helps guests select wine and cocktails. ( )

4:30pm

Chefs Andy and Fernando give themselves a coffee break. They crouch outside together in the little tin shed they built on their own — a minute's peace before what they hope will be a busy night.

4:50pm

But the hoped-for rush will have to wait. Andy comes back inside and finds Bridget.

"Hey Bridget. Do you want some good news?" he asks with a grimace.

"No. Don't tell me. What's broken?" says Bridget, her eyes widening.

"The pilot on the fryer has gone out."

Bridget momentarily closes her eyes. "We won't get anyone to fix it now. It's almost the weekend," she says.

The two discuss options. Not much can be done this close to dinner. One fryer is still working but just like the heat lamp, one will now be out of action.

They let the floor staff know to hold back on pushing menu items that need to be deep-fried.

Meanwhile, Bridget throws the problem into the Stanley Street WhatsApp group, and someone comes up with a repair contact right away.

"We can't have someone come here during service, and we can't afford the Sunday call-out fee, so it'll have to be Monday," she says.

"Hopefully we won't get stung with an 'urgent' loading."

Bridget Raffal and Harry Hunter need flexibility to respond to the unexpected. ( )

5:18pm

Bridget checks the bookings for the night — just 34 covers in a venue that comfortably seats 60. Most are peripheral industry people — friends and colleagues they know — with a handful of first timers.

A couple comes in and orders glasses of wine.

"You're a very good addition to Stanley Street," the gentleman tells Bridget. "If you keep your heads above water you're going to do well."

Friends and family are an important part of Claret Club's customer base. It's also a big part of what makes the restaurant feel personal and welcoming. "Our whole business is built around relationships: we try to know everyone's name, if they've just had a baby and it's their first time out of the house," Bridget says.

Building relationships is at the heart of what Bridget and Harry aim to do. ( )

Bridget likes to tell a story of how she does her banking at a branch in Marrickville, close to their other venue. One day her regular teller said she was planning to book Claret Club for dinner.

"When I saw her name on the bookings and when she showed up, that really meant a lot," Bridget says.

Just as often, strangers become friends. "We're a neighbourhood venue. We want the three generations, the kids, the place people think of for their special birthday every year."

In many ways this word of mouth is more effective than any marketing. "The old wisdom is everyone works really hard to capture new guests, and of course we do that," she says. "But if you work to get them back the returns are much higher."

10:00pm

The night has been busier than expected. But it's still quiet enough that Bridget has time to sit down and try Andy's red mullet with velouté.

10:37pm

Just four groups remain. Everyone is taking their time to finish a final few languid glasses of wine, while Bridget and Harry stop repeatedly at the groups to chat.

It's a long night yet again, but the team still look like they are in their element.

"We do it for the love of food and wine, really," Bridget says. "Connecting with people over those things is really fulfilling and restorative. Those little moments when people really get what we're doing and who we are — that's what makes it all worth it."

Bridget says connecting with customers is what makes the job worth it. ( )

11:23pm

The team looks tired, though they make plans for a couple of beers next door, like last night. For Bridget and Harry especially, Claret Club is more than just a workplace, it's the heart of their lives.

Bridget rests her head briefly on Harry's shoulder.

"The last thing we say before we go to sleep isn't 'I love you baby'," she says. "It's 'Did we do well today?'"

After a long day at work only one question remains: DId we do well? ( )

Credits

Words: Alexandra Carlton

Photographs: Teresa Tan
