World.title: Met Police received letter about Meghan Markle's father in 2019
World.content:
London's Metropolitan Police has confirmed the force received a letter about Meghan Markle's father in January 2019 but did not share it with other agencies.

In a statement received by the ABC, a spokesperson for the Met Police said the letter contained "a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom".

It comes after Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, revealed on Friday that she was informed in 2018 about "disturbing allegations" against her father, Thomas Markle, which prompted her to keep her children away from him.

Loading...

International media earlier reported claims that child sexual abuse material had been found at Mr Markle's former home in the Philippines.

In an interview with the Daily Mail, Mr Markle denied possessing the images, calling the accusations "sick lies".

The 2019 letter was referred to MPS Protection Command "to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex" and to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

But it was not shared with other law enforcement agencies, the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson added that the force was reviewing its handling of the matter, including whether it should call in the police watchdog.

The Met Police received the letter in 2019. (Reuters: Justin Tallis)

Authorities in the Philippines are investigating the allegations, according to UK media.

In the US, an FBI spokesperson said it was "aware of the allegations and would provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities".

Prince Harry, the second son of King Charles III and estranged brother of heir to the throne Prince William, married Meghan at Windsor Castle in May 2018.

The couple left Britain and quit royal duties in 2020.

But they made an unexpected return with their two children to live in the United Kingdom in August.

ABC/Wires

World.title: Ukraine says Starlink at normal speed after delays impede military
World.content:
Ukraine says the Starlink satellite system is back to operating at high speeds after restrictions disrupted Ukraine's military operations and intensified tensions with the US.

Problems with Elon Musk's SpaceX-owned Starlink and its military version, Starshield, came after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel, while pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries.

Neither Elon Musk or the US government has acknowledged responsibility for delays in satellite speed. (Reuters: Nathan Howard)

Ukrainian officials said the restrictions hampered the military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations.

"Ukraine's Ministry of Defence monitoring systems are officially recording the restoration of Starlink/Starshield operating speeds," the ministry said in a post to Telegram.

"Connectivity remains stable at speeds exceeding 400km per hour," it added.

The Ukrainian military does not disclose the systems' maximum operating speeds, and the defence ministry did not say whether service had been fully restored.

A Ukrainian serviceman prepares a Starlink satellite internet system at a frontline position in the Donetsk region. (Reuters: Inna Varenytsia)

When limitations were in place, Ukraine experienced problems trying to operate at speeds over 160kph.

Ukraine does not rely on the systems for long-range drone operations on Russian territory, but Starlink is vital for frontline communications and Starshield is used for military operations in occupied territories.

The restrictions sparked outrage in Ukraine, particularly as they coincided with disruptions to allied warnings about incoming Russian missile attacks.

Kyiv later said it continued to receive US intelligence.

Neither Elon Musk or the US government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine.

Both said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hugs US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff. (NTB/Heiko Junge/via Reuters)

It was reported by Reuters that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House.

Previously, US administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn Starlink on or off in various countries, sources said.

Trump said on Friday that if problems persisted, he would "get it straightened out".

Reuters

World.title: WA premier confronted by South Hedland community members
World.content:
South Hedland residents have confronted the West Australian Premier during a five-hour visit to the northern town — his first since the state government announced a coronial inquest into the deaths of three local children.

The renewed investigation into Margaret Hawke's 2022 killing of her 10-year-old daughter, seven-year-old son and four-month-old baby came after sustained political and media pressure over failures by WA's Department of Child Protection.

Child protection authorities are under fire after it was reported more than a dozen children were living alone in a house in South Hedland (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

Recent weeks have seen a steady stream of political drop-ins to South Hedland, more than 1,600 kilometres north of Perth, with the premier arriving on Saturday to declare a contractor had been selected to construct a long-promised $22 million MRI facility.

However, the spotlight remained on reports first appearing in The Australian newspaper that up to 15 children had been living unsupervised in a state-owned home until September.

The Premier was accompanied by Child Protection Minister Jessica Stojkovski — her fourth trip to South Hedland in nine weeks — for an agenda dominated by closed-door discussions with government agencies and their partners.

"You've gotta come back sit with us here, camp with us and roam the streets with us, so they can see for themselves what's actually happening," said Nyamal-Pitjikarli elder Doris Eaton, who spoke with the pair at a snap meeting during their visit.

" You can't see it from Perth, you can't do fly in and fly out. "

Doris Eaton (far left) met with the premier, alongside fellow elders Linda Doogiebee and Pat Mason. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

Departing talks with community organisation Hedland Aboriginal Strong Leaders, Mr Cook and Ms Stojkovski came under fire from a community member who identified herself as a former foster carer.

"When is the department going to be accountable and when are you going to speak to the community?" she said.

The ABC spoke with multiple other residents who expressed their frustration with the government response.

"I get confronted by people all the time. That's part of the job," Mr Cook said.

"But I fully appreciate that everyone wants to see things improve."

Progress being made, government says

There were no policy announcements about child protection during the premier's visit, nor did he meet with families impacted by the crisis.

Mr Cook said the emphasis was on consulting with the people "who are delivering the services in the community".

Dorothy Papertalk believes a coronial inquest would provide answers about what happened to her grandchildren. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

The ABC understands Dorothy Papertalk, mother of Margaret Hawke and the children's grandmother, declined an invitation to meet with the premier.

Ms Papertalk led the campaign for an inquest, which was denied by the coroner in 2025. Ms Papertalk has requested privacy at this time.

"There are a range of families that are receiving good services, there's others that we can improve," Mr Cook said.

"The department's in a process of continuous improvement all the time."

Ms Stojkovski has ordered an assurance review of the department's handling of the Hawke murders. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

When questioned, Ms Stojkovski could not point to how many full-time equivalent staff positions had been filled since it was revealed in WA Parliament the Pilbara region had 11 child protection caseworker vacancies.

A relief team has been sent to South Hedland in response.

"Having those senior staff from the group, the relieving team, is really important and it's been very helpful for our staff here on the ground," Ms Stojkovski said.

The minister expects to be handed an assurance review of recommendations made in the wake of the Hawke murders by the end of the month.

'National shame': WA opposition

On Thursday, WA Commissioner for Children and Young People Jacqueline McGowan-Jones tabled a scathing assessment of the state's child protection system in parliament.

The report considered the experiences of 19 children who were placed into a secure care centre multiple times and made 56 recommendations.

"If children are brought into out-of-home care, it is because they are apparently at risk at home," Ms McGowan-Jones told the ABC.

" They were equally, if not more so, at risk, being brought into the state system. "

Jacqueline McGowan-Jones handed down her review on Thursday. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

WA opposition leader Basil Zempilas said it was "insulting" that the premier was not visiting affected families.

"I am absolutely astounded after nine weeks of this being in the national spotlight, the premier has finally gone up — finally — but is not meeting with any families," he said.

"This is a shocking and ignorant lack of leadership."

World.title: Young investors love AI stocks. Are they falling into a debt trap?
World.content:
MoneyInvestingAI Opinion Young investors love AI stocks. Are they falling into a debt trap? Victoria Devine Money columnist October 25, 2026 — 5:08am

October 25, 2026 — 5:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It was only earlier this month and here in this very column that I wrote about the importance of doing your research and seriously considering your appetite for risk before investing in the tech sector. And as if right on cue, the market demonstrated exactly why people are increasingly recommending investors move with caution. The latest AI models are far more advanced than expected and pose a substantial risk to existing cybersecurity defences. Getty Over the course of a single week of trading last week, more than $US1 trillion ($1.43 billion) was wiped from the stocks of 20 of the world’s biggest semiconductor and AI companies. That sounds pretty bad, right? Well, skip to this week, and the share prices of many of those same companies were already enjoying a rebound. Unlike more established investment industries, there is still a lot we simply do not know about where the AI train is headed, which is in part what makes it so volatile – and the potential rewards so appealing.



While for some seasoned investors riding this rollercoaster is simply part of the experience, two interesting things are taking place that make paying attention to this specific issue especially important, and worth me banging on about. The first is that according to a new report from the ASX, more Australians are now investing than ever before. The second is that thanks to the hype surrounding the AI industry generally and the looming IPOs for two major artificial intelligence companies – Anthropic and OpenAI – many Australian investors, and specifically young investors with decades of portfolio time on their side, are seriously considering putting their hard-earned money into this sector. Most analysts agree the AI industry overall is still solid, but that doesn’t inherently make it a safe investment with a guaranteed return. What’s more, the timing of all of this matters, and not just because of those IPOs. For a while now, AI stocks have stood out in part because of the seemingly unrelenting unpredictability of the sector, and in part because market experts are increasingly worried about the fact that most of these companies are reliant on debt to fund their growth. And as interest rates in the US rise (and US Treasury yields in the bond market hit increasingly higher levels), that has the potential to become a massive, expensive problem.



Take CoreWeave, an American cloud computing and data centre operator whose IPO in March 2025 marked the biggest public debut for a tech company since 2021. By June 2025, just three months later, the company reached a market cap of $US90 billion and shareholders were feeling pretty happy about getting in early on the neocloud company (these businesses rent computing power to companies building AI). Editor's pick Opinion

Credit cards Backlash: Why the ATO’s credit card ban missed the mark Victoria Devine Money columnist At the end of last year, they had about $US30 billion of debt and liabilities on its balance sheet. By the second quarter of this year, the debt figure had grown to $US52 billion. Even worse is when you cut to today, where CoreWeave stocks have dropped by 30 per cent this month alone, and its valuation has been virtually cut by two thirds of what it was 18 months ago – diving to about $US34 billion. In large part, this decline is because CoreWeave is reliant on debt to fund its growth and is not yet profitable. So, those rising interest rates are hitting pretty hard – to the point where its bond yields rose to levels that generally signal distress. While this is just one company, it is causing investment experts to ask important questions about the tech sector and if the boom times it has been enjoying can really last.



Last month, Deutsche Bank published a research note that warned the level of AI spending we’re currently seeing is unsustainable. But, it noted, if spending slows before the sector’s promises come to fruition, it could wreak economic havoc. As the bank’s head of FX Research George Saravelos wrote, market growth “is not coming from AI itself, but from building the factories to generate AI capacity”. In other words, many of these companies are selling future potential, not a verified reality. Sam Altman, chief executive officer and co-founder of OpenAI. Bloomberg Earlier this month, the global investment bank RBC Capital Markets issued a recommendation that their clients reduce their tech holdings, after previously recommending higher than average holdings. In downgrading the tech sector’s outlook from “overweight” to “market weight”, RBC also said investors should instead look at more traditionally safe stocks such as healthcare – because sectors like these tend to perform well irrespective of what’s happening in an economy because people will always need access to medicine and medical care.



Now, at this point it is sounding a bit doom and gloom, which is not entirely the case. In his note to Deutsche Bank investors, Saravelos noted that “AI machines – in quite a literal sense – appear to be saving the US economy right now”. He also said that “In the absence of tech-related spending, the US would be close to, or in, recession this year.” In other words, it’s still doing well, but there is a lot riding on that not changing, and it’s important to be keenly aware of that risk. While most analysts agree that the sheer level of demand for AI – as in, people continue to use it and remain willing to pay for the services – means the industry overall is still very much safe, that doesn’t inherently make it a safe investment with a guaranteed return. And when you’re talking about people investing their savings as a means of creating long-term wealth (as opposed to investors with several more zeros to their bank balances), this matters an awful lot. As I’ve said a hundred times, one of the most important factors your money can have is time in the market. For some investors, being able to ride the highs and lows of volatile stock over a long period of time might be OK.



But another important factor is ensuring that your money is working for you in a way that will help you achieve your financial goals. If you’re planning to one day access that money to put towards something like a house or as you move towards retirement, there’s a very real risk that when you go to sell a volatile stock, you won’t be able to do so without losing money. That will mean you either have to wait out the dip, or eat the loss – neither of which are especially great options. The added layer of difficulty in all of this is that if you ask 10 experts, there’s a good chance you’ll get at least five different perspectives. But to my mind, that’s why doing your research and backing your own decision once it’s informed, is the foundation to good investing – especially when risk and volatility are involved. Victoria Devine is an award-winning retired financial adviser, a bestselling author and host of Australia’s No.1 finance podcast, She’s on the Money. She is also founder and director of Zella Money. World.title: Will I still have to pay the 30% tax if only sell a few shares?
World.content:
MoneyTaxAsk an expert Opinion Will I still have to pay the 30% tax if only sell a few shares? Paul Benson Money contributor October 25, 2026 — 5:01am

October 25, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I’ve had many questions from readers seeking clarification to a response I gave last week in relation to a person who was inheriting shares. There seems to be considerable confusion arising from conflicting commentary around the application of the minimum 30 per cent tax that will be introduced from next financial year. The specifics of the new tax laws appear to be confusing many. AFR This is the statement as published by Treasury on May 28, 2026: “In addition to indexation, a minimum tax rate of 30 per cent will apply to real capital gains accruing from July 1, 2027.” This statement makes it clear that the minimum 30 per cent tax does not apply to gains that accrued before the new rules take effect. It’s also worth highlighting that those receiving the age pension, even a small part pension, are specifically exempt from the 30 per cent minimum capital gains tax on gains accruing post 1 July 2027. In my response I mentioned that “it may be possible to sell small amounts each year and keep under the tax-free threshold.” ‘May be possible’ carries a significant load here and warrants further explanation.



This will depend on what the CBA share price does after July 1, 2027, and whether the person receives an age pension. For self-funded retirees, the minimum 30 per cent tax will apply on real gains that arise from 1 July 2027 onwards, no matter how small the value of shares sold. I’ve really appreciated the engagement from so many readers, so please, if you see something that you feel isn’t clear (or, heaven forbid, wrong!), do email and let me know. I’m trying to work out if I can afford to retire next year. I’m finding my conclusion changes considerably depending on how much I assume my spending will be in the future. I’ve never worked to a budget, but I tried using an online calculator. The answer it came up with seems too low, so I must be missing things. I’ve found the figure of $56,000 a year mentioned online, but I don’t feel like I’m “average”. Any tips? Everyone who tries to work out what they currently spend via a budget app underestimates, so rest assured that you are running with the pack here. We’ve found that reverse-engineering your current spending is the best starting point. Determine your after-tax income from the past year. Then calculate how much your savings rose, or your debt reduced. Subtract this movement from the income, and the figure you get must be what you spent.



As an example, let’s say you earned $100,000 in the past year after tax. Your savings account increased by $20,000. The rest of your balance sheet was unchanged, other than market movements (super can be ignored here). This would imply that you spent $80,000 in the past year. Related Article Opinion

Ask an expert Will inheriting my mum’s CBA shares trigger a big capital gains tax? Paul Benson Money contributor With this as your starting point, you can now consider what your spending is likely to be once retired. Commute costs often decrease, but maybe (hopefully) you will spend more socialising. Often people will spend more money early in retirement, as they tick off some travel bucket list items. We might build in an extra $20,000 per person for the first decade of retirement to cover this need. Research points to retirement spending following a “smile” pattern. Higher at the beginning to cover fun things, and then higher at the end for care-related costs, with a lull in the middle. In your calculations, be sure to allow for inflation. Over a 20-year-plus retirement, inflation impact is significant. Paul Benson is a Certified Financial Planner at Guidance Retirement Planning. He hosts the Financial Autonomy podcast. World.title: The European river ship so good, other cruise lines copy it
World.content:
★★★★ Reviews & adviceShip reviews The European river ship so good, other cruise lines copy it Brian Johnston October 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

VIKING SKIRNIR AND VIKING MODI Launched 2015

2015 The cruise Rhine & Main Explorer, 11 days

Rhine & Main Explorer, 11 days Passengers 190

190 Crew 53

53 Decks Four

Four Length 135 metres

135 metres Suites 95 A Viking ship on the Rhine THE SHIP Owing to a stretch of too-shallow Rhine, I’m on two Viking Longships (Skirnir and Modi), but the coach transfer is made with remarkable efficiency and without much disruption to the itinerary. Because all of Viking’s Longships (there are currently 69) are virtually identical, the onboard experience is uncannily the same.



BOARDING 



The decor is unassuming but, when I look closely, I find interesting touches, such as Viking-style axes above the computer terminals, and black-and-white photos of company founder Torstein Hagen’s family. Viking’s educational ethos is alive and well in the quality of the book selection. THE SPACES The lounge is expansive and bartenders at its U-shaped bar are always busy. Grouped seating means guests can socialise in whatever sized gathering the mood takes them. At its front end the lounge dissolves into Aquavit Terrace, a delightful spot at the ship’s prow for informal dining with forward-facing views. The top Sun Deck has shuffleboard, a walking track and putting green, seating and strips of herbs that get regular haircuts to supply the galley. However, low bridges on the Main River, the longest tributary of the Rhine, mean it can’t be used throughout much of this particular cruise.



The library is understandably, given the limited space on river ships, simply a lobby space with a wall of books, two desktop computers and four armchairs around a coffee table often taken up by jigsaw-puzzle solvers. Viking’s educational ethos is alive and well in the quality of the book selection. One of seven Veranda Suites on the ship. THE STATEROOM Among cabin categories are Standard Staterooms which have but a porthole, French Balcony Staterooms, and Veranda Staterooms. Outlook and size vary but decor and amenities are very similar. I’m in stateroom 316, one of seven Veranda Suites (there are also two larger Explorer Suites). It’s a generous 25.5 square metres and divided into a lounge with enough room for a sofa and armchair, as well as a modest desk that doubles as a dressing table. The bedroom has a queen-sized bed good enough for Goldilocks. Praise be for sensible pillows uncommon in Europe, one thin and one fat, to suit your favourite neck position. The suite’s beige, brown and blue decor is relaxing, and a cool comfort to return to in the full blast of Europe’s heatwave.



Some arty photos of European river scenes might have been more interesting than the couple of small and undistinguished abstract artworks. Nice touches include a pair of binoculars, reading lights in the bedhead, heated bathroom floors, and an anti-fog bathroom mirror. Suites benefit from complimentary laundry. Menus run the gamut of international favourites including pannacotta. THE FOOD The food is very satisfying, and can’t be faulted for quality and freshness. Regional dishes are among the choices every evening, among which are standouts such as braised beef with onion sauce, sausages and sauerkraut, and bienenstich or bee-sting cake, an almond layered biscuit cake with vanilla cream. Both lunch and dinner are a la carte. At lunch, chefs are present to prepare salads and cook pasta, and guests help themselves to salads, bread, cheese and dessert. Three-course dinners are more formally served. All the tables in the main restaurant are shared. Alternative Aquavit Terrace is more informal with some limited tables for two that are always in high demand. Menus run the gamut of international favourites from French onion soup to steamed cod, rib-eye steak to involtini, rounding off with classic desserts or cheese and fruit plates. I become a little obsessed with the lunchtime Nicoise salad. Although excellent, the dining is mainstream rather than adventurous and, on a cruise that spends far more time in Germany than France, I’d have preferred a German buffet evening. Instead, it’s French and rather unexciting, with cheese plates peculiarly promoted as an appetiser. WELLNESS



I’ve often wondered why cruise ships, and especially river ships, devote space to gyms that only a minority of guests use. No such mistake on Viking Longships. You don’t need a gym on a European river cruise: every port has kilometres of promenades and cycle paths. The Main River has amiable cycleways that contour the river for almost its full length. No wellness area either. Wellness consists of enjoying the top deck in the fresh air as lovely scenery drifts past, instead of huddling in a perfumed room. Space for shuffleboard, a walking track and a putting green. Aquavit Terrace is an informal dining spot at the ship’s prow. ENTERTAINMENT There’s no regular nightly entertainment except trivia competitions, although occasionally a local music group is invited on board. A pianist glassy-eyed with boredom tinkles on a grand piano in the lounge. I suspect he can play Rachmaninov, but is doomed to produce dreary elevator music. Lectures and talks that provide informative background to local history, politics and society used to be a hallmark of Viking’s river cruises. Disappointing that these have been abandoned but for one mundane lecture on the rise of the Nazis.



THE CREW Founder Torstein Hagen is a Harvard-educated Norwegian who once worked for an American ocean cruise line, and his company has headquarters in America and Switzerland. The crew on both ships seem infused both with Swiss-Norwegian efficiency and the relaxed friendliness of American service: a winning combination. THE VERDICT I’ve been on several Viking river cruises, but the last one was probably a decade ago. Rediscovering that little has changed is slightly disconcerting but ultimately a pleasure. Why change something that works so well? DETAILS

World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life ‘We understood each other’: Why writer Jon Ronson says he and Monica Lewinsky bonded Robyn Doreian October 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. This story is part of the October 25 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

Author Jon Ronson is best known for writing books including The Psychopath Test and Them: Adventures with Extremists. Here, the 59-year-old talks about the women who have influenced his life, including a peripatetic aunt, his wife, Elaine, and Monica Lewinsky, with whom he shared a professional connection. Jon Ronson’s mother urged him to volunteer at a local radio station, which kickstarted his career. “That was the best thing she did for me.” Emli Bendixen www.emli.co.uk I grew up in a boring suburban house in Cardiff, Wales. My father, David, managed a warehouse. When I was 19 and had moved to London, my parents bought a hotel. It was a pretty middle-class, non-glamorous life. My father’s sister, Auntie Mavis, however, was an adventurer. At the age of 19 she and her friend from London went off on a seven-year odyssey. There are photos of her on a shipwrecked beach with opium smugglers. When she returned, she wrote a book and became a Magnum [photographic agency] photographer. I found photographs of the Rolling Stones in my grandfather’s London kitchen for her series, Rock Stars In The Kitchen. When I was four, Auntie Mavis took a special liking to me. She was like, “He’s the one who’s going to have an amazing life.” She lived in London and sent me cassettes of David Bowie; she was the coolest. Auntie Mavis died of cancer when I was 10. By far, she was the earliest formative woman in my life.



My mother, Paula, is in a home now, but she was always very kind. I remember her taking my older brother, Daniel, and me fossil hunting on the beaches in Penarth, near Cardiff. When I was a feckless 16-year-old, she got me to volunteer at my local radio station. It got me a place in media studies at the Polytechnic of Central London, which set me on my way. That was the best thing she did for me. Growing up, I was awkward in my own skin and a misfit. I would go to Jewish summer and winter camps where I’d meet really cool girls. The camp wasn’t weird or religious, more listening to Simon & Garfunkel and learning how to smoke. These 15-, 16-year-old girls from London were sassy and funny. It was probably where I had my first kiss. Our marriage works because we are not controlling of each other. We let the other do whatever they want. But we also watch TV together every night. While I was at college I had an incredible one-night stand with Clare. She looked like [the actress] Nastassja Kinski. I thought she was amazing. We are still in touch and have a friendship that has endured for life. David Cardiff was one of my teachers at college. He was a very elegant man who was married to the journalist Lynn Barber – she wrote An Education, which was made into a movie. I was a big fan of hers. After David died in 2003, I got to know Lynn. From her, I learnt how to ask impudent interview questions in ways that didn’t offend.



I met my wife, Elaine, while working for Time Out magazine – she was one of the editors and I was a columnist. She was very together and I was very un-together. We hit it off. She had a beautiful flat and was very glamorous and impressive. Related Article Sunday Life ‘People come at you from all over’: How fame changed Sarah Cracknell’s outlook on love We got married in the late 1990s on a whim. We were on a safari in Africa for a month and were staying in a Victoria Falls hotel, which is now in disrepair. But rules prevented us from marrying in Zimbabwe, so we went to Nantucket, in Massachusetts, and married there. Elaine is an art consultant and an aesthete. I am not. I never think about the way things look. She did a brilliant job of doing up our barn in upstate New York. Our marriage works because we are not controlling of each other. We let the other do whatever they want. But we also watch TV together every night. Our son, Joel, 28, is practical, thoughtful and sociable, just like Elaine. Monica Lewinsky and I both started talking about cancel culture at the same time – her 2015 TED Talk, and my book about public shaming. I really like Monica. We’ve met a bunch of times and have done TED events together. We had this shared strangeness in that we started a conversation that had taken over the world. We were both badly bullied at school. I think we understood each other a bit better because of that shared experience. I think she’s done really well at correcting her narrative.



Jon Ronson is currently touring Australia. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.

World.content:
NationalNSWParramatta Billionaires, immortality and barbecues: Sci-fi author ready for arrival at Powerhouse Michael Ruffles October 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Ted Chiang has been thinking about some of the worst people in the world. Considered one of the greatest living science-fiction writers and known for fighting the rapacious rise of artificial intelligence, the New York-born, Seattle-based writer is bound for Sydney for Powerhouse Parramatta’s 23-day opening festival. Chiang will give a keynote address on November 8 about billionaires and capitalism and whether immortality can be pursued ethically. Author Ted Chiang will make a guest appearance for the opening of Powerhouse Parramatta in November. Kate Joyce Spoiler alert: probably not. “It seems like a lot of the people who are interested in pursuing immortality in recent years, they seem like the worst people in the world,” Chiang says. “I guess this raises a couple of questions. You know, like one is, would you really want to spend eternity in the company of these people?”



The other question Chiang is pondering is along these lines: “If the worst people in the world seem to be the only ones who are really interested in that, does that tell you anything about that thing that they are interested in?” There have been headline-grabbing examples of biohacking, and the longevity billionaires are a class of ultrawealthy individuals who seem intent on testing the theory that money cannot buy more time. Chiang doesn’t name anyone, but points out those in such a socioeconomic stratosphere already live pretty long lives. “For us to have good evidence that [these treatments] are working, we’ll need to see a significant number of them living over 100 or like 120 or something like that, and so you know that’s decades away.” In a sense, the ultra-rich have bought time anyway, since they do not have to bother themselves with such mundane tasks as dishes and laundry, or driving around to hardware stores to swap the gas bottle.



“That’s another version of the question of, ‘Why does anyone continue to pursue wealth?’ There’s a level of wealth which is modest by billionaire standards but is really more than anyone could actually want in terms of improving the quality of their life. “If you have $10 million, I don’t know how much better your life is going to get with additional money, but you know, obviously, billionaires – they have 100 times that. “Now there are people who have $10 billion or $100 billion. Why do they keep pursuing that? It’s not because it will help improve their life in any meaningful way. It’s just because, arguably, it’s the only thing they know how to do. You know, they can’t think of anything else to do.” In the film Arrival, adapted from Ted Chiang’s story, Amy Adams plays a linguist who tries to interpret for visiting aliens. Alamy One of Chiang’s early stories, his 1998 novella Story of Your Life, was the basis of Eric Heisserer’s screenplay for the award-winning Denis Villeneuve film Arrival. But another, The Tower of Babylon, was the inspiration for one of the blockbuster opening exhibitions for the Powerhouse Parramatta.



For Task Eternal, billed as “one of the most ambitious aerospace exhibitions ever staged” and located in the museum’s largest space, the architects drew on the story for an ascending design in four acts, titled Skyward, Power, Off-Earth and The Return. About 30 minutes into the interview, I throw a barbie into the conversation as we veer from billionaires’ quixotic quests to the inevitable heat death of the universe. In Chiang’s Hugo award-winning story Exhalation, the title work from his 2019 collection, long-lived mechanical beings come to grips with the inevitability of their own demise when they realise the differences in air pressure that power them will eventually equalise and their universe will be rendered inert. Mortality, or immortality, was not front of mind. “I can understand why you might be reminded of that story, but I guess I want to clarify that that story is just about thermodynamics,” Chiang says. “Sometimes people interpret the story as maybe being about climate change. It is absolutely not about climate change because climate change is not inevitable, whereas the heat death of the universe is inevitable.”



Early on, there’s a passage about how swapping depleted lungs for full canisters can sometimes be a joyous communal event, and sometimes as perfunctory as changing the batteries in the remote. I’d read it when the bottle under the barbecue had run empty, so fossil fuels were front of mind. Not so for the author. “I certainly never expected people to interpret Exhalation as being about climate change. That was not something that ever, ever occurred to me. But yeah, that’s just another example of how it is impossible to anticipate how people will read your work.” Chiang was named among Time’s 100 most influential figures in artificial intelligence for his criticism of the technology and the companies profiting from it. His work has dealt with fate and mortality, along with thermodynamics. “Trying to make peace with one’s mortality is, yeah, I think a really central part of what it means to be a human. What I want is not to live forever, but I want to be at peace with my mortality.” If writing might be an easier way to achieve immortality, “that has never crossed my mind”. “When people crave immortality, mostly what they want is actual physical immortality. I don’t think that having a long-lasting reputation is a substitute for physical immortality,” he says.

World.content:
InspirationNorth America Forgotten forest secrets in Canada’s greenest city Jim Darby October 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. “We are the land and the land is us,” explains Talaysay Campo, born and raised in the Squamish and Sechelt cultures of Canada’s First Nations. On Campo’s Talking Trees tour in Vancouver’s Stanley Park, the city’s vast green 400-hectare lung, we are introduced to the plants, medicines and technologies of her people. Vancouver’s Stanley Park stays lush and green thanks to 169 days of rain a year. iStock First, we meet the vine maple tree. “It doesn’t know personal space – it likes to branch out and reach for that sunshine,” Talaysay says. Its wood is strong but flexible so it is useful for constructing shelters. If the tree arched in shape, then that shape would form the frame for a shelter. Next, we meet the mighty Douglas fir, which soars into the sky with bark so thick it resists forest fires but, ironically, there’s an element in its sap that helps start fires, and it was tapped for just that purpose.



Deeper into the forest we find salmonberries, huckleberries and more. “This is one of the first laws we learn: you never take the first berry, and you never take the last berry,” says Talaysay. 



There are rules for the bark harvest: “If you can reach around the tree and touch your hands, move on because the tree is too small. When you find a tree old enough, measure two hand widths, make a cut and pull the bark away. That might strip as much as five metres, it will stop where the tree wants it to stop.” From that park full of trees, stroll along the shores of English Bay and catch a ferry to Granville Island. While the First Canadians would harvest from the forest, here’s where the locals harvest their fresh food today. “The market is who we are,” says my Vancouver Foodie tour guide Sandra Trotter. “Here’s the best of Vancouver – food, wine and the outdoors. We aim for this to be the world’s best market.” The morning is sunny and the crowds are building. There are no franchise outlets on the island and most of the produce we taste on this tour with Trotter is local and artisan. The Benton Brothers make their small-batch cheese from the milk that comes in from the Okanagan region. Oyama Sausage makes its meaty creations from five generations of charcutiers.



Fresh produce at the Granville Island Public Market. Bloomberg Wild salmon from Longliner Seafoods. And the morsels of wild-caught Canadian salmon we try at Longliner Seafoods (the maple candy salmon is what I’m going back for) is another story of the generations. Jim Moorehead, himself a longline fisher, founded the business in the late 1970s and was one of the market’s original tenants. Back then, the island was mainly used for warehousing and as a base for the local fishing fleet. Beyond the market, you’ll find those warehouses have been transformed into studios for artists and artisans – painters, jewellers, glassblowers, even broom makers. And before it hosted those warehouses, the island’s sandbars were a food source for the First Canadians. When the tide was out, the food was on. And so it continues.

Event season is kicking off, and if you’re in the market for a skin refresh before hitting the party circuit, it pays to find one with minimal downtime. Cosmetic physician Dr Joseph Hkeik, of Sydney’s All Saint Clinic, offers CoolPeel, a laser resurfacing procedure with about two days of downtime. “This helps to brighten skin and rebuild collagen,” he says.

Looking for a skin refresh this time of year? Pick a cosmetic treatment with minimal downtime. Getty Images

Of course, regardless of which treatment you choose, it’s essential to pay attention to appropriate after-care. Following the procedure, keep your skincare routine simple to support the barrier and protect it from sun damage.

Dr Hkeik suggests using a gentle, non-active cleanser and a moisturising SPF50+ sunscreen, and taking an ingestible marine collagen supplement such as Par Olive’s Marine Collagen. “It’s paired with vitamin C from the Kakadu plum, which is exactly what skin needs to keep producing its own collagen once the treatment is done,” he says.

Once your skin has bounced back from the treatment, at around the two-week mark, you can reinstate your active skincare products.

World.title: Young investors love AI stocks. Are they falling into a debt trap?
World.content:
MoneyInvestingAI Opinion Young investors love AI stocks. Are they falling into a debt trap? Victoria Devine Money columnist October 25, 2026 — 5:08am

October 25, 2026 — 5:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It was only earlier this month and here in this very column that I wrote about the importance of doing your research and seriously considering your appetite for risk before investing in the tech sector. And as if right on cue, the market demonstrated exactly why people are increasingly recommending investors move with caution. The latest AI models are far more advanced than expected and pose a substantial risk to existing cybersecurity defences. Getty Over the course of a single week of trading last week, more than $US1 trillion ($1.43 billion) was wiped from the stocks of 20 of the world’s biggest semiconductor and AI companies. That sounds pretty bad, right? Well, skip to this week, and the share prices of many of those same companies were already enjoying a rebound. Unlike more established investment industries, there is still a lot we simply do not know about where the AI train is headed, which is in part what makes it so volatile – and the potential rewards so appealing.



While for some seasoned investors riding this rollercoaster is simply part of the experience, two interesting things are taking place that make paying attention to this specific issue especially important, and worth me banging on about. The first is that according to a new report from the ASX, more Australians are now investing than ever before. The second is that thanks to the hype surrounding the AI industry generally and the looming IPOs for two major artificial intelligence companies – Anthropic and OpenAI – many Australian investors, and specifically young investors with decades of portfolio time on their side, are seriously considering putting their hard-earned money into this sector. Most analysts agree the AI industry overall is still solid, but that doesn’t inherently make it a safe investment with a guaranteed return. What’s more, the timing of all of this matters, and not just because of those IPOs. For a while now, AI stocks have stood out in part because of the seemingly unrelenting unpredictability of the sector, and in part because market experts are increasingly worried about the fact that most of these companies are reliant on debt to fund their growth. And as interest rates in the US rise (and US Treasury yields in the bond market hit increasingly higher levels), that has the potential to become a massive, expensive problem.



Take CoreWeave, an American cloud computing and data centre operator whose IPO in March 2025 marked the biggest public debut for a tech company since 2021. By June 2025, just three months later, the company reached a market cap of $US90 billion and shareholders were feeling pretty happy about getting in early on the neocloud company (these businesses rent computing power to companies building AI). Editor's pick Opinion

Credit cards Backlash: Why the ATO’s credit card ban missed the mark Victoria Devine Money columnist At the end of last year, they had about $US30 billion of debt and liabilities on its balance sheet. By the second quarter of this year, the debt figure had grown to $US52 billion. Even worse is when you cut to today, where CoreWeave stocks have dropped by 30 per cent this month alone, and its valuation has been virtually cut by two thirds of what it was 18 months ago – diving to about $US34 billion. In large part, this decline is because CoreWeave is reliant on debt to fund its growth and is not yet profitable. So, those rising interest rates are hitting pretty hard – to the point where its bond yields rose to levels that generally signal distress. While this is just one company, it is causing investment experts to ask important questions about the tech sector and if the boom times it has been enjoying can really last.



Last month, Deutsche Bank published a research note that warned the level of AI spending we’re currently seeing is unsustainable. But, it noted, if spending slows before the sector’s promises come to fruition, it could wreak economic havoc. As the bank’s head of FX Research George Saravelos wrote, market growth “is not coming from AI itself, but from building the factories to generate AI capacity”. In other words, many of these companies are selling future potential, not a verified reality. Sam Altman, chief executive officer and co-founder of OpenAI. Bloomberg Earlier this month, the global investment bank RBC Capital Markets issued a recommendation that their clients reduce their tech holdings, after previously recommending higher than average holdings. In downgrading the tech sector’s outlook from “overweight” to “market weight”, RBC also said investors should instead look at more traditionally safe stocks such as healthcare – because sectors like these tend to perform well irrespective of what’s happening in an economy because people will always need access to medicine and medical care.



Now, at this point it is sounding a bit doom and gloom, which is not entirely the case. In his note to Deutsche Bank investors, Saravelos noted that “AI machines – in quite a literal sense – appear to be saving the US economy right now”. He also said that “In the absence of tech-related spending, the US would be close to, or in, recession this year.” In other words, it’s still doing well, but there is a lot riding on that not changing, and it’s important to be keenly aware of that risk. While most analysts agree that the sheer level of demand for AI – as in, people continue to use it and remain willing to pay for the services – means the industry overall is still very much safe, that doesn’t inherently make it a safe investment with a guaranteed return. And when you’re talking about people investing their savings as a means of creating long-term wealth (as opposed to investors with several more zeros to their bank balances), this matters an awful lot. As I’ve said a hundred times, one of the most important factors your money can have is time in the market. For some investors, being able to ride the highs and lows of volatile stock over a long period of time might be OK.



But another important factor is ensuring that your money is working for you in a way that will help you achieve your financial goals. If you’re planning to one day access that money to put towards something like a house or as you move towards retirement, there’s a very real risk that when you go to sell a volatile stock, you won’t be able to do so without losing money. That will mean you either have to wait out the dip, or eat the loss – neither of which are especially great options. The added layer of difficulty in all of this is that if you ask 10 experts, there’s a good chance you’ll get at least five different perspectives. But to my mind, that’s why doing your research and backing your own decision once it’s informed, is the foundation to good investing – especially when risk and volatility are involved. Victoria Devine is an award-winning retired financial adviser, a bestselling author and host of Australia’s No.1 finance podcast, She’s on the Money. She is also founder and director of Zella Money. World.title: Will I still have to pay the 30% tax if only sell a few shares?
World.content:
MoneyTaxAsk an expert Opinion Will I still have to pay the 30% tax if only sell a few shares? Paul Benson Money contributor October 25, 2026 — 5:01am

October 25, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I’ve had many questions from readers seeking clarification to a response I gave last week in relation to a person who was inheriting shares. There seems to be considerable confusion arising from conflicting commentary around the application of the minimum 30 per cent tax that will be introduced from next financial year. The specifics of the new tax laws appear to be confusing many. AFR This is the statement as published by Treasury on May 28, 2026: “In addition to indexation, a minimum tax rate of 30 per cent will apply to real capital gains accruing from July 1, 2027.” This statement makes it clear that the minimum 30 per cent tax does not apply to gains that accrued before the new rules take effect. It’s also worth highlighting that those receiving the age pension, even a small part pension, are specifically exempt from the 30 per cent minimum capital gains tax on gains accruing post 1 July 2027. In my response I mentioned that “it may be possible to sell small amounts each year and keep under the tax-free threshold.” ‘May be possible’ carries a significant load here and warrants further explanation.



This will depend on what the CBA share price does after July 1, 2027, and whether the person receives an age pension. For self-funded retirees, the minimum 30 per cent tax will apply on real gains that arise from 1 July 2027 onwards, no matter how small the value of shares sold. I’ve really appreciated the engagement from so many readers, so please, if you see something that you feel isn’t clear (or, heaven forbid, wrong!), do email and let me know. I’m trying to work out if I can afford to retire next year. I’m finding my conclusion changes considerably depending on how much I assume my spending will be in the future. I’ve never worked to a budget, but I tried using an online calculator. The answer it came up with seems too low, so I must be missing things. I’ve found the figure of $56,000 a year mentioned online, but I don’t feel like I’m “average”. Any tips? Everyone who tries to work out what they currently spend via a budget app underestimates, so rest assured that you are running with the pack here. We’ve found that reverse-engineering your current spending is the best starting point. Determine your after-tax income from the past year. Then calculate how much your savings rose, or your debt reduced. Subtract this movement from the income, and the figure you get must be what you spent.



As an example, let’s say you earned $100,000 in the past year after tax. Your savings account increased by $20,000. The rest of your balance sheet was unchanged, other than market movements (super can be ignored here). This would imply that you spent $80,000 in the past year. Related Article Opinion

Ask an expert Will inheriting my mum’s CBA shares trigger a big capital gains tax? Paul Benson Money contributor With this as your starting point, you can now consider what your spending is likely to be once retired. Commute costs often decrease, but maybe (hopefully) you will spend more socialising. Often people will spend more money early in retirement, as they tick off some travel bucket list items. We might build in an extra $20,000 per person for the first decade of retirement to cover this need. Research points to retirement spending following a “smile” pattern. Higher at the beginning to cover fun things, and then higher at the end for care-related costs, with a lull in the middle. In your calculations, be sure to allow for inflation. Over a 20-year-plus retirement, inflation impact is significant. Paul Benson is a Certified Financial Planner at Guidance Retirement Planning. He hosts the Financial Autonomy podcast. VIKING SKIRNIR AND VIKING MODI Launched 2015

2015 The cruise Rhine & Main Explorer, 11 days

Rhine & Main Explorer, 11 days Passengers 190

190 Crew 53

53 Decks Four

Four Length 135 metres

135 metres Suites 95 A Viking ship on the Rhine THE SHIP Owing to a stretch of too-shallow Rhine, I’m on two Viking Longships (Skirnir and Modi), but the coach transfer is made with remarkable efficiency and without much disruption to the itinerary. Because all of Viking’s Longships (there are currently 69) are virtually identical, the onboard experience is uncannily the same.



BOARDING 



The decor is unassuming but, when I look closely, I find interesting touches, such as Viking-style axes above the computer terminals, and black-and-white photos of company founder Torstein Hagen’s family. Viking’s educational ethos is alive and well in the quality of the book selection. THE SPACES The lounge is expansive and bartenders at its U-shaped bar are always busy. Grouped seating means guests can socialise in whatever sized gathering the mood takes them. At its front end the lounge dissolves into Aquavit Terrace, a delightful spot at the ship’s prow for informal dining with forward-facing views. The top Sun Deck has shuffleboard, a walking track and putting green, seating and strips of herbs that get regular haircuts to supply the galley. However, low bridges on the Main River, the longest tributary of the Rhine, mean it can’t be used throughout much of this particular cruise.



The library is understandably, given the limited space on river ships, simply a lobby space with a wall of books, two desktop computers and four armchairs around a coffee table often taken up by jigsaw-puzzle solvers. Viking’s educational ethos is alive and well in the quality of the book selection. One of seven Veranda Suites on the ship. THE STATEROOM Among cabin categories are Standard Staterooms which have but a porthole, French Balcony Staterooms, and Veranda Staterooms. Outlook and size vary but decor and amenities are very similar. I’m in stateroom 316, one of seven Veranda Suites (there are also two larger Explorer Suites). It’s a generous 25.5 square metres and divided into a lounge with enough room for a sofa and armchair, as well as a modest desk that doubles as a dressing table. The bedroom has a queen-sized bed good enough for Goldilocks. Praise be for sensible pillows uncommon in Europe, one thin and one fat, to suit your favourite neck position. The suite’s beige, brown and blue decor is relaxing, and a cool comfort to return to in the full blast of Europe’s heatwave.



Some arty photos of European river scenes might have been more interesting than the couple of small and undistinguished abstract artworks. Nice touches include a pair of binoculars, reading lights in the bedhead, heated bathroom floors, and an anti-fog bathroom mirror. Suites benefit from complimentary laundry. Menus run the gamut of international favourites including pannacotta. THE FOOD The food is very satisfying, and can’t be faulted for quality and freshness. Regional dishes are among the choices every evening, among which are standouts such as braised beef with onion sauce, sausages and sauerkraut, and bienenstich or bee-sting cake, an almond layered biscuit cake with vanilla cream. Both lunch and dinner are a la carte. At lunch, chefs are present to prepare salads and cook pasta, and guests help themselves to salads, bread, cheese and dessert. Three-course dinners are more formally served. All the tables in the main restaurant are shared. Alternative Aquavit Terrace is more informal with some limited tables for two that are always in high demand. Menus run the gamut of international favourites from French onion soup to steamed cod, rib-eye steak to involtini, rounding off with classic desserts or cheese and fruit plates. I become a little obsessed with the lunchtime Nicoise salad. Although excellent, the dining is mainstream rather than adventurous and, on a cruise that spends far more time in Germany than France, I’d have preferred a German buffet evening. Instead, it’s French and rather unexciting, with cheese plates peculiarly promoted as an appetiser. WELLNESS



I’ve often wondered why cruise ships, and especially river ships, devote space to gyms that only a minority of guests use. No such mistake on Viking Longships. You don’t need a gym on a European river cruise: every port has kilometres of promenades and cycle paths. The Main River has amiable cycleways that contour the river for almost its full length. No wellness area either. Wellness consists of enjoying the top deck in the fresh air as lovely scenery drifts past, instead of huddling in a perfumed room. Space for shuffleboard, a walking track and a putting green. Aquavit Terrace is an informal dining spot at the ship’s prow. ENTERTAINMENT There’s no regular nightly entertainment except trivia competitions, although occasionally a local music group is invited on board. A pianist glassy-eyed with boredom tinkles on a grand piano in the lounge. I suspect he can play Rachmaninov, but is doomed to produce dreary elevator music. Lectures and talks that provide informative background to local history, politics and society used to be a hallmark of Viking’s river cruises. Disappointing that these have been abandoned but for one mundane lecture on the rise of the Nazis.



THE CREW Founder Torstein Hagen is a Harvard-educated Norwegian who once worked for an American ocean cruise line, and his company has headquarters in America and Switzerland. The crew on both ships seem infused both with Swiss-Norwegian efficiency and the relaxed friendliness of American service: a winning combination. THE VERDICT I’ve been on several Viking river cruises, but the last one was probably a decade ago. Rediscovering that little has changed is slightly disconcerting but ultimately a pleasure. Why change something that works so well? DETAILS



Related Article River cruises What Europe’s record-low rivers mean for cruising Viking Cruises’ 11-day Rhine & Main Explorer river cruise from Basel to Nuremberg (or the reverse) has limited remaining departures in November 2026. It resumes between May and November 2027. From $7795 a person twin share in 2027, including dining, beverages with meals, Wi-Fi, a shore excursion in every port and gratuities. Economy flights are included on new bookings on selected 2027 sailings made before November 30, 2026. Phone 138 747; see vikingrivercruises.com.au RATING OUT OF FIVE ★★★★ SWELL



Unflappable efficiency both on and off the ship has been the hallmark of all my river and ocean cruises with Viking, and this is no exception. NOT SO SWELL The ship’s air-conditioning copes well with Europe’s heatwave, but only when the engines are running. In Basel and Strasbourg, ships must connect to shore power, and reduced electric capacity means several sweltering mealtimes. Cabins aren’t as badly affected. The writer was a guest of Viking Cruises

World.title: ‘We understood each other’: Why writer Jon Ronson says he and Monica Lewinsky bonded
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life ‘We understood each other’: Why writer Jon Ronson says he and Monica Lewinsky bonded Robyn Doreian October 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This story is part of the October 25 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

Author Jon Ronson is best known for writing books including The Psychopath Test and Them: Adventures with Extremists. Here, the 59-year-old talks about the women who have influenced his life, including a peripatetic aunt, his wife, Elaine, and Monica Lewinsky, with whom he shared a professional connection. Jon Ronson’s mother urged him to volunteer at a local radio station, which kickstarted his career. “That was the best thing she did for me.” Emli Bendixen www.emli.co.uk I grew up in a boring suburban house in Cardiff, Wales. My father, David, managed a warehouse. When I was 19 and had moved to London, my parents bought a hotel. It was a pretty middle-class, non-glamorous life. My father’s sister, Auntie Mavis, however, was an adventurer. At the age of 19 she and her friend from London went off on a seven-year odyssey. There are photos of her on a shipwrecked beach with opium smugglers. When she returned, she wrote a book and became a Magnum [photographic agency] photographer. I found photographs of the Rolling Stones in my grandfather’s London kitchen for her series, Rock Stars In The Kitchen. When I was four, Auntie Mavis took a special liking to me. She was like, “He’s the one who’s going to have an amazing life.” She lived in London and sent me cassettes of David Bowie; she was the coolest. Auntie Mavis died of cancer when I was 10. By far, she was the earliest formative woman in my life.



My mother, Paula, is in a home now, but she was always very kind. I remember her taking my older brother, Daniel, and me fossil hunting on the beaches in Penarth, near Cardiff. When I was a feckless 16-year-old, she got me to volunteer at my local radio station. It got me a place in media studies at the Polytechnic of Central London, which set me on my way. That was the best thing she did for me. Growing up, I was awkward in my own skin and a misfit. I would go to Jewish summer and winter camps where I’d meet really cool girls. The camp wasn’t weird or religious, more listening to Simon & Garfunkel and learning how to smoke. These 15-, 16-year-old girls from London were sassy and funny. It was probably where I had my first kiss. Our marriage works because we are not controlling of each other. We let the other do whatever they want. But we also watch TV together every night. While I was at college I had an incredible one-night stand with Clare. She looked like [the actress] Nastassja Kinski. I thought she was amazing. We are still in touch and have a friendship that has endured for life. David Cardiff was one of my teachers at college. He was a very elegant man who was married to the journalist Lynn Barber – she wrote An Education, which was made into a movie. I was a big fan of hers. After David died in 2003, I got to know Lynn. From her, I learnt how to ask impudent interview questions in ways that didn’t offend.



I met my wife, Elaine, while working for Time Out magazine – she was one of the editors and I was a columnist. She was very together and I was very un-together. We hit it off. She had a beautiful flat and was very glamorous and impressive. Related Article Sunday Life ‘People come at you from all over’: How fame changed Sarah Cracknell’s outlook on love We got married in the late 1990s on a whim. We were on a safari in Africa for a month and were staying in a Victoria Falls hotel, which is now in disrepair. But rules prevented us from marrying in Zimbabwe, so we went to Nantucket, in Massachusetts, and married there. Elaine is an art consultant and an aesthete. I am not. I never think about the way things look. She did a brilliant job of doing up our barn in upstate New York. Our marriage works because we are not controlling of each other. We let the other do whatever they want. But we also watch TV together every night. Our son, Joel, 28, is practical, thoughtful and sociable, just like Elaine. Monica Lewinsky and I both started talking about cancel culture at the same time – her 2015 TED Talk, and my book about public shaming. I really like Monica. We’ve met a bunch of times and have done TED events together. We had this shared strangeness in that we started a conversation that had taken over the world. We were both badly bullied at school. I think we understood each other a bit better because of that shared experience. I think she’s done really well at correcting her narrative.



Jon Ronson is currently touring Australia. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.

World.title: Billionaires, immortality and barbecues: Sci-fi author ready for arrival at Powerhouse
World.content:
NationalNSWParramatta Billionaires, immortality and barbecues: Sci-fi author ready for arrival at Powerhouse Michael Ruffles October 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Ted Chiang has been thinking about some of the worst people in the world. Considered one of the greatest living science-fiction writers and known for fighting the rapacious rise of artificial intelligence, the New York-born, Seattle-based writer is bound for Sydney for Powerhouse Parramatta’s 23-day opening festival. Chiang will give a keynote address on November 8 about billionaires and capitalism and whether immortality can be pursued ethically. Author Ted Chiang will make a guest appearance for the opening of Powerhouse Parramatta in November. Kate Joyce Spoiler alert: probably not. “It seems like a lot of the people who are interested in pursuing immortality in recent years, they seem like the worst people in the world,” Chiang says. “I guess this raises a couple of questions. You know, like one is, would you really want to spend eternity in the company of these people?”



The other question Chiang is pondering is along these lines: “If the worst people in the world seem to be the only ones who are really interested in that, does that tell you anything about that thing that they are interested in?” There have been headline-grabbing examples of biohacking, and the longevity billionaires are a class of ultrawealthy individuals who seem intent on testing the theory that money cannot buy more time. Chiang doesn’t name anyone, but points out those in such a socioeconomic stratosphere already live pretty long lives. “For us to have good evidence that [these treatments] are working, we’ll need to see a significant number of them living over 100 or like 120 or something like that, and so you know that’s decades away.” In a sense, the ultra-rich have bought time anyway, since they do not have to bother themselves with such mundane tasks as dishes and laundry, or driving around to hardware stores to swap the gas bottle.



“That’s another version of the question of, ‘Why does anyone continue to pursue wealth?’ There’s a level of wealth which is modest by billionaire standards but is really more than anyone could actually want in terms of improving the quality of their life. “If you have $10 million, I don’t know how much better your life is going to get with additional money, but you know, obviously, billionaires – they have 100 times that. “Now there are people who have $10 billion or $100 billion. Why do they keep pursuing that? It’s not because it will help improve their life in any meaningful way. It’s just because, arguably, it’s the only thing they know how to do. You know, they can’t think of anything else to do.” In the film Arrival, adapted from Ted Chiang’s story, Amy Adams plays a linguist who tries to interpret for visiting aliens. Alamy One of Chiang’s early stories, his 1998 novella Story of Your Life, was the basis of Eric Heisserer’s screenplay for the award-winning Denis Villeneuve film Arrival. But another, The Tower of Babylon, was the inspiration for one of the blockbuster opening exhibitions for the Powerhouse Parramatta.



For Task Eternal, billed as “one of the most ambitious aerospace exhibitions ever staged” and located in the museum’s largest space, the architects drew on the story for an ascending design in four acts, titled Skyward, Power, Off-Earth and The Return. About 30 minutes into the interview, I throw a barbie into the conversation as we veer from billionaires’ quixotic quests to the inevitable heat death of the universe. In Chiang’s Hugo award-winning story Exhalation, the title work from his 2019 collection, long-lived mechanical beings come to grips with the inevitability of their own demise when they realise the differences in air pressure that power them will eventually equalise and their universe will be rendered inert. Mortality, or immortality, was not front of mind. “I can understand why you might be reminded of that story, but I guess I want to clarify that that story is just about thermodynamics,” Chiang says. “Sometimes people interpret the story as maybe being about climate change. It is absolutely not about climate change because climate change is not inevitable, whereas the heat death of the universe is inevitable.”



Early on, there’s a passage about how swapping depleted lungs for full canisters can sometimes be a joyous communal event, and sometimes as perfunctory as changing the batteries in the remote. I’d read it when the bottle under the barbecue had run empty, so fossil fuels were front of mind. Not so for the author. “I certainly never expected people to interpret Exhalation as being about climate change. That was not something that ever, ever occurred to me. But yeah, that’s just another example of how it is impossible to anticipate how people will read your work.” Chiang was named among Time’s 100 most influential figures in artificial intelligence for his criticism of the technology and the companies profiting from it. His work has dealt with fate and mortality, along with thermodynamics. “Trying to make peace with one’s mortality is, yeah, I think a really central part of what it means to be a human. What I want is not to live forever, but I want to be at peace with my mortality.” If writing might be an easier way to achieve immortality, “that has never crossed my mind”. “When people crave immortality, mostly what they want is actual physical immortality. I don’t think that having a long-lasting reputation is a substitute for physical immortality,” he says.

World.title: Forgotten forest secrets in Canada’s greenest city
World.content:
InspirationNorth America Forgotten forest secrets in Canada’s greenest city Jim Darby October 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

“We are the land and the land is us,” explains Talaysay Campo, born and raised in the Squamish and Sechelt cultures of Canada’s First Nations. On Campo’s Talking Trees tour in Vancouver’s Stanley Park, the city’s vast green 400-hectare lung, we are introduced to the plants, medicines and technologies of her people. Vancouver’s Stanley Park stays lush and green thanks to 169 days of rain a year. iStock First, we meet the vine maple tree. “It doesn’t know personal space – it likes to branch out and reach for that sunshine,” Talaysay says. Its wood is strong but flexible so it is useful for constructing shelters. If the tree arched in shape, then that shape would form the frame for a shelter. Next, we meet the mighty Douglas fir, which soars into the sky with bark so thick it resists forest fires but, ironically, there’s an element in its sap that helps start fires, and it was tapped for just that purpose.



Deeper into the forest we find salmonberries, huckleberries and more. “This is one of the first laws we learn: you never take the first berry, and you never take the last berry,” says Talaysay. 



There are rules for the bark harvest: “If you can reach around the tree and touch your hands, move on because the tree is too small. When you find a tree old enough, measure two hand widths, make a cut and pull the bark away. That might strip as much as five metres, it will stop where the tree wants it to stop.” From that park full of trees, stroll along the shores of English Bay and catch a ferry to Granville Island. While the First Canadians would harvest from the forest, here’s where the locals harvest their fresh food today. “The market is who we are,” says my Vancouver Foodie tour guide Sandra Trotter. “Here’s the best of Vancouver – food, wine and the outdoors. We aim for this to be the world’s best market.” The morning is sunny and the crowds are building. There are no franchise outlets on the island and most of the produce we taste on this tour with Trotter is local and artisan. The Benton Brothers make their small-batch cheese from the milk that comes in from the Okanagan region. Oyama Sausage makes its meaty creations from five generations of charcutiers.



Fresh produce at the Granville Island Public Market. Bloomberg Wild salmon from Longliner Seafoods. And the morsels of wild-caught Canadian salmon we try at Longliner Seafoods (the maple candy salmon is what I’m going back for) is another story of the generations. Jim Moorehead, himself a longline fisher, founded the business in the late 1970s and was one of the market’s original tenants. Back then, the island was mainly used for warehousing and as a base for the local fishing fleet. Beyond the market, you’ll find those warehouses have been transformed into studios for artists and artisans – painters, jewellers, glassblowers, even broom makers. And before it hosted those warehouses, the island’s sandbars were a food source for the First Canadians. When the tide was out, the food was on. And so it continues.
